As such to deny the benefit of waste and scrap on the ground that the same was not an input was not justified. 4.3 Damaged goods - In CCE v. Tulsyan NEC Ltd. 2007 (207) ELT 209 (Kar.), it has been held that an assessee is entitled to claim CENVAT credit on the inputs destroyed in a fire accident; but in the event of settlement by the insurance company they would remit the benefit back to the department.

Inclusive Part

5. The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

In Indo Rama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (219) ELT 122 (Bom.), the High Court held that the credit of duty paid on the goods or fuel used in the generation of electricity is available, provided the electricity is used for the manufacture of final product. The use of electricity must have nexus with goods manufactured in the factory.

5.1 Primary packing material - In Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 201 (Punj. & Har.), it was held that it is not a matter of dispute that chewing gum/bubble gums manufactured by the assessees are directly or primarily packed with the printed aluminium foils without tattoos. It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

CENTRAL EXCISE - TREATMENT OF WASTE

1. We have two factories registered under central excise with the following details —

1st Factory - Manufacturer of fine chemicals falling under Chapter 34

2nd Factory - Declared as job worker (a bottling plant) of first factory.

We sent 100 Kgs. of chemicals to be packed in 100 gms. bottles to bottling plant. After completion of packing in small packs we received only 90 Kgs. chemicals packed in small container. What would be the treatment of non-collectible waste of 10% (10 Kgs. out of every lot of 100 kgs.) ?

It is clearly stated by you that both the factories are registered separately. In this case the manufacturing factory is clearing 100 Kgs. to job-worker and receiving back the same in entirety (subject to processing loss). The process loss of 10% will not be chargeable to duty, only if the same is normal process loss.

The benefit may be claimed under rule 21 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, as —

the same is due to natural causes or unavoidable reasons, and

is incurred prior to removal of finished goods from the factory.

An alternative view may be that only 90 Kg. is the manufactured product, because manufacture under section 2(f) is complete only after the completion of all incidental or ancillary processes, which include packing/bottling.

In any case, the duty can be levied only on 90 Kgs.

CENTRAL EXCISE - WHETHER IN CASE OF EXPORT UNDER CLAIM OF REBATE, EXCISE DUTY MAY BE PAID THROUGH CENVAT CREDIT

2. We are exporters of a final product. Export is made under claim of rebate. Please clarify whether we can set-off/adjust excise duty payable under the option of "Export under claim of Rebate" through Cenvat credit or not ? Whether rebate would be allowed even in that case ?

As per rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, credit is allowed of duty or tax paid on inputs or input services or capital goods used in factory/manufacture purposes.

The said credit may be used to pay duty on final product. Goods exported under claim of rebate are cleared on payment of duty and said duty can very well be paid by using Cenvat credit as per rule 3(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In fact, Form ARE-1 itself in Part A provides for certification as follows —

Certified that 1. duty has been paid by debit entry in the Personal Ledger Account No. .........and/or CENVAT Account Entry No. .……or recorded as payable in Daily Stock Account, on the goods described overleaf.

(Emphasis Supplied)

Therefore, for purpose of export under claim of rebate, duty may be paid using balance in Cenvat Credit Account.

The query has been replied in two parts —

Part - I : Input v. Capital Goods

Taking classification put forth by you to be correct, since the goods are classifiable under Chapter 44, they are not listed in any of the categories of capital goods as provided in rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. However, if —

they are purchased as 'components or spares or accessories' of some other machinery ; and

such other machinery is a capital goods under rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004,

then the said mill/ball would be classifiable as capital goods under rule 2(a)(A)(iii) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In any other event the same would be eligible for credit as an 'input', as the same is presumably used within the factory.

Part - II : Relevant treatment under Financial Accounts

The classification and treatment under financial accounts is not relevant for the purpose of deciding eligibility to Cenvat credit.

In other words, even if the said goods are inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, they may be 'fixed assets' under the accounting standards issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and would, accordingly, be eligible for depreciation.

The two things must be viewed separately.

In such case, CENVAT Credit is available on such capital goods, if final product is chargeable to duty - CBEC Circular No. 665/56/2002-CX, dated 25-9-2002.

(k) Project imports - These are also eligible for CENVAT Credit. If some capital goods are eligible while some may not be eligible, the breakup value of capital goods eligible for CENVAT can be certified by a Cost Accountant in the prescribed form - MF (DR) Circular No. 351/67/97-CX., dated 5-11-1997.

(m) Exclusion of equipment/appliances used in an office - Rule 2 specifically excludes use of capital goods like equipment or appliances in an office.

(n) Other capital goods - Capital goods other than those mentioned above, are not eligible for CENVAT Credit.

(o) Capital goods removed as scrap after use - In such circumstances, it cannot be said that these are removal ‘as such’. Hence, no excise duty is payable. Wear/Tear cannot be said to be manufactured, and is not liable for duty - CCE v. Birla Corpn. Ltd. 2005 (181) ELT 263 (Tri. - Delhi).

(p) Sale of factory - If factory is sold, it is not removal of capital goods ‘as such’. Hence, no duty is payable on capital goods - Jamna Auto Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2001 (130) ELT 181 (Tri. - Delhi).

(q) Capital goods removed after use for some years - As per the Board’s Circular No. 643/34/2002, CX, dated 1-7-2002 the value on which the supplier of capital goods has paid duty would be a reasonable basis for paying duty with depreciation as per Letter F. No. 495/16/93, CUS VI, dated 26-5-1993.

(r) Use of capital goods by service provider - In case of output service provider, the capital goods should be used for providing output services. The use may be anywhere and even part use is sufficient.

(s) Installation is not required for taking CENVAT Credit - Installation or use is not a precondition for taking CENVAT Credit. On mere receipt in the factory, CENVAT Credit can be availed on capital goods.

(t) Eligibility to be decided on the basis of date of receipt - Eligibility of CENVAT Credit on capital goods is required to be decided on the basis of eligibility on the date when goods were received in the factory. Subsequent eligibility will not help - CCE v. Surya Roshini Ltd. 2003 (155) ELT 581 (Tri. - Delhi).

(u) Capital goods used by service provider - Service provider can also send out capital goods for providing output service, but they should be brought back within 180 days.

Difference between CENVAT Credit on capital goods and Input

4. The difference between Cenvat Credit on capital goods & inputs is explained hereunder :

(a)In the case of inputs, CENVAT Credit is available as soon as input is received in the factory, whereas for capital goods up to 50 per cent Credit is available in current year and balance in subsequent year.

(b)CENVAT Credit utilised on inputs has to be reversed on stock of inputs, when the assessee opts out of CENVAT. This rule is not applicable for capital goods.

(c)The eligible inputs and capital goods have been given in CENVAT Rules.

(d)Inputs are to be used in or in relation to manufacture while in respect of capital goods the only requirement is that it should be used in the factory.

CHALLENGES AND FUTURE UNCERTAINTY

While MOOWR is a beneficial scheme, these challenges are hindering its performance.

Complex compliance: Filing multiple BOEs for each DTA sale is time-consuming and complex.

No depreciation is allowed when capital goods are sold in the domestic market—duty is on full import value.

No RODTEP or Drawback: MOOWR-based exports are less competitive given they are not eligible for RODTEP scrips or Drawback. Typically benefits RODTEP and Drawback would be in the range of 4-5% of the value of exported good, which is significant for a lot of exporters.

New concern: The Finance Act 2024 empowered the Government of India to exclude certain goods or operations from the applicability of MOOWR scheme. This adds unpredictability, making long-term planning difficult for businesses relying on this scheme and creating an unease in doing business.

Takeaways

If you are importing raw materials or machinery regularly, consider obtaining a MOOWR license.

Be prepared for higher compliance costs.

Evaluate if loss of RODTEP/Drawback is offset by duty deferment benefits.

MOOWR is one of the most flexible and cash-flow-friendly customs schemes available in India. It's ideal for businesses that import raw material or machinery and sell their finished goods either in domestic market or export market.

Small and Mid-sized manufacturers initially hesitate to register under MOOWR because of compliance worries. But once they set up the systems, the cash flow benefits are too significant to ignore.

They also periodically sold items such as scraps, unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, rims, etc., Issue before the Court was whether these sales were 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' to the business ?

Before the above case, the Hon. Madras High Court in the case of Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. Sri Thirumagal Mills Limited [1967] 20 STC 287 had taken a view that even if by way of amendment to the definition of 'business' profit motive is deleted as an ingredient, still the ancillary activity has to be of commercial nature. It should still partake the nature of 'trade, commerce, manufacture, etc.' specified in the first limb and only then it can be taxed. Hence, it was held that turnover of fair price shop run for the employees will not be leviable to tax.

The Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court on the contrary in the case of Hyderabad Asbestos Cement Products Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh [1969] 24 STC 487 (SC) had taken a view that for an ancillary sale to be taxed it is not required that the same must be done with an intention of doing business. Any ancillary sale connected with the business shall be taxable.

The Hon. Supreme Court in the case of Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Co. of India Ltd. (supra) did not agree with the decision of the Hon. Madras High Court and affirmed the ratio decided by the Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court.

It held that the Hon. Madras High Court had not paid sufficient attention to word 'such' as appearing in clause 'any transaction in connection with, or incidental or ancillary to, such trade, commerce, manufacture,adventure or concern'. Hence, it held that after the omission of profitmotive, any sale which is ancillary to business whether or not made with an intention to do business of such ancillary goods shall be taxable. The Hon. Supreme Court thus held that once a transaction is covered within the ambit of terms 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' the same shall be taxable, whether or not there was any intention to do business in the commercial sense of 'business' in these ancillary goods.

In the given case the Apex Court held that whether sale of scrap such unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, etc, is ancillary to the business is a finding of fact. However, it observed that as the respondent was an oil company, all those items were parts of the business activity of trading in oil and, hence, the same were taxable. In respect of marketing items like calendars, wallets, etc. it was observed that such goods were given to dealers for increasing the sales. Hence, the same were also ancillary to business. With regard to canteen sales it was observed that Government Order specifically provided for exemption to sales made by canteen and, hence, the same must be considered by lower authorities.

CENTRAL EXCISE - WRONG SCN - WHETHER COMPENSATION CAN BE CLAIMED FROM THE DEPARTMENT ?

1. Though our Query is academic, we would like to know whether where any officer, purely out of ill-will, creates allegations against the assessees by issuance of unwarranted show-cause notices, can assessees seek compensation from the department of all the expenses ? What about filing of civil suit ?

Section 40 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and corresponding provisions under various other laws provide protection to Central Government and its officers.

Section 40(1) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 provides that -

no suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie

against the Central Government or any officer of the Central Government or a State Government

for anything which is done, or intended to be done,

in good faith, in pursuance of this Act or any rule made thereunder.

Further, section 40(2) provides that no proceeding, other than a suit, shall be initiated against the Central Government or any officer of the Central Government or a State Government for anything done or purported to have been done in pursuance of this Act or any rule made thereunder, -

without giving the Central Government or such officer a month's previous notice in writing of the intended proceeding and of the cause thereof, or

after the expiration of three months from the accrual of such cause.

Thus, any of the proposed actions must conform to the requirements of section 40 and corresponding provisions in other law.

Further, unless otherwise proved with clear evidence, the benefit of doubt goes to the Central Government and its officers, etc.

A criminal proceeding is generally entertained subject to evidence and time-bar created in section 40(2). A civil proceeding entails voluminous work/evidences.

Introduction

1. To be liable to excise duty, a product must be manufactured, movable, marketable and mentioned in First Schedule to Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 as subject to duty of excise duty. From 1-3-2015, even if goods are non-excisable, they continue to be exempted goods and, therefore, credit relatable thereto has to be reversed.

Demand of duty on Bagasse/Zinc-Dross, etc. has been subject matter of repeated litigation since decades. The Department has been making all efforts (and CBEC upholding said efforts by issuance of circulars) to demand excise duty on Bagasse/Zinc-Dross. However, the Courts have been holding otherwise.

This article makes an attempt to analyse the position of law vis-à-vis recent landmark judgments on the issue and Circular No.1027/15/2016-CX, dated 25-4-2016.

Position prior to 10-5-2008

2. Prior to 10-5-2008, concept of marketability was not defined in the Central Excise Act, 1944 and for being marketable, goods were required to be known as such in market and capability of being commercially bought and sold as 'goods'. Thus, waste and residue of many kinds were held non-marketable. In this regard, to be brief, we may be conclude that —

bagasse was held not excisable goods in Commissioner v. Balrampur Chini Mills Ltd. - 2015 (320) ELT A258 (SC)]. This view was accepted by CBEC itself in its Circular No. 941/2/2011-CX., dated 14-2-2011

zinc dross was held non-manufactured/non-marketable in Collector v. Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. - 2004 (165) ELT 386 (SC) and Commissioner v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 2006 (203) ELT 3 (SC).

The Department's demand of excise duty on said goods was therefore, set aside. The Department's demand of reversal of credit under rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 (and its earlier counterparts) was set aside on ground that since they were not marketable and non-excisable, hence, they were not even 'exempted goods' as defined in the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Hence, no payment of duty/credit was required prior to 10-5-2008.

Period 10-5-2008 to 28-2-2015

3. Vide amendment by Finance Act, 2008, as Explanation was inserted in section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 defining the concept of marketability. It was provided that "goods" includes any article, material or substance which is capable of being bought and sold for a consideration and such goods shall be deemed to be marketable. Thus, capability of being bought and sold for a consideration would constitute marketability and there would be no need for the goods to be commercially tradeable or known as such in the market.

3.1 Circular of 2009 and 2011 : Relying upon this amendment, the CBEC issued Circular No. 904/24/2009-CX., dated 28-10-2009 (reiterated in Circular No. 941/2/2011-CX., dated 14-2-2011) that (paras 2 to 5 of the Circular of 2009, relevant extracts) :

Excisability of bagasse and similar waste products arising during the course of manufacture has been under dispute for a long period of time.

In the budget of 2008, the definition of "excisable goods" in clause (d) of section 2 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 was amended by adding an explanation that for the purposes of this clause, "goods" include any article, material or substance which is capable of being bought and sold for a consideration and such goods shall be deemed to be marketable.

It is clarified that with this amendment in section 2(d), the bagasse, aluminium/zinc dross and other such products termed as waste, residue or refuse which arise during the course of manufacture and are capable of being sold for consideration would be excisable goods and chargeable to payment of excise duty.

1. We purchased wire rods, availed Cenvat credit thereon and sent them to the job worker [who is a related party] for drawing them [procedure under rule 4(5)(a) has been followed]. The job worker is an exporter also. Instead of sending the drawn rods back to us, it was decided that the job-workers would export the same to its own customers. Can it be done ? We are ready to pay duty on cost (raw material plus job work charges plus 10% net profit margin) by issuing invoice in name of job worker. Will it be in accordance with law ? You may please advise us as regards any other formality to be observed under the law ?

One can presume that yourself (the principal manufacturer) want to sell the finished goods to the job-worker himself and the job-worker would export the same. There is absolutely no embargo thereupon i.e., you may sell the goods to job-worker. In fact, rule 4(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 permits direct clearance from factory of job-worker. Instead of receiving finished goods back and again selling them to job-worker, you may definitely raise a sale bill in the name of job-worker.

Since it is claimed that you are related parties, the value of 'drawn rods' (final product) would be determined as per rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000, read with rules 9 and 10 ibid.

Since the job-worker would act as merchant exporter, he may avail of facilities under rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, i.e., procurement without payment of duty or any other export incentive for which necessary procedures would have to be complied with. If the facility under rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 in relation to procurement of goods without payment of duty for export is availed, no duty would be payable on drawn rods.

CENVAT CREDIT - FAQs (PART 3)

In this article, the author has discussed some very common questions in respect of capital goods used by manufacturer of excisable goods or provider of taxable services.

Is Cenvat credit available on capital goods if acquired on lease, hire-purchase or loan ?

1. YES, it is allowed under rule 4(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

What if capital goods are removed from factory/service premises ‘as such’ or ‘if removed as scrap’ or ‘before put to use’ or ‘after being used’?

2. Rule 3(5) and 3(5A)/(5B) defines four types of situations and provides guidelines what is to be done. All these situations are detailed below.

Here there is no question of bona fide or mala fide intention due to which no penalty provision would be attracted.

(a) Capital goods removed ‘as such’ - ‘As such’ means, in the same position in which purchase is done. Whatever Cenvat Credit is taken/availed, it has to be paid to the account of the Central Government. No such type of payment is required to be made if the capital goods is/are removed for providing output service.

(b) Capital goods removed ‘as scrap’ - If capital goods are removed ‘as scrap’, then manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the duty leviable on transaction value.

(c) Capital goods removed ‘before put to use’ - Here manufacturer is required to pay full amount of duty which has been taken as Cenvat credit. This situation is different from the situation given in (a) above, as here it might be possible that the capital goods which are purchased may not be in ‘intact’ position, say, for example machines are purchased and installed and are made ready to use, but ultimately it is decided that these should not be used but to be removed.

(d) Capital goods removed ‘after put to use’ - What amount of Cenvat credit has been taken in the books of account is required to be depreciated by 2.5 per cent (i.e., reduced) per quarter and the balance amount is required to be paid to the account of the Central Government.

What if capital goods are sent for jobwork outside factory or office premises and not received back in 180 days ?

3. Rule 4(5a ) clarifies this situation. Once capital goods which are purchased are removed from the factory or the premises of the service provider for providing output taxable services, then such capital goods must be received back in the factory or the premises of service provider within the period of 180 days. If such capital goods are not received within the abovesaid period, then manufacturer or service provider (as the case may be) shall pay an amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the inputs or capital goods by debiting the Cenvat credit account or otherwise. Here the option of payment by debiting cenvat account is given.

What is 8 per cent/10 per cent option which is newly introduced under rule 6 ?

4. This is new provision which has been introduced under rule 6. It is made clear that Cenvat credit is not allowed for the input/capital goods/input services which are used in the process of manufacture of non-excisable goods or for providing non-taxable services.

However, this new provision allows the manufacturer or service provider to take 100 per cent Cenvat credit, by paying 10 per cent of the value of exempted goods (for manufacturer) or 8 per cent of the value of exempted services (for service provider).

Is Cenvat credit on mobile phone available ?

5. Yes, this is a very debatable issue, but the same has been resolved by Circular No. 59/8/2003-ST, dated June 20, 2003 in the context of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002.

As per the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002, Cenvat credit for service tax paid on telephone bills which are installed in office premises was available.

However, under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the same condition was totally removed. This rule came in force with effect from September 10, 2004.

Recently, further notifications and clarifications were issued on May 20, 1994, in order to overcome these difficulties. The following are the important points to be noted from these amendments :

(i)Under the original rule, if the capital goods, on which MODVAT credit was taken were removed from the factory, the assessee was required to clear the same on payment of duty, not lesser than the amount of credit which was previously taken thereon. As per the amended notification, this requirement applies only where the capital equipment is sought to be removed from the factory without being used in the manufacture of excisable goods.

As per the amendment, if the machinery is sought to be removed from the factory after being used therein, then the payment of excise duty has to be made after allowing a deduction of 2.5 per cent of the credit taken earlier for each quarter of a year of usage from the date of taking the credit. The amended notification further provides that if the machinery has been sold for any reason as scrap, this duty shall be paid at the rate applicable to such scrap.

It would appear that the normal life of the machinery, for this purpose, is estimated at 10 years, and a distinction is drawn between used and unused machinery and also between usable and scrapped machinery.

(ii)A new sub-rule has also been added, permitting removal of capital goods for tests or repairs for reconditioning, provided the same are returned to the factory for further use as capital goods. Prior to this amendment, it was thought that even in such cases of removal of capital goods duty was required to be reimbursed.

(iii)The earlier requirement was that before the assessee takes MODVAT credit on capital goods, such goods have to be verified by the Excise Superintendent. This requirement, which was considered impractical and susceptible to misuse, has now been removed by another amended notification.

(iv)Yet another welcome amendment is that the assessee can now take credit on capital goods on the basis of an invoice or bill of entry or other duty-paying document as against the cumbersome procedure prescribed earlier.

These amendments are in the right direction, as a result of which, most of the practical difficulties are considered to have been removed.

2.4 Case of goods obtained on lease or hire purchase - According to the existing provisions, MODVAT credit on capital goods is not permissible in respect of the equipment acquired on lease or hire purchase. Several representations were made in this regard by the industry. It was reported that the Government has decided to amend the relevant rules so as to extend MODVAT credit to capital goods acquired through leasing and hire purchase also. But the relevant notification has not yet been issued and it is hoped that it would be done soon.

2.5 MODVAT credit vs. Depreciation - It is specifically provided that no credit of the duty paid on capital goods shall be allowed, if the assessee claims depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 on that part of the value of capital goods which represents the amount of specified duty paid on such goods. In other words, a manufacturer has the option to claim MODVAT credit on the duty paid or forego the same if he opts to claim income-tax depreciation on the duty portion of the capital goods. If the manufacturer has opted for taking MODVAT credit, income-tax depreciation on such capital goods can be claimed only on the net cost as reduced by the duty paid thereon.

definition of ‘manufacture’ as contained in the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The term ‘manufacture’ is borrowed from the Central Excise Act, 1944 and this is one of the terms which never reached finality in the matter of dispute regarding process to be considered as a manufacture or not. There is a catena of judgments on the subject ‘Manufacture’, and there are books written on this subject which show the significance of the term under the Excise Law. The definition under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act can be divided into three parts:

First part of the definition refers to "any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product". This term has been interpreted by various forums including the Apex Court and what emerges out is presence of the following criteria to constitute manufacture:

u A process should be carried out.

u Such process should result into a distinctly new product, commercially known as such.

u The resultant product should be moveable and marketable.

For example, processes like Electroplating, Teflon Coating, Anodising, Heat Treatment, Powder Coating, etc., are no doubt a process carried out, but no new product emerges out of such process and, hence, this cannot be described as process amounting to manufacture and job workers undertaking the above activities are required to pay service tax.

The second part of the definition under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 is introduced from March 1, 1986, which reads as under:

"‘Manufacture’ includes any process,—

(i )** ** **

(ii )which is specified in relation to any goods in the section or Chapter Notes of the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 as amounting to manufacture;"

This is a major change in the definition of ‘Manufacture’ and the interesting aspect of this definition is that whatever is mentioned in the Section Notes or Chapter Notes will be applicable to only those goods falling in the respective Sections/Chapter of the Tariff. For example, in respect of food preparations, chemicals and pharmaceutical products, even the process of labelling and re-labelling, repacking from bulk packs to retail packs or adoption of any other treatment to render the product marketable to the consumer, shall amount to manufacture. If the product falling under the respective Chapters undergoes the above process, it will be treated as ‘Manufacture’ and all excise formalities will have to be complied with. To appreciate and understand whether a particular process amounts to manufacture or not, one has to refer to Section Notes and Chapter Notes under the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

The third part of the definition is a recent addition which came into effect from March 1, 2003 which reads as under:

"‘Manufacture’ includes any process,—

(i )and (ii) ** ** **

(iii )which, in relation to the goods specified in the Third Schedule, involves packing or repacking of such goods in a unit container or labelling or re-labelling of containers including the declaration or alteration of retail sale price on it or adoption of any other treatment on the goods to render the product marketable to the consumer,"

The above definition applies only to goods specified in the Third Schedule which comprises of 99 items which are incidentally same items which attract excise duty based on MRP/RSP under section 4A of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

Thus, the term ‘Manufacture’ spreads its wings all over, which leaves very little scope for escape from excise levy. When the manufacturers themselves are contesting the term ‘Manufacture’ with the Excise authorities resulting in never ending disputes arising out of the same, it is time for job workers to understand and appreciate the concept which is now defined in a detailed way as explained above.

4. It is interesting to note that production or processing of goods for or on behalf of the client is one of the notified services under the term ‘Business Auxiliary Service’. The definition ends with a clear note that the term ‘Business Auxiliary Service’ does not include any activity that amounts to manufacture within the meaning of clause (f) of section 2 of the Central Excise Act, 1944. Therefore, if the job worker carries out any manufacturing process under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 falling under one of the three categories of the definition discussed above, he can safely remain out of service tax net. 4.2-5 Clearance of waste by service provider

Following provisions will apply to a service provider, who is not a 'manufacturer' -

Inputs becoming waste while providing output service - If some inputs become waste while providing output services, they are 'used in provision of output services'. In such case, no 'amount' or 'duty' is payable when he sells them as scrap, as it cannot be said that he has 'manufactured' them.

Sale of empty packing material - A service provider availing Cenvat on inputs is not required to pay any 'amount' on packing material/empty drums sold by him, even if he had availed Cenvat on such inputs.

Sale of goods on which no Cenvat was availed - A service provider is not required to pay any 'amount' if he sells/disposes of inputs or goods on which he has not availed Cenvat credit.

Scrap — Whether it covers the defective items?

Defective does not mean scrap. Defective G.I. Sheets and the rejected items (steel wires, for example) do not fall under iron scrap. The mere fact that something is defective would not convert them into scrape. Scrapes, in common parlance, contemplate old and broken articles, not fit for use as such item. [Banaras Iron Scrap Merchants Association v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1978 UPTC 632].

The term "scrap", according to dictionary meaning, means 'waste'. 'Anything discarded', 'worn out', 'dead' or 'useless'. In commercial or popular sense also scrap appears to be understood in the sense of waste or the thing being of no use. It cannot be equated with 'defectives, rejects, cuttings or end pieces' mentioned in clause (xvi) of Section 14. These expressions have their own connotation in business circle. For instance defectives or rejects would normally be those goods which for some reason did not come upto standard or specification but were otherwise all right. The argument is therefore not acceptable that tin scrap is covered in clause (xvi). [Cheap Hardware Store v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1982 UPTC 201, decided on 24.12.1981 by Allahabad High Court].

Defective products not usable as such are 'waste and scrap' - Defective products unusable have to be taken as 'scrap and waste' - Panchmahal Steels Ltd. v. CCE 1997(93) ELT 516 (CEGAT). No duty on scrap if final product is exempt, if assessee manufacturing exclusively exempted product or paying 1% duty - It may happen that an item may be exempt from duty under some notification. However, some scrap, waste or paring may get produced while manufacturing the final product (which is exempt from duty). In such case, the waste, scrap and parings are fully exempt from duty. This exemption is available only to those who are exclusively manufacturing exempted final product. If assessee manufactures both excisable and exempt goods, the exemption to waste and scrap is not available. This exemption is not applicable in case of SSI concession, which is applicable on the basis of turnover of the unit. - Notification No. 89/1995-CE dated 18-5-1995.

Similarly, if assessee is manufacturing goods bearing 1% excise duty under Notification Nos. 1/2001-CE dated 1-3-2011 and 20/2011-CE dated 24-3-2011, the waste and scrap arising out of such manufacture is exempted if the manufacturer is engaged solely in the manufacture of goods under 1% effective rate - Notification No. 27/2011-CE dated 24-3-2011.

CCE (2007) 209 ELT 95 (CESTAT), it was confirmed that if assessee is manufacturing both exempt and dutiable products, the waste and scrap arising while manufacturing exempted final product will not be exempt i.e. duty will be payable.

Assessee paid duty on scrap proportional to waste and scrap which was used in respect wagons cleared on payment of duty. It was held that no duty is payable on balance scrap, which was actually recycled.

In Maheshwari Solvent Extraction Ltd. v. CCE (2014) 299 ELT 116 (CESTAT), it was held that the exemption is available even if the waste is sold at a price.

In Saraiwalla Agro Refineries v. Coaches (Condemned) sold by the Railways in auction

The condemned coaches are sold by the Railways on the condition that wheel sets, non-ferrous or stainless steel metal and other goods, as are indicated by the Railways, shall have to be returned by the purchaser to the Railways, and to separate these goods, the purchaser has to dismantle the goods sold in auction in the Railway premises itself. So long as these goods are not returned to the Railways, the purchaser cannot take away the goods obtained as a result of dismantling. Therefore, it is clear that the property in goods (of the goods sold in auction) does not pass to the purchaser so long as the goods returnable to the railways are not returned to them. It is clear that only the goods remaining at the end of dismantling are auctioned, and it will, therefore, be proper to hold that the goods auctioned fall in the category of Iron scrap. Since the work of dismantling is done by the purchaser on behalf of the Railways, therefore, the purchaser cannot be said to be the manufacturer. Scrap Waste Product

The contention of the applicant is that the copper and iron scrap obtained in the process of manufacture of electrical stampings and ceiling fans is waste product which is approximately 52 per cent of the raw material. Their further contention is that the scrap under consideration, being waste products, its sale is exempted in their hands because they are new units and sale of waste product by the new unit is also exempted from tax, as per Circular No. New Unit – 29 dated 24.4.1992 issued by the Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P., Lucknow.

The contention of the Counsel for the applicant is devoid of force that the copper and iron scrap obtained in the process of manufacture of electrical stampings and ceiling fan is waste product, because according to the Oxford Dictionary, "scrap" means the useless bye product of the manufacturer. Scrap is waste material but not the waste product. Scrap is the commodity from which goods may be manufactured after reprocessing it, but waste product cannot be used in remanufacture. Since the scrap is not waste product, it is not exempted from tax. [Khaitan Fans (India) Ltd., NOIDA, decided on 7.1.1994, u/s. 35 by Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P., Lucknow]

The question for consideration is as to under which entry the old aluminum vessels purchased for conversion thereof into new aluminum utensils fall. Held by the Supreme Court- A finding of fact has been arrived at by the Tribunal that the appellant used to purchase the old aluminium vessels and scrap which were used for conversion to new household utensils. The dictionary meaning of scrap is "a small piece or amount of something especially one that is left over after the greater part has been used or material, especially metal, discarded for reprocessing".

The Entries contained in the First Schedule appended to the Act are in three parts. Entry 5 deals with aluminium household utensils. Entry 6 deals with aluminium products and aluminium alloys and entry 83 deals with metal scraps. Indisputably, aluminium metal scraps would also come within the purview of Entry 83. As the appellant deals in metal scrap, its case will come within the purview of Entry 83. All aluminium products do not come within the purview of Entry 5. It deals with only domestic utensils. For other aluminium products a different rate of tax has been provided in Entry 6. If there exists an entry which covers the goods in question, by necessary implication the same would be considered to have been excluded from another entry.

We will assume that the Entry 5 is capable of two interpretations. It may be read in the manner in which the Tribunal did, but it can also be read as "household utensils made up of aluminium or aluminium alloy." Use of the word "Aluminium" at the beginning may be superfluous. In any event the dealer cannot be said to be dealing with aluminium household utensils or household utensils made up of aluminium and aluminium alloys. We, therefore, are of the opinion that it was entry 83 which is attracted to the facts of the present case. [Baby Varghese v. The definition of 'scrap' as given in Explanation (b) is not limited to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone but extends to cover 'waste' also. Therefore, the scope of the term 'scrap' as defined in Explanation (b) cannot be interpreted so as to restrict its application to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone. The first part of the definition of 'scrap' in Explanation (b) refers not only to scrap from the 'manufacture' but also to 'mechanical working of materials'. Both the phrases, namely, manufacture and mechanical working of materials differ in their meaning and content. 'Mechanical working of materials' refers to physical operations on materials. It signifies physical operations to bring about physical change to which the material is subjected in order to change its shape, properties or structure. In order to fall in the definition of 'scrap', it is not necessary that the same should occur in the course of manufacture; it can also occur in the course of mechanical working of materials, i.e., in the course of physical operations on materials. Thus, both the operations/processes, namely, the manufacture and mechanical working of materials, can give rise to scrap. Any article or thing arising from the physical operations on materials which is not usable as such would therefore fall in the category of 'scrap'. As stated earlier, the second part of the definition, i.e., 'which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons' also throws light on the scope of the term 'scrap' inasmuch as it seeks to define the characteristics of scrap. In order to constitute 'scrap', the article or thing must not be usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. The use of the words 'other reasons' in the second part of the definition of 'scrap' is significant. In order to constitute 'scrap', what is contemplated by Explanation (b) is the non-usability of materials as such, which could even be for a reason other than breakage, cutting up and wear. The phraseology employed in Explanation (b) shows that the term 'scrap' has been defined in wide terms so as to include both (i) waste, and (ii) scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials. However, both of them have been used as one phrase, i.e., as 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials', for the second part of the definition and, therefore, both of them should definitely be not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear or other reasons.

CCE (2004) 165 ELT 314 (CESTAT), it was held that scrap paper generated during manufacture of cigarettes it not result of manufacturing process - quoted and stay granted in International Tobacco Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 292 ELT 97 (CESTAT). - same view in ITC Ltd. v. CCE (2016) 341 ELT 417 (CESTAT).

Waste of black carbon during manufacture of electrodes - Waste of black carbon during manufacture of electrodes is not 'goods' even if it fetches some value. It is not necessary to enter those goods in Daily Stock Account but the time of its sale. Application for remission of duty is also not required - Eveready Industries v. CCE (2014) 307 ELT 556 (CESTAT).

Waste and scrap not goods if not marketable

3.2-1 Carbide sludge arising in manufacture of acetylene gas is not marketable and hence not liable to duty - CCE v. Bansal Indus. Gases 2003(151) ELT 4 (SC 3 member bench). Spent Nickel Catalyst arising during manufacture of soap is not an excisable commodity as department failed to prove that it is a marketable commodity. - CCE v. Hindustan Lever 2003(151) ELT 10 (SC).

In CCE v. MRF Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 595 (CEGAT - 3 member bench), it was held that rubber scrap obtained by cutting defective rubber tubes are not 'goods'.

Calcium carbide slag is waste and not marketable. It is not excisable goods - CCE v. DCW Ltd. (2008) 222 ELT 79 (CESTAT).

Just because assessee has found some use of waste, it does not mean that the waste is marketable, if it has no specific composition or identity - Gujarat State Fertilisers v. CCE (2009) 234 ELT 532 (CESTAT).

In UP State Sugar Corpn v. CCE 2000(119) ELT 74 (CEGAT), it was held that press-mud arising during manufacture of sugar is only a residual waste. It is not marketable and is not excisable. - view upheld in CCE v. Titawi Sugar Complex 2003(152) ELT 21 (SC)- - - followed in CCE v. Cheyyar Coop Sugar Mills (2009) 240 ELT 417 (CESTAT SMB) accepted by department - CBEC circular No. 730/46/2003-CX dated 31-7-2003 [However, in another matter, departmental appeal has been admitted - 199 ELT A70].

In CCE v. Tony Electronics 2000(119) ELT 139 (CEGAT), it was held that waste and scrap in the course of manufacture of audio/video magnetic tape is not marketable and hence not excisable.

Waste like floor sweeping, processed defective cakes etc. are not marketable.- CCE v. Delta Foods (2011) 30 STT 121 (CESTAT SMB) * Delta Foods v. CCE (2012) 277 ELT 352 (CESTAT) (Hence rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules is not applicable as payment of 'amount' is not required)

Stray or distress sale does not mean goods are 'marketable'.

3.2-2 Stray or distress sale does not prove marketability

Stray sale does not mean goods are marketable - If the product is generally not sold, stray sales do not mean that the product is marketable - Gujarat State Fertilizers v. CCE - (1996) 84 ELT 539 (CEGAT) - correct decision as 'one swallow does not make a summer'.

In CCE v. Ranger Breweries Ltd. 2000(122) ELT 447 = 39 RLT 1065 (CEGAT), it was observed that stray incidents of sale does not give characteristics of marketability to the goods - same view in CCE v. Karnataka Vidyuth Karkhane (2009) 239 ELT 165 (CESTAT).

Distress sale does not mean goods are marketable - In Britannia Industries Ltd. v. CCE 1997(93) ELT 719 (CEGAT), it was held that waste cannot be treated as excisable goods merely because it is capable of fetching some sale price, if such sale is distress sale and sale price is determined at the whims of the buyers as there is no ready market for regular sale.

Rejected, Defectives, Cuttings and End Pieces of Iron Sheet – Whether they fall within 'Iron Scraps"?

On a perusal of Photo and Sample of the goods, it is evident that the goods referred by the applicant are not iron scrap, they are defective pieces and cuttings of iron sheet. These are not useless or old broken items. The defectives, rejected and end pieces obtained during manufacture cannot be categorized as scrap. Sellers have also described them in the bills as "rejected CR or HR sheet". They can be used as new sheet as well. Hence these items do not fall within iron scrap mentioned in clause (i) of Section 14(iv) of the Central Sales Tax Act, but they fall within clause (xvi) of Section 14(iv) of the Central Sales Tax Act. Hence they are not exempted from the payment of entry tax. FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. On appeal, the revenue contended, inter alia, that sections 41(1) and 41(2) were applicable to profits derived from sale of scrap metal and drums.

HELD: Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

HELD: Scrap--Drums (Empty) of calcium carbide are not "goods" cleared in terms of Rule 57F(2) CER, but "scrap" arising in preparatory stage, of manufacturing process in terms of Rule 57F(4) and duty can be demanded at the rate applicable to scrap (i.e. drums as such in the form they are cleared).

"After the Modvat credit was taken, the status of the goods changed and instead of the goods being considered as duty paid goods these became goods as if these are the manufacture of the appellants' factory. But there is no controversy that what was removed from the appellants' factory were not the goods as these were brought in i.e. Calcium Carbide filled in the drums but only empty drums. The empty drums, therefore, cleared from the appellants' factory cannot be taken to be goods cleared as such in terms of Rule 57F(2) from the appellants' factory. However, we observe that the Calcium Carbide drums for the purpose of taking the Calcium Carbide into use had to be opened and the remaining empty drums can be taken to be scrap which arose in the preparatory stages of the manufacturing process. In that view of the matter we hold that the drums can be considered as scrap in terms of Rule 57F(4) and duty on the same can be demanded under the Tariff Heading and the rate applicable to the scrap as such i.e. the rate applicable to the drums as such in the form these are cleared."

HELD: In Fenner (India) Ltd. v. CIT (No. 2) [2000] 241 ITR 803, the Madras High Court expressed the view that the scrap materials has direct link or nexus with the industrial undertaking and, therefore, profit from the sale of the scrap materials should be eligible for deduction under section 80HH. Following that decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the relief under section 80HH was allowable to the assessee on profit on sale of scrap. [Para 13]

, 'which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons' refers to the characteristics which a material has to possess in order to fall in the category of 'scrap'.

The second part of definition, being integral part of the definition, also throws light on the scope and ambit of the term 'scrap' and, therefore, needs to be taken into consideration while interpreting the first part of the definition of 'scrap'. [Para 24] The first part of the definition, namely, 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials' seeks to cover both 'waste' as well as 'scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials'. In the absence of any definition of the term 'waste' in the Act, one has to turn to its meaning as it is understood in common parlance.

In common parlance, 'waste' is understood as something unusable or unwanted material. According to the Concise Oxford Dictionary, 'waste' is something which has been 'eliminated or discarded as no longer useful or required'. 'Scrap', on the other hand, represents something which is left over after the greater part has been used or consumed. 'Scrap' thus refers to the incidental residue derived from certain types of manufacture, which is recoverable without further processing.

It is in this context that the words 'from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials' qualify the preceding word 'scrap' and not 'waste'. The definition of 'scrap' as given in Explanation (b) is not limited to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone but extends to cover 'waste' also. Therefore, the scope of the term 'scrap' as defined in Explanation (b) cannot be interpreted so as to restrict its application to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone.

While 'waste' covers everything that is unusable or has been discarded as no longer useful as such, 'scrap' covers everything that arises from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials. By its very nature, 'waste' is a term of wider import while 'scrap' is narrower in its scope. [Para 25]

The first part of the definition of 'scrap' in Explanation (b) refers not only to scrap from the 'manufacture' but also to 'mechanical working of materials'. Both the phrases, namely, manufacture and mechanical working of materials differ in their meaning and content. [Para 26]

'Mechanical working of materials' refers to physical operations on materials. It signifies physical operations to bring about physical change to which the material is subjected in order to change its shape, properties or structure. In order to fall in the definition of 'scrap', it is not necessary that the same should occur in the course of manufacture; it can also occur in the course of mechanical working of materials, i.e., in the course of physical operations on materials.

Thus, both the operations/processes, namely, the manufacture and mechanical working of materials, can give rise to scrap. Any article or thing arising from the physical operations on materials which is not usable as such would therefore fall in the category of 'scrap'.

As stated earlier, the second part of the definition, i.e., 'which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons' also throws light on the scope of the term 'scrap' in as much as it seeks to define the characteristics of scrap. In order to constitute 'scrap', the article or thing must not be usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. The use of the words "other reasons" in the second part of the definition of 'scrap' is significant.

In order to constitute 'scrap', what is contemplated by Explanation (b) is the non-usability of materials as such, which could even be for a reason other than breakage, cutting up and wear. The phraseology employed in Explanation (b) shows that the term 'scrap' has been defined in wide terms so as to include both (i) waste, and (ii) scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials.

However, both of them have been used as one phrase, i.e., as 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials', for the second part of the definition and, therefore, both of them should definitely be not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear or other reasons. [Para 26]

It was submitted by the assessee that the use of the word 'and' in the expression 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials' suggests that both of them, namely, waste and scrap, must arise from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials and that waste per se cannot be scrap unless it, like scrap, also arises from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials.

It is correct that the word 'and' in the said expression joins both the words, namely, (i) waste; and (ii) scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials and to that extent they constitute one phrase, i.e., 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials' and that is why the words "which is" have been used as link between the first part and second part of the definition.

HELD: Computation of Section 80HHC deduction

The deduction under section 80HHC, subject to several other conditions, incorporated in the section, is determined as under: Thus, if the total turnover increases, the advantage which the assessee would get under section 80HHC would decrease because the amount deductible substantially depends upon the ratio between the export turnover and total turnover. If the export turnover is higher, comparatively the amount deductible under section 80HHC would be more; or in other words, if compared to total turnover, export turnover is less the amount deductible from the income under section 80HHC would be reduced. [Para 10]

Meaning of the term 'turnover'

The term 'turnover' had neither been defined in the Act nor has been explained by any of the CBDT circulars. [Para 17]

In the aforesaid circumstances, one has to look at the meaning of the term 'turnover' in ordinary accounting or commercial parlance. [Para 18]

Normally, the term 'turnover' would show the sale effected by a business unit. It may happen that in the course of the business, in addition to the normal sales, the business unit may also sell some other things. [Para 19]

In ordinary accounting parlance, as approved by all accountants and auditors, the term 'sales', when reflected in the profit and loss account, would indicate sale proceeds from sale of the articles or things in which the business unit is dealing. When some other things like old furniture or a capital asset, in which the business unit is not dealing are sold, the sale proceeds therefrom would not be included in 'sales' but it would be shown separately. [Para 20]

In simple words, the word 'turnover' would mean only the amount of sale proceeds received in respect of the goods in which an assessee is dealing in. [Para 21]

So far as the scrap is concerned, the sale proceeds from the scrap may either be shown separately in the profit and loss account or may be deducted from the amount spent by the manufacturing unit on the raw material, which is steel in the case of the respondent-assessee, as the respondent-assessee is using stainless steel as raw material, from which utensils are manufactured. The raw material, which is not capable of being used for manufacturing utensils will have to be either sold as scrap or might have to be re-cycled in the form of sheets of stainless steel, if the manufacturing unit is also having its re-rolling plant. If it is not having such a plant, the manufacturer would dispose of the scrap of steel to someone who would re-cycle the said scrap into steel so that the said steel can be re-used. [Para 22]

When such scrap is sold, the sale proceeds of the scrap cannot be included in the term 'turnover' for the reason that the respondent-unit is engaged primarily in the manufacturing and selling of steel utensils and not scrap of steel. Therefore, the proceeds of such scrap would not be included in 'sales' in the Profit and Loss Account of the respondent-assessee. [Para 23]

The situation would be different in the case of the buyer, who purchases scrap from the respondent-assessee and sells it to someone else. The sale proceeds for such a buyer would be treated as 'turnover' for a simple reason that the buyer of the scrap is a person who is primarily dealing in scrap. In the case on hand, as the respondent-assessee is not primarily dealing in scrap but is a manufacturer of stainless steel utensils, only sale proceeds from sale of utensils would be treated as his 'turnover'. [Para 24]

The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India ('ICAI') has published some material under the head 'Guidance Note on Tax Audit under section 44AB'. The said material has been published so as to guide the members of the ICAI. In our opinion, when a recognized body of Accountants, after due deliberation and consideration publishes certain material for its members, one can rely upon the same. Para 5 of the said Note deals with 'Sales', 'turnover' and 'gross receipts'. The meaning given by the ICAI clearly denotes that in normal accounting parlance the word 'turnover' would mean 'total sales' as explained hereinabove. The said sales would definitely not include the scrap material which is either to be deducted from the cost of raw material or is to be shown separately under a different head. There is no reason for not accepting the meaning of the term 'turnover' given by a body of Accountants, which is having a statutory recognition. [Para 25]

If all accountants, auditors, businessmen, manufacturers etc. are normally interpreting the term 'turnover' as sale proceeds of the commodity in which the business unit is dealing, there is no reason to take a different view than the view normally taken by the persons who are concerned with the said term. [Para 26]

HEADNOTE: Section 80HH of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from hotels or industrial undertaking, etc., in backward areas - Assessment year 1994-95 - Assessee, engaged in running of steel and iron re-rolling mill, derived income from sale of brass scrap which he obtained from dismantling certain guns purchased in auction and which could not be used for re-rolling - He claimed deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I on such income which was denied as it was not considered as income arising from industrial undertaking - Assessee had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware that inside guns, there was brass scrap which was removed - Thus, it was only a fortuitous circumstance that, in relevant assessment year, assessee had purchased guns without knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in process of manufacture - Whether since brass was not an essential raw material of industrial unit, in question and brass was not at all connected with steel re-rolling, there was no nexus between brass scrap obtained on dismantling of guns and main activity of assessee of steel re-rolling and, therefore, separation of brass could not be said to be in process of manufacture or a product or by-product of activity of assessee’s industrial undertaking - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, profit on sale of brass scrap could not be said to be profit and gain derived from industrial undertaking so as to be entitled to deduction under sections 80HHC and 80-I - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, engaged in the manufacture of re-rolled products of iron and steel in his re-rolling mill, filed his return of income which was accepted as such. In the course of the survey conducted under section 133A, the assessee had offered to pay tax on Rs. 10 lakhs. When required to explain the surrender, the assessee submitted that he had purchased certain guns in auction and certain quantity of brass scrap was obtained from breaking and dismantling those guns and the balance was iron scrap. It was contended that the said activity tantamounted to production of goods and, hence, income from industrial undertaking. The Assessing Officer, however, did not consider the income from sale of brass scrap as arising from industrial undertaking for purposes of allowing deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I and allowed the claim only in respect of other income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s submission. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal reversed the impugned order and allowed the revenue’s appeal. It accepted the plea that the assessee had purchased guns and the income from brass scrap which could not be used for re-rolling, thus, was not entitled to deduction under sections 80HH and 80-I.

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: The assessee in his explanation had stated that he dealt in steel scrap and was not aware of the fact that inside the guns, there was brass scrap which was removed. Thus, it was clear from the reply that brass was not an ingredient used in the process of manufacture in industrial undertaking of the assessee. The brass scrap had no direct nexus with the appellant’s industrial undertaking. It could not be said that brass scrap was a profit or gain which directly flowed, neither it had close connection with undertaking of the assessee. By removal of brass scrap which was not useful for steel rerolling work no different and distinct article came into existence, it was only incidental as was apparent from the assessee’s reply. [Paras 13 and 14]

Further, composition of brass scrap was not at all changed, that was only removed as that was not useful to the assessee for the activity of manufacturing which he was carrying on. It was only a fortuitous circumstance that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee had purchased the guns without the knowledge that brass scrap was inside them which was separated and it could not be said to be a by-product obtained in the process of manufacture. There was no nexus between brass and activity of steel rerolling. Brass was not at all an input in the process of manufacture of steel rerolling. It was not a raw material at all for the process of rerolling in which the assessee was involved. It was purely incidental that brass was found inside guns which were purchased in that year. Guns might have several components, sometimes brass or some other articles which may not be connected at all with the manufacturing process of the industrial undertaking. [Paras 22, 23, 24 and 25]
