Introduction

1. To be liable to excise duty, a product must be manufactured, movable, marketable and mentioned in First Schedule to Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 as subject to duty of excise duty. From 1-3-2015, even if goods are non-excisable, they continue to be exempted goods and, therefore, credit relatable thereto has to be reversed.

Demand of duty on Bagasse/Zinc-Dross, etc. has been subject matter of repeated litigation since decades. The Department has been making all efforts (and CBEC upholding said efforts by issuance of circulars) to demand excise duty on Bagasse/Zinc-Dross. However, the Courts have been holding otherwise.

This article makes an attempt to analyse the position of law vis-à-vis recent landmark judgments on the issue and Circular No.1027/15/2016-CX, dated 25-4-2016.

Position prior to 10-5-2008

2. Prior to 10-5-2008, concept of marketability was not defined in the Central Excise Act, 1944 and for being marketable, goods were required to be known as such in market and capability of being commercially bought and sold as 'goods'. Thus, waste and residue of many kinds were held non-marketable. In this regard, to be brief, we may be conclude that —

bagasse was held not excisable goods in Commissioner v. Balrampur Chini Mills Ltd. - 2015 (320) ELT A258 (SC)]. This view was accepted by CBEC itself in its Circular No. 941/2/2011-CX., dated 14-2-2011

zinc dross was held non-manufactured/non-marketable in Collector v. Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. - 2004 (165) ELT 386 (SC) and Commissioner v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 2006 (203) ELT 3 (SC).

The Department's demand of excise duty on said goods was therefore, set aside. The Department's demand of reversal of credit under rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 (and its earlier counterparts) was set aside on ground that since they were not marketable and non-excisable, hence, they were not even 'exempted goods' as defined in the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Hence, no payment of duty/credit was required prior to 10-5-2008.

Period 10-5-2008 to 28-2-2015

3. Vide amendment by Finance Act, 2008, as Explanation was inserted in section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 defining the concept of marketability. It was provided that "goods" includes any article, material or substance which is capable of being bought and sold for a consideration and such goods shall be deemed to be marketable. Thus, capability of being bought and sold for a consideration would constitute marketability and there would be no need for the goods to be commercially tradeable or known as such in the market.

3.1 Circular of 2009 and 2011 : Relying upon this amendment, the CBEC issued Circular No. 904/24/2009-CX., dated 28-10-2009 (reiterated in Circular No. 941/2/2011-CX., dated 14-2-2011) that (paras 2 to 5 of the Circular of 2009, relevant extracts) :

Excisability of bagasse and similar waste products arising during the course of manufacture has been under dispute for a long period of time.

In the budget of 2008, the definition of "excisable goods" in clause (d) of section 2 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 was amended by adding an explanation that for the purposes of this clause, "goods" include any article, material or substance which is capable of being bought and sold for a consideration and such goods shall be deemed to be marketable.

It is clarified that with this amendment in section 2(d), the bagasse, aluminium/zinc dross and other such products termed as waste, residue or refuse which arise during the course of manufacture and are capable of being sold for consideration would be excisable goods and chargeable to payment of excise duty.

CENTRAL EXCISE - JOB-WORK - DIRECT EXPORT

1. We purchased wire rods, availed Cenvat credit thereon and sent them to the job worker [who is a related party] for drawing them [procedure under rule 4(5)(a) has been followed]. The job worker is an exporter also. Instead of sending the drawn rods back to us, it was decided that the job-workers would export the same to its own customers. Can it be done ? We are ready to pay duty on cost (raw material plus job work charges plus 10% net profit margin) by issuing invoice in name of job worker. Will it be in accordance with law ? You may please advise us as regards any other formality to be observed under the law ?

One can presume that yourself (the principal manufacturer) want to sell the finished goods to the job-worker himself and the job-worker would export the same. There is absolutely no embargo thereupon i.e., you may sell the goods to job-worker. In fact, rule 4(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 permits direct clearance from factory of job-worker. Instead of receiving finished goods back and again selling them to job-worker, you may definitely raise a sale bill in the name of job-worker.

Since it is claimed that you are related parties, the value of 'drawn rods' (final product) would be determined as per rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000, read with rules 9 and 10 ibid.

Since the job-worker would act as merchant exporter, he may avail of facilities under rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, i.e., procurement without payment of duty or any other export incentive for which necessary procedures would have to be complied with. If the facility under rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 in relation to procurement of goods without payment of duty for export is availed, no duty would be payable on drawn rods.

It is advised that an informed decision be made, after analyzing pros and cons.

2. We are manufacturers of TV sets. In some cases we purchase completed TV sets from third parties and sell them to customers. We are availing of marketing services. Purchase and sale of goods does not amount to 'manufacture'. Further, the same does not amount to an 'output service' under rule 2(p) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, as first of all, the same is not a service under section 65B(44) of the Finance Act, 1994 and secondly, the same falls in negative list under section 66D(e) of the Finance Act, 1994 [Trading of Goods].

Since trading of goods is neither manufacture nor provision of service, any service used therefor is not eligible for credit under rule 3, read with rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In case you have taken credit, you are advised to reverse the same to avoid applicability of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

CENVAT CREDIT - FAQs (PART 3)

In this article, the author has discussed some very common questions in respect of capital goods used by manufacturer of excisable goods or provider of taxable services.

Is Cenvat credit available on capital goods if acquired on lease, hire-purchase or loan ?

What if capital goods are removed from factory/service premises ‘as such’ or ‘if removed as scrap’ or ‘before put to use’ or ‘after being used’?

2. Rule 3(5) and 3(5A)/(5B) defines four types of situations and provides guidelines what is to be done. All these situations are detailed below.

Here there is no question of bona fide or mala fide intention due to which no penalty provision would be attracted.

(a) Capital goods removed ‘as such’ - ‘As such’ means, in the same position in which purchase is done. Whatever Cenvat Credit is taken/availed, it has to be paid to the account of the Central Government. (b) Capital goods removed ‘as scrap’ - If capital goods are removed ‘as scrap’, then manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the duty leviable on transaction value.

(c) Capital goods removed ‘before put to use’ - Here manufacturer is required to pay full amount of duty which has been taken as Cenvat credit. This situation is different from the situation given in (a) above, as here it might be possible that the capital goods which are purchased may not be in ‘intact’ position, say, for example machines are purchased and installed and are made ready to use, but ultimately it is decided that these should not be used but to be removed.

(d) Capital goods removed ‘after put to use’ - What amount of Cenvat credit has been taken in the books of account is required to be depreciated by 2.5 per cent (i.e., reduced) per quarter and the balance amount is required to be paid to the account of the Central Government.

Recently, further notifications and clarifications were issued on May 20, 1994, in order to overcome these difficulties. The following are the important points to be noted from these amendments :

(i)Under the original rule, if the capital goods, on which MODVAT credit was taken were removed from the factory, the assessee was required to clear the same on payment of duty, not lesser than the amount of credit which was previously taken thereon. As per the amended notification, this requirement applies only where the capital equipment is sought to be removed from the factory without being used in the manufacture of excisable goods.

As per the amendment, if the machinery is sought to be removed from the factory after being used therein, then the payment of excise duty has to be made after allowing a deduction of 2.5 per cent of the credit taken earlier for each quarter of a year of usage from the date of taking the credit. The amended notification further provides that if the machinery has been sold for any reason as scrap, this duty shall be paid at the rate applicable to such scrap.

It would appear that the normal life of the machinery, for this purpose, is estimated at 10 years, and a distinction is drawn between used and unused machinery and also between usable and scrapped machinery.

(ii)A new sub-rule has also been added, permitting removal of capital goods for tests or repairs for reconditioning, provided the same are returned to the factory for further use as capital goods. Prior to this amendment, it was thought that even in such cases of removal of capital goods duty was required to be reimbursed.

(iii)The earlier requirement was that before the assessee takes MODVAT credit on capital goods, such goods have to be verified by the Excise Superintendent. This requirement, which was considered impractical and susceptible to misuse, has now been removed by another amended notification.

(iv)Yet another welcome amendment is that the assessee can now take credit on capital goods on the basis of an invoice or bill of entry or other duty-paying document as against the cumbersome procedure prescribed earlier.

These amendments are in the right direction, as a result of which, most of the practical difficulties are considered to have been removed.

2.4 Case of goods obtained on lease or hire purchase - According to the existing provisions, MODVAT credit on capital goods is not permissible in respect of the equipment acquired on lease or hire purchase. Several representations were made in this regard by the industry. It was reported that the Government has decided to amend the relevant rules so as to extend MODVAT credit to capital goods acquired through leasing and hire purchase also. But the relevant notification has not yet been issued and it is hoped that it would be done soon.

2.5 MODVAT credit vs. Depreciation - It is specifically provided that no credit of the duty paid on capital goods shall be allowed, if the assessee claims depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 on that part of the value of capital goods which represents the amount of specified duty paid on such goods. In other words, a manufacturer has the option to claim MODVAT credit on the duty paid or forego the same if he opts to claim income-tax depreciation on the duty portion of the capital goods. definition of ‘manufacture’ as contained in the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The term ‘manufacture’ is borrowed from the Central Excise Act, 1944 and this is one of the terms which never reached finality in the matter of dispute regarding process to be considered as a manufacture or not. There is a catena of judgments on the subject ‘Manufacture’, and there are books written on this subject which show the significance of the term under the Excise Law. The definition under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act can be divided into three parts:

First part of the definition refers to "any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product". This term has been interpreted by various forums including the Apex Court and what emerges out is presence of the following criteria to constitute manufacture:

u A process should be carried out.

u Such process should result into a distinctly new product, commercially known as such.

u The resultant product should be moveable and marketable.

For example, processes like Electroplating, Teflon Coating, Anodising, Heat Treatment, Powder Coating, etc., are no doubt a process carried out, but no new product emerges out of such process and, hence, this cannot be described as process amounting to manufacture and job workers undertaking the above activities are required to pay service tax.

The second part of the definition under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 is introduced from March 1, 1986, which reads as under:

"‘Manufacture’ includes any process,—

(i )** ** **

(ii )which is specified in relation to any goods in the section or Chapter Notes of the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 as amounting to manufacture;"

This is a major change in the definition of ‘Manufacture’ and the interesting aspect of this definition is that whatever is mentioned in the Section Notes or Chapter Notes will be applicable to only those goods falling in the respective Sections/Chapter of the Tariff. For example, in respect of food preparations, chemicals and pharmaceutical products, even the process of labelling and re-labelling, repacking from bulk packs to retail packs or adoption of any other treatment to render the product marketable to the consumer, shall amount to manufacture. If the product falling under the respective Chapters undergoes the above process, it will be treated as ‘Manufacture’ and all excise formalities will have to be complied with. To appreciate and understand whether a particular process amounts to manufacture or not, one has to refer to Section Notes and Chapter Notes under the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

The third part of the definition is a recent addition which came into effect from March 1, 2003 which reads as under:

"‘Manufacture’ includes any process,—

(i )and (ii) ** ** **

(iii )which, in relation to the goods specified in the Third Schedule, involves packing or repacking of such goods in a unit container or labelling or re-labelling of containers including the declaration or alteration of retail sale price on it or adoption of any other treatment on the goods to render the product marketable to the consumer,"

The above definition applies only to goods specified in the Third Schedule which comprises of 99 items which are incidentally same items which attract excise duty based on MRP/RSP under section 4A of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

Thus, the term ‘Manufacture’ spreads its wings all over, which leaves very little scope for escape from excise levy. When the manufacturers themselves are contesting the term ‘Manufacture’ with the Excise authorities resulting in never ending disputes arising out of the same, it is time for job workers to understand and appreciate the concept which is now defined in a detailed way as explained above.

Business Auxiliary Service, meaning of

4. It is interesting to note that production or processing of goods for or on behalf of the client is one of the notified services under the term ‘Business Auxiliary Service’. The definition ends with a clear note that the term ‘Business Auxiliary Service’ does not include any activity that amounts to manufacture within the meaning of clause (f) of section 2 of the Central Excise Act, 1944. Therefore, if the job worker carries out any manufacturing process under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 falling under one of the three categories of the definition discussed above, he can safely remain out of service tax net. On account of introduction of service tax on job work, it will be a tough time for job workers to convince the excise authorities that the process carried out by them amounts to manufacture. Before introduction of service tax on job work, the job workers were fighting with the department that the process carried out by them does not amount to manufacture to remain out of the excise net, whereas the present scenario is a reverse situation. One has to go by the decisions of the Tribunal, High Court or Supreme Court when claim is made for remaining away from service tax net on the ground that the process carried out amounts to manufacture.

If the job workers carry out the process on the material supplied to them which amounts to manufacture, service tax is not payable in view of the definition of ‘Business Auxiliary Service’ as discussed above.

CENVAT CREDIT - REVERSAL ON EXEMPTED SERVICE AND SERVICES COVERED UNDER FULL REVERSE CHARGE ?

We are manufacturing goods which are 100% excisable and are also providing Goods Transport Agency's Services, which are exempt as per mega exemption notification (transport of defence and military equipments). When taking and availing cenvat, is it necessary to reverse cenvat on exempted service as per rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 ? Is it necessary to reverse credit, even if service is provided on reverse charge mechanism ? Kindly clarify.

Reversal under rule 6 would apply to exempted services provided by service provider. Hence, it would equally apply to exempt Goods Transport Agency's Services.

Supply of bed rolls in trains is a taxable service and is not eligible for any exemption or abatement. The abatement relates only to 'transport of passengers by railways' and the service in question is altogether different.

8. If outdoor caterer is providing catering service in a mess within the factory premises : Is the service exempt as per the mega exemption notification ?

Entries 19 and 19A of the Mega Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012 read as follows :

"19. Services provided in relation to serving of food or beverages by a restaurant, eating joint or a mess, other than those having the facility of air-conditioning or central air-heating in any part of the establishment, at any time during the year;";

19A. Services provided in relation to serving of food or beverages by a canteen maintained in a factory covered under the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948), having the facility of air-conditioning or central air-heating at any time during the year."

It appears that mess would be covered by Entry 19A (if maintained as per Factories Act and having AC) or Entry 19 (if non-AC).

Some experts would suggest that mess services are provided by company to employees and not by outdoor caterer and hence, exemption cannot be availed. However, the most important fact to be noted is that 'company has hired outdoor caterer to run mess' in compliance with law and therefore, mess is run/operated by caterer and mess services would thus, be exempt as aforesaid. Employer-company is not the service provider; in fact, it is duty bound to arrange for canteen and canteen/mess services are provided only by the caterer.

4.2-5 Clearance of waste by service provider

Following provisions will apply to a service provider, who is not a 'manufacturer' -

Inputs becoming waste while providing output service - If some inputs become waste while providing output services, they are 'used in provision of output services'. In such case, no 'amount' or 'duty' is payable when he sells them as scrap, as it cannot be said that he has 'manufactured' them.

Input becoming waste/scrap before putting to use - If the inputs become waste even before taking them out of stores, an 'amount' equal to Cenvat taken will be payable. The reason is that in such case, it cannot be said that the inputs were used 'for providing output services'.

Sale of empty packing material - A service provider availing Cenvat on inputs is not required to pay any 'amount' on packing material/empty drums sold by him, even if he had availed Cenvat on such inputs.

Sale of goods on which no Cenvat was availed - A service provider is not required to pay any 'amount' if he sells/disposes of inputs or goods on which he has not availed Cenvat credit.

Defective does not mean scrap. Defective G.I. Sheets and the rejected items (steel wires, for example) do not fall under iron scrap. Clearance of waste by service provider

28.6-2 Following provisions will apply to a service provider, who is not a 'manufacturer'-

Inputs becoming waste while providing output service - If some inputs become waste while providing output services, they are 'used in provision of output services'. In such case, no 'amount' or 'duty' is payable when he sells them as scrap, as it cannot be said that he has 'manufactured' them.

Input becoming waste/scrap before putting to use - If the inputs become waste even before taking them out of stores, an 'amount' equal to Cenvat taken will be payable. The reason is that in such case, it cannot be said that the inputs were used 'for providing output services'.

Sale of empty packing material - A service provider availing Cenvat on inputs is not required to pay any 'amount' on packing material/empty drums sold by him, even if he had availed Cenvat on such inputs.

Sale of goods on which no Cenvat was availed - A service provider is not required to pay any 'amount' if he sells/disposes of inputs or goods on which he has not availed Cenvat credit.

Scrap Waste Product

The contention of the applicant is that the copper and iron scrap obtained in the process of manufacture of electrical stampings and ceiling fans is waste product which is approximately 52 per cent of the raw material. Their further contention is that the scrap under consideration, being waste products, its sale is exempted in their hands because they are new units and sale of waste product by the new unit is also exempted from tax, as per Circular No. New Unit – 29 dated 24.4.1992 issued by the Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P., Lucknow.

The contention of the Counsel for the applicant is devoid of force that the copper and iron scrap obtained in the process of manufacture of electrical stampings and ceiling fan is waste product, because according to the Oxford Dictionary, "scrap" means the useless bye product of the manufacturer. CCE 1997(94) ELT 268 (CEGAT).

Old Aluminium Utensils/Vessels purchased for converting them into new aluminium utensils

There were three entries under consideration –

Entry 5 read "Aluminium household utensils whether made of aluminium and aluminium alloys".

Entry 6 read "Aluminium products (including aluminium extrusion) and products, aluminium alloys not elsewhere mentioned in this Schedule."

Entry 83 read "Metal scraps other than those specified in the second Schedule."

The question for consideration is as to under which entry the old aluminum vessels purchased for conversion thereof into new aluminum utensils fall. The Tribunal held that prior to amendment of entry 5, the word 'and" was there between "aluminum" and "household" and it appears to have been left inadvertently to be mentioned in the revised entry. The Tribunal held the word "and" should still be read there and finally held that "old aluminum vessel" fell in entry 5 and not in entry 83.

Held by the Supreme Court- A finding of fact has been arrived at by the Tribunal that the appellant used to purchase the old aluminium vessels and scrap which were used for conversion to new household utensils. Old aluminium vessels are pressed to convert the same into scrap. Appellant, thus, is a scrap dealer and not a dealer in aluminium vessels within the meaning of Entry 5.

The dictionary meaning of scrap is "a small piece or amount of something especially one that is left over after the greater part has been used or material, especially metal, discarded for reprocessing".

The Entries contained in the First Schedule appended to the Act are in three parts. Entry 5 deals with aluminium household utensils. Entry 6 deals with aluminium products and aluminium alloys and entry 83 deals with metal scraps. Indisputably, aluminium metal scraps would also come within the purview of Entry 83. As the appellant deals in metal scrap, its case will come within the purview of Entry 83. All aluminium products do not come within the purview of Entry 5. It deals with only domestic utensils. For other aluminium products a different rate of tax has been provided in Entry 6. If there exists an entry which covers the goods in question, by necessary implication the same would be considered to have been excluded from another entry.

We will assume that the Entry 5 is capable of two interpretations. It may be read in the manner in which the Tribunal did, but it can also be read as "household utensils made up of aluminium or aluminium alloy." Use of the word "Aluminium" at the beginning may be superfluous. In any event the dealer cannot be said to be dealing with aluminium household utensils or household utensils made up of aluminium and aluminium alloys. We, therefore, are of the opinion that it was entry 83 which is attracted to the facts of the present case. [Baby Varghese v. State of Kerala, VSTI 2008 …B-436; VSTI 2008 (Delhi, Punjab, Haryana)...B-607; 2008 NTN (Vol. 38) – 123; (2008) 32 PHT 185 (SC); (2008) 16 VST 448 (SC); (2010) 56 S.T.A. 73, decided on 1.8.2008 by the Supreme Court]

Aluminium Utensils/Vessels (Old) purchased for converting them into scrap

Entry 5 read "Aluminium household utensils whether made of aluminium

and aluminium alloys".

Entry 6 read "Aluminium products (including aluminium extrusion) and products, aluminium alloys not elsewhere mentioned in this Schedule."

Alloy Aluminium scrap turning and boring

Alloy Aluminium scrap turning and boring is taxable under the entry "All kinds of metals and scraps and alloy including sheets and circles used in the manufacture of brasswares, except those included in any other entry or any other notification issued under the Act." [Agarwal Disposal and Metal Works, Kanpur decided on 17.9.1984 u/s. 35 by Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P., Lucknow]

Old Battery Scraps

They are taxable @4% under Entry 51 of Schedule II, Part A that reads "Old, discarded, obsolete, unserviceable machinery, stores and vehicle including waste products". [M/s Metal Alloy, Varanasi, Application No. 33/2008 decided on 17.3.2008, by the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, U.P. under Section 59 of the VAT Ordinance, 2008 NTN (Vol. 37) Tribunal and Commissioner's decision 79, 2008 VLJ (Volume 8) Statutes, Notifications & Circulars - 25]

Batteries sold as scrap by radio head office

They are taxable @4% under Entry 51 of Schedule II, Part A that reads "Old, discarded, obsolete, unserviceable machinery, stores and vehicle including waste products". [M/s Sahayak Radio Adhikari Pravidhik, U.P. Police radio, Lucknow, Application No. 100/2008 decided on 17.3.2008, by the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, U.P. under Section 59 of the VAT Ordinance, 2008 NTN (Vol. 37) Tribunal and Commissioner's decision 59; 2008 VLJ (Volume 8) Statutes, Notifications and Circulars -39]

Aluminium Vessels (Old) purchased for metal value

Old aluminium vessels purchased for metal value and used for reprocessing is aluminium scrap.[Prabhat Rolling Metal Works v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, (1988) 69 STC 359 (Kar.)]

Machinery Part obtained after getting the machinery cut

The contention of the assessee is that since he sold the machinery parts after getting the machinery cut, they should be taxed as iron scrap and not as "old, discarded, unserviceable or obsolete machinery…." The interpretation suggested by the assessee cannot be accepted for in that case every assessee will simply get his machinery cut and then sell it as scrap, thus making the entry redundant. Unless the machinery has been cut or broken to the extent that it is no longer possible to call it machinery, it cannot be called scrap. No facts have been given by the assessee as to the extent to which the machinery has been cut or dismembered. Hence the machinery parts in question cannot be called scrap. [U.P. State Sugar Corporation of India Ltd. v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1992 UPTC 1344].

Rail Line Scrap – Whether it is iron scrap?

Anything which has been rendered useless and worn out or is a waste would be a scrap and it is different from material which is defective or rejected but the real test to distinguish between the two would only be by ascertaining the nature of the material in the hands of the party selling it i.e. the railways in the present case. It cannot be decided simply on the basis of entries made in Form 38 because generally the persons filling the forms are technical persons. [Prince Industries v. Commissioner, Commercial Tax, U.P., Lucknow, (2012) 19 VLJ 187, decided on 15.5.2012 by the Allahabad High Court]

TTJ 1/27 ITR (Trib.) 611 (Rajkot) (SB)

The definition of 'scrap' as given in Explanation (b) is not limited to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone but extends to cover 'waste' also. Therefore, the scope of the term 'scrap' as defined in Explanation (b) cannot be interpreted so as to restrict its application to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone. The first part of the definition of 'scrap' in Explanation (b) refers not only to scrap from the 'manufacture' but also to 'mechanical working of materials'. Both the phrases, namely, manufacture and mechanical working of materials differ in their meaning and content. 'Mechanical working of materials' refers to physical operations on materials. It signifies physical operations to bring about physical change to which the material is subjected in order to change its shape, properties or structure. In order to fall in the definition of 'scrap', it is not necessary that the same should occur in the course of manufacture; it can also occur in the course of mechanical working of materials, i.e., in the course of physical operations on materials. Thus, both the operations/processes, namely, the manufacture and mechanical working of materials, can give rise to scrap. Any article or thing arising from the physical operations on materials which is not usable as such would therefore fall in the category of 'scrap'. As stated earlier, the second part of the definition, i.e., 'which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons' also throws light on the scope of the term 'scrap' inasmuch as it seeks to define the characteristics of scrap. In order to constitute 'scrap', the article or thing must not be usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. The use of the words 'other reasons' in the second part of the definition of 'scrap' is significant. In order to constitute 'scrap', what is contemplated by Explanation (b) is the non-usability of materials as such, which could even be for a reason other than breakage, cutting up and wear. The phraseology employed in Explanation (b) shows that the term 'scrap' has been defined in wide terms so as to include both (i) waste, and (ii) scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials. However, both of them have been used as one phrase, i.e., as 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials', for the second part of the definition and, therefore, both of them should definitely be not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear or other reasons.

Non Ferrous Metal Scrap – Whether it is included in "All Non Ferrous Metal including ores and concentrates"?

The entry under consideration was "All non ferrous metals including ores and concentrates". The question was as to whether non ferrous metal scrap was covered in it as non ferrous metal?

Held – The words "non ferrous metal" refer to any metal (other than iron and its alloys) which is used or intended to be used as a raw material for the manufacture or production of any metal product. When bars, wires, flats, plates are used in the manufacture of metal products, bits, pieces, shavings, fragments are generated as waste. Such metal scrap is purchased by the appellant from outside the State and brought into the State for the purpose of melting it and produce rods, wires, etc. Such metal scrap will therefore be metal. Therefore, non ferrous metal scrap intended to be melted to produce metal or metal product is also non ferrous metal falling under entry 29-A of the second Schedule to the Act. [Bhandarai Metals ands Alloys (P) Limited v. State of Karnataka (2004) 136 STC 292 (Kar.), decided on 8.3.2004 by the Division Bench of Karnataka High Court]

Old Aluminium Vessels purchased for metal value

Old aluminium vessels purchased for metal value and used for reprocessing is aluminium scrap. [Prabhat Rolling Metal Works v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, (1988) 69 STC 359 (Kar.)]

Scrap Machinery - totally unserviceable purchased for melting and recasting

According to Webster's Dictionary, "Scrap" is (1) "a small piece; a little bit; a fragment; as scrap of metal; (2) discarded metal in the form of machinery, auto parts, etc., suitable only for reprocessing."

It is evident from these dictionary meanings that broken parts or fragments of a machinery would undoubtedly be considered as "Scrap".

Speaking of the facts of the case, the old machinery and spare parts of which the assessee is found to have paid tax, at the time of their purchase has actually been put to use as metal and not as machinery because it is an admitted position that they have been melted and recast. Under the circumstances even applying common parlance test, machinery which is totally unserviceable can be treated as scrap. [Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Bharat Iron and Brass Foundries, (1971) 28 STC 455 (Guj)].*

*Note — It appears as if there was no provision or notification under The Gujarat Sales Tax Act specifically taxing "old, discarded, obsolete and unserviceable machinery."

Tin Drums & Drum made of Iron

Drums and Tins made of iron are not covered in "wares made of any metal or alloy other than brass or aluminium or gold or silver" because in Hindi version of the notification words "Bartan" have been used for the English word "wares". Therefore only those articles would fall in this notification as are called "Utensils". Since Drums and Tins made of iron are not called utensils, they are not covered under this entry. [Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Agrawal Tin Supply Company, 1976 UPTC 583: (1977) 39 STC 172 (All) on 23.7.1976 by the Division Bench of the Hon'ble Allahabad High Court]

Machinery totally unserviceable purchased for melting and recasting — Whether it is taxable as iron and steel scrap?

According to Webster's Dictionary, "Scrap" is (1) "a small piece; a little bit; a fragment; as scrap of metal; (2) discarded metal in the form of machinery, auto parts, etc., suitable only for reprocessing."

It is evident from these dictionary meanings that broken parts or fragments of a machinery would undoubtedly be considered as "Scrap".

Speaking of the facts of the case, the old machinery and spare parts on which the assessee is found to have paid tax, at the time if their purchase has actually been put to use as metal and not as machinery because it is an admitted position that they have been melted and recast. Under the circumstances even applying common parlance test, machinery which is totally unserviceable can be treated as scrap. [Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Bharat Iron and Brass Foundries, (1971) 28, STC 455 (Guj)].*

*Note — It appears as if there was no provision or Notification under The Gujarat Sales Tax Act specifically taxing "old, discarded, obsolete and unserviceable machinery."

German Silver Rods

The word "scrap" has not been defined in the notification but as commonly understood, it refers to used and discarded material, which is not fit for use for the purpose for which it was made. Hindi version of the words "Scrap meant for melting and sheets containing circles meant for making brasswares and containing only, any or all of the said metals viz. copper, tin, nickel and Zinc" is "Pighlaye jane ke liye dhatu ka raddi mal jismen aisi gol katrane (circles) bhee hain jinka upyog pital ke bartan banane ke liye kiya jata hai…" German Silver Rods do not answer the description of 'raddi mal' as they cannot be said to old and discarded material and it is not the assessee's case that they were unfit for the purpose for which they were made. Further it is only such scrap, which is meant for melting that falls within the purview of this notification. There is no finding that german silver rods were meant for melting. They are not the circles, as the circle that are contemplated by the notification are cut material meant for melting, and not solid rods manufactured by the assessee. Thus the german silver rods sold by the assessee would not fall within the term 'scrap' under the notification under consideration.

It cannot be decided whether or not they fall in the category of alloys containing any of the metals "copper, tin, Zinc or nickel only" because the Tribunal has not addressed itself to this question. [Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Hastkala Pital Udyog Sahkari Samiti, Varanasi, 1979 UPTC 1065, decided on 26.2.1979 by Allahabad High Court].

they are neither by-products of the final product nor subsidiary product. To be dutiable, waste and scrap must arise regularly and continuously produced in the course of manufacturing business of the product manufactured by the assessee. Goods are not excisable merely because of their specification in a particular tariff entry. Goods are not excisable unless they are manufactured in India. Repairing is not 'manufacture' - Grasim Industries v. UOI (2011) 273 ELT 10 (SC). [Waste generated during manufacture of spare parts is excisable - UOI v. Grasim Industries (2008) 229 ELT 328 (Raj HC DB) - reversing Grasim Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (203) ELT 603 (CESTAT SMB) - followed in Birla Corporation Ltd. v. CCE (2011) 266 ELT 275 (CESTAT). The decision has now been reversed by SC]

Waste arising during process which is not manufacture is not dutiable - In Rail Coach Factory v. CCE (2009) 236 ELT 160 (CESTAT), waste was generated during cutting/slitting of HR/CR coils. It was held that this process is not 'manufacture'. Hence, waste arising during such process (which is not manufacture) may not be dutiable (prima facie view at the time of stay).

Waste arising out of remnants, old material, building material is not dutiable - In Hindalco Industries v. CCE 2002(144) ELT 339 = 101 ECR 357 (CEGAT), it was held that only waste and scrap arising from manufacture or mechanical working of iron or steel is liable to duty. Metal scrap arising from dismantling of buildings, old machine parts, remnants of duty paid steel used in plant, discarded packing material, old electrical parts etc. are not dutiable - followed in Kumbhi Kasari SSK Ltd. v. CCE 2004 (173) ELT 61 (CESTAT) - same view in Deepak Fertilisers v. CCE 2004 (174) ELT 468 (CESTAT) * Zuari Cement v. CCE 2007 (210) ELT 219 (CESTAT) * Panasonic Carbon India v. CCE (2007) 213 ELT 391 (CESTAT).

Waste material (MS scrap) of building construction is not dutiable as it did not arise from manufacturing process - UOI v. Banswara Syntex (2008) 221 ELT 360 (Raj HC DB) - confirming Banswara Syntex v. CCE (2006) 203 ELT 51 (CESTAT).

Steel rolls used in rolling mills which have outlived their utility and are worn out are not 'manufacture' and not dutiable - Steel Authority of India v. CCE (2007) 211 ELT 564 (CESTAT SMB)

In Steel Authority of India v. CCE 2006 (201) ELT 580 (CESTAT), conveyor belts installed in steel mills were removed when worn out and sold. It was held that this is not 'manufacture' and no duty is payable.

Waste Oil remaining after manufacture - In Vikrant Tyres v. CCE (2004) 171 ELT 23 (CESTAT), it was held that waste oil does not emerge from process of manufacture and hence is not dutiable.

Scrap arising during construction activity is not dutiable - Scrap arising during construction activity (which is separate from manufacturing) is not liable to excise duty - Rashtriya Ispat Nigam v. CCE (2005) 2 STT 117 = 184 ELT 57 (CESTAT) * Apollo Tyres v. CCE 2005 (185) ELT 183 (CESTAT).

Waste and scrap arising in ancillary process is not dutiable

3.3-2 In UOI v. Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd. 2003 AIR SCW 5529 = 134 STC 24 = 158 ELT 3 (SC), it has been held that waste arising in ancillary process is not 'manufacture'. In this case, coal was used as a fuel to produce steam. The steam was used in manufacturing process. After coal was burnt, 'cinder' was left.

In National Fertilizer v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 56 (CEGAT), 'gauzes' were used in manufacture as catalyst. After continuous use, they became 'saturated gauzes' and hence ineffective. These were cleared for refining and re-fabrication. It was held that the process is not 'manufacture' even if mentioned in tariff. It was observed that gauze remains gauze after use. If department's contention is accepted, every machine used in the manufacture, which is scrapped after prolonged use, must suffer duty as waste and scrap of metal - Departmental civil appeal dismissed by SC - 173 ELT A190.

WASTE AND SCRAP - EXPLANATION (b) TO SECTION 206C

1065. Navine Fluorine International Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2011] 45 SOT 86/139 TTJ 248/10 taxmann.com 78 (Ahd.)

The words 'waste and scrap' are as one item. Thereafter, the word used is 'from' the manufacture or mechanical working of material. It would mean that the waste and scrap being one item should arise from the manufacture or mechanical working of material. It is, therefore, necessary to read the words waste and scrap together which are generated out of manufacturing process of the assessee. The words 'waste and scrap' should have nexus with the manufacturing or mechanical working of material. Thereafter, the words used are 'which is' definitely not usable. The word 'is' as used in this definition of the scrap is meant for a singular item i.e., 'waste and scrap'. The words 'which is' denote singular item and, thus, the singular item would be waste and scrap. The words waste and scrap, thus, cannot be read differently.

♦♦

CIT v. Priya Blue Industries (P.) Ltd. [2016] 65 taxmann.com 206/237 Taxman 1/381 ITR 210/286 CTR 210 (Guj.)

The expression 'scrap' is defined under clause (b) to the Explanation to section 206, to mean waste and scrap from manufacture or mechanical working of materials which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. On a plain reading of the said expression, it is evident that any material which is as such would not fall within the ambit of the expression 'scrap' as envisaged under clause (b) of the Explanation to section 206C.

♦♦

Nawanshahar Co-op. Sugar Mills Ltd. v. ITO, (TDS) [2013] 32 taxmann.com 279/153 TTJ 493 (Asr.)

Molasses is not waste or scrap and cannot be used as such. Thus, it does not fall within the meaning of scrap as defined in Explanation (b) to section 206C.

♦♦

Bharti Auto Products v. CIT [2013] 37 taxmann.com 37/145 ITD 1/157 TTJ 1/27 ITR (Trib.) 611 (Rajkot) (SB)

The definition of 'scrap' as given in Explanation (b) is not limited to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone but extends to cover 'waste' also. Therefore, the scope of the term 'scrap' as defined in Explanation (b) cannot be interpreted so as to restrict its application to scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials alone.

Turning Boring Scrap of Alloy Aluminium

Alloy Aluminium scrap turning and boring is taxable under the entry "All kinds of metals and scraps and alloy including sheets and circles used in the manufacture of brasswares, except those included in any other entry or any other notification issued under the Act." [Agarwal Disposal and Metal Works, Kanpur decided on 17.9.1984 u/s. 35 by Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P., Lucknow]

appear to be very convincing].

In Wimco Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 230 ELT 106 (CESTAT), assessee purchased paper and paperboard for manufacture of printed paperboard box for matches. During process, waste and scrap of paper and paperboard arises. It was held that such waste is not an intermediate product of any excisable goods. Assessee has no intention to manufacture such scrap. Waste paper arising during manufacture of matches is not excisable. Waste paper during manufacture of cigarettes is not 'manufactured' product - In International Tobacco Ltd. v. CCE (2004) 165 ELT 314 (CESTAT), it was held that scrap paper generated during manufacture of cigarettes it not result of manufacturing process - quoted and stay granted in International Tobacco Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 292 ELT 97 (CESTAT). - same view in ITC Ltd. v. CCE (2016) 341 ELT 417 (CESTAT).

Waste of black carbon during manufacture of electrodes - Waste of black carbon during manufacture of electrodes is not 'goods' even if it fetches some value. It is not necessary to enter those goods in Daily Stock Account but the time of its sale. Application for remission of duty is also not required - Eveready Industries v. CCE (2014) 307 ELT 556 (CESTAT).

Waste and scrap not goods if not marketable

3.2-1 Carbide sludge arising in manufacture of acetylene gas is not marketable and hence not liable to duty - CCE v. Bansal Indus. Gases 2003(151) ELT 4 (SC 3 member bench). Spent Nickel Catalyst arising during manufacture of soap is not an excisable commodity as department failed to prove that it is a marketable commodity. - CCE v. Hindustan Lever 2003(151) ELT 10 (SC).

In CCE v. MRF Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 595 (CEGAT - 3 member bench), it was held that rubber scrap obtained by cutting defective rubber tubes are not 'goods'.

Calcium carbide slag is waste and not marketable. It is not excisable goods - CCE v. DCW Ltd. (2008) 222 ELT 79 (CESTAT).

Just because assessee has found some use of waste, it does not mean that the waste is marketable, if it has no specific composition or identity - Gujarat State Fertilisers v. CCE (2009) 234 ELT 532 (CESTAT).

In UP State Sugar Corpn v. CCE 2000(119) ELT 74 (CEGAT), it was held that press-mud arising during manufacture of sugar is only a residual waste. It is not marketable and is not excisable. - view upheld in CCE v. Titawi Sugar Complex 2003(152) ELT 21 (SC)- - - followed in CCE v. Cheyyar Coop Sugar Mills (2009) 240 ELT 417 (CESTAT SMB) accepted by department - CBEC circular No. 730/46/2003-CX dated 31-7-2003 [However, in another matter, departmental appeal has been admitted - 199 ELT A70].

In CCE v. Tony Electronics 2000(119) ELT 139 (CEGAT), it was held that waste and scrap in the course of manufacture of audio/video magnetic tape is not marketable and hence not excisable.

Waste like floor sweeping, processed defective cakes etc. are not marketable.- CCE v. Delta Foods (2011) 30 STT 121 (CESTAT SMB) * Delta Foods v. CCE (2012) 277 ELT 352 (CESTAT) (Hence rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules is not applicable as payment of 'amount' is not required)

Stray or distress sale does not mean goods are 'marketable'.

3.2-2 Stray or distress sale does not prove marketability

Stray sale does not mean goods are marketable - If the product is generally not sold, stray sales do not mean that the product is marketable - Gujarat State Fertilizers v. CCE - (1996) 84 ELT 539 (CEGAT) - correct decision as 'one swallow does not make a summer'.

In CCE v. Ranger Breweries Ltd. 2000(122) ELT 447 = 39 RLT 1065 (CEGAT), it was observed that stray incidents of sale does not give characteristics of marketability to the goods - same view in CCE v. Karnataka Vidyuth Karkhane (2009) 239 ELT 165 (CESTAT).

Distress sale does not mean goods are marketable - In Britannia Industries Ltd. v. CCE 1997(93) ELT 719 (CEGAT), it was held that waste cannot be treated as excisable goods merely because it is capable of fetching some sale price, if such sale is distress sale and sale price is determined at the whims of the buyers as there is no ready market for regular sale.

Rejected, Defectives, Cuttings and End Pieces of Iron Sheet – Whether they fall within 'Iron Scraps"?

On a perusal of Photo and Sample of the goods, it is evident that the goods referred by the applicant are not iron scrap, they are defective pieces and cuttings of iron sheet. These are not useless or old broken items. The defectives, rejected and end pieces obtained during manufacture cannot be categorized as scrap. Sellers have also described them in the bills as "rejected CR or HR sheet". They can be used as new sheet as well. Hence these items do not fall within iron scrap mentioned in clause (i) of Section 14(iv) of the Central Sales Tax Act, but they fall within clause (xvi) of Section 14(iv) of the Central Sales Tax Act. Hence they are not exempted from the payment of entry tax. [M/s Pawan Enterprises, 77/2 Halsi Road, Kanpur, Application No. 045/14 decided on 05.01.2015 by the Commissioner, Commercial Tax, U.P., Lucknow under Section 59 of the U.P. Value Added Tax Act, 2008, reported in 2015 (Vol. 27) VLJ (Commissioner Decisions) 73; 2015 NTN (Vol.-57)-26 (Commissioner Decision's); 2015 (63) STJ 167]

WHETHER ASSESSEE WAS ENTITLED TO DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH IN

WHETHER ASSESSEE COULD ALSO CLAIM DEDUCTION UNDER SECTION 80HH IN RESPECT OF PROFITS DERIVED FROM SALE OF DRUMS, USED FOR STORING

as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking. While giving the relief under section 80HH, value of closing stock of scrap would also have to be included. The sale proceeds of drums used for storing water and which had become useless could not, however, be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manufactur-ing activity in which the assessee was involved. This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and it is in the course of the manufacturing activity that waste material, viz., scrap metal was obtained. We hold that the assessee is entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking, as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking. The value of the scrap was shown at Rs. 75,665 and the value of the closing stock of scrap was shown as Rs. 1,581. In all, the value of the scrap comes to Rs. 77,246 and on the basis of working of the assessee, relief under section 80HH would have to be given at the prescribed percentage including this amount.

The balance of Rs. 16,702 was shown as sale proceeds of drums. According to the learned counsel appearing for the assessee, section 80HH applies even to sale proceeds of the drums. The sale proceeds of the drums used for storing water and which had become useless, cannot be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manfac-turing activity in which the assessee was involved. The surplus is also of the nature falling under section 41(2). Therefore, the assessee is not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to Rs. 16,702 under section 80HH.

19. Appeal is allowed in part.

Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

Further, the particular receipt under consideration is, insofar as scrap was concerned, realisation from the sale of waste material from manufacturing activity of the assessee-company and it was not a receipt from the sale of some of its old machinery, plant or building resulting in balancing charge as contemplated under section 41(2) . Therefore, section 41( 2) also had no application to the facts of the instant case as far as scrap was concerned. The section could be attracted insofar as the sale price of drums was concerned.

In fact, the assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains from newly established industrial undertaking as contemplated under section 80HH in relation to profits from sale of scrap since this scrap, being a waste product which had a commercial value, was directly derived from the industrial undertaking which the assessee was carrying on and was sold in the normal course of running the industrial undertaking.

While giving the relief under section 80HH, value of closing stock of scrap would also have to be included. The sale proceeds of drums used for storing water and which had become useless could not, however, be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manufactur-ing activity in which the assessee was involved. This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.

8. The assessee is a domestic company in which the public are not substantially interested. Its main activity was manufacture and sale of super-enamelled aluminium, copper wire and DPC wires. The assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 46,393 under section 80HH, being 20 per cent of Rs. 2,31,963 in the revised return filed. This deduction was claimed as allowable on the profits and gains derived from the industrial under- taking. According to the ITO, it was seen from the profit and loss account that the profits and gains include a sum of Rs. 93,948 (Rs. 92,367—sale of scrap and drums, and Rs. 1,581—value of scrap at close), which, according to the ITO, cannot be said to have been derived from the industrial undertaking. The ITO, in arriving at this conclusion, drew support from the decision of the Supreme Court in Cambay Electric Supply Industrial Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1978] 113 ITR 84 and the decision in the case of CIT v. Cochin Refineries Ltd. [1982] 135 ITR 278 (Ker.). Accordingly, he came to the conclusion that the sum of Rs. 28,410 alone is allowable as deduc-tion on the profits and gains of Rs. 1,47,051 being 20 per cent thereof.

9. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), considering the nature of the business carried on by the assessee, came to the conclusion that the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Cambay Electric Supply Industrial Co. Ltd. (supra) and that of the Kerala High Court in the case of Cochin Refineries Ltd. ( supra), will not stand in the way in arriving at the conclusion that the scrap metal is a direct offshoot of the manufactur-ing, activity of the assessee and, eventually, it cannot be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product is derived. Accordingly, he held as under:

"I am, therefore, of the considered opinion that in the appellant's case, the realisations from the waste material like scrap metal and empty drums, etc., will have to be construed as income derived from the industrial under- taking and the Income-tax Officer is, accordingly, directed to take that also into account for the purpose of allowing relief under section 80HH. In passing, however, I may mention that in any event, the Income-tax Officer is certainly not right in excluding the entire sale proceeds from the purview of relief under section 80HH as if it represented net profits. The point for consideration in this appeal is whether the assessee is entitled to relief under section 80HH on profits attributable to sale value of scrap and drums. According to section 80HH, where the gross total income of an assessee includes any profits or gains 'derived from' an industrial undertaking, or the business of a hotel, to which the section applies, there shall, in accordance with and subject to the provisions of the section, be allowed, in computing the total income of the assessee, a deduction from such profits and gains of an amount equal to 20 per cent thereof. The assessee-company was manufacturing super- enamelled aluminium, copper wires and DPC wires in respect of which the turnover of Rs. 56.68 lakhs was accounted and under miscellaneous receipts was registered sale of scrap of Rs. 75,665 and drums of Rs. 16,702, aggregating to Rs. 92,367. The value of stock of scrap was Rs. 1,581. According to the learned counsel appearing for the assessee, the main activity of the assessee being manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires, it is in the course of the manufacturing activity that scrap metal was obtained. The scrap metal, he stated, is the direct outcome from the materials used in the manufacture of different varieties of metallic wires. Therefore, this amounts, if nothing else, to a by-product of the main product manufactured. Therefore, the scrap metals being directly derived from the industrial undertaking which was earned on by the assessee, profit derived from the sale therefrom would qualify for relief under section 80HH. Adverting to the drums, it was stated they were purchased for storing water and were sold when they became useless.

12. There is the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Cambay Electric Supply Industrial Co. Ltd. (supra ). In the said judgment, there was an observation to the effect that the expression 'attributable to' occurring in section 80E of the Act is certainly wider in import than the expression ‘derived from’. It was also pointed out therein that had the expression ‘derived from’ been used, it could have, with some force, been contended that a balancing charge arising from the sale of old machinery and build-ings cannot be regarded as profits and gains derived from the conduct of the business of generation and distribution of electricity. Taking a clue from the abovesaid observation, the learned departmental representative pointed out that inasmuch as the words 'derived from' are used in section 80HH, it will mean only direct receipts from a business of specified nature but does not include receipts which have no direct link with the business. Accord-ingly, the expression 'derived from', as occurring in section 80HH, will have a restricted meaning, whereby profit from the sale proceeds of the scrap metal obtained by the assessee in manufacturing various metallic wires cannot be considered as 'derived from' the manufacturing activity of the assessee.

13. The learned departmental representative also drew support from the decision of the Kerala High Court in Cochin Refineries Ltd.'s case (supra), wherein the Kerala High Court followed the decision of the Supreme Court in Cambay Electric Supply Industrial Co. Ltd.'s case (supra). In Cochin Refineries Ltd.'s case (supra), the Kerala High Court held as under:

". . . the words 'derived from' in section 80J of the Act cannot have a wide import so as to include any income which can in some manner be attributed to the business. The derivation of the income must be directly connected with the business in the sense that the income is generated by the business. It would not be sufficient if it is generated by the exploita- tion of a business asset. . . ." (p. 279)

4.2-5 Clearance of waste by service provider

Following provisions will apply to a service provider, who is not a 'manufacturer' -

Inputs becoming waste while providing output service - If some inputs become waste while providing output services, they are 'used in provision of output services'. In such case, no 'amount' or 'duty' is payable when he sells them as scrap, as it cannot be said that he has 'manufactured' them.

Input becoming waste/scrap before putting to use - If the inputs become waste even before taking them out of stores, an 'amount' equal to Cenvat taken will be payable. The reason is that in such case, it cannot be said that the inputs were used 'for providing output services'.

Sale of empty packing material - A service provider availing Cenvat on inputs is not required to pay any 'amount' on packing material/empty drums sold by him, even if he had availed Cenvat on such inputs.

Sale of goods on which no Cenvat was availed - A service provider is not required to pay any 'amount' if he sells/disposes of inputs or goods on which he has not availed Cenvat credit.

Scrap — Whether it covers the defective items?

Defective does not mean scrap. Defective G.I. Sheets and the rejected items (steel wires, for example) do not fall under iron scrap. The mere fact that something is defective would not convert them into scrape. Scrapes, in common parlance, contemplate old and broken articles, not fit for use as such item. [Banaras Iron Scrap Merchants Association v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1978 UPTC 632].

The term "scrap", according to dictionary meaning, means 'waste'. 'Anything discarded', 'worn out', 'dead' or 'useless'. In commercial or popular sense also scrap appears to be understood in the sense of waste or the thing being of no use. It cannot be equated with 'defectives, rejects, cuttings or end pieces' mentioned in clause (xvi) of Section 14. These expressions have their own connotation in business circle. For instance defectives or rejects would normally be those goods which for some reason did not come upto standard or specification but were otherwise all right. The argument is therefore not acceptable that tin scrap is covered in clause (xvi). [Cheap Hardware Store v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1982 UPTC 201, decided on 24.12.1981 by Allahabad High Court].

This Court in a case concerning the same assessee in Pandian Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 254 ITR 562, had held, inter alia, that scrap not being a necessary by product in the process of manufacturer, the income from the sale of scrap could not be regarded as income derived from the industrial undertaking.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the income from the sale of scrap was not relatable to the industrial activities of the assessee for the purpose of section 80HH.

HELD: Scrap--Drums (Empty) of calcium carbide are not "goods" cleared in terms of Rule 57F(2) CER, but "scrap" arising in preparatory stage, of manufacturing process in terms of Rule 57F(4) and duty can be demanded at the rate applicable to scrap (i.e. drums as such in the form they are cleared).

"After the Modvat credit was taken, the status of the goods changed and instead of the goods being considered as duty paid goods these became goods as if these are the manufacture of the appellants' factory. But there is no controversy that what was removed from the appellants' factory were not the goods as these were brought in i.e. Calcium Carbide filled in the drums but only empty drums. The empty drums, therefore, cleared from the appellants' factory cannot be taken to be goods cleared as such in terms of Rule 57F(2) from the appellants' factory. However, we observe that the Calcium Carbide drums for the purpose of taking the Calcium Carbide into use had to be opened and the remaining empty drums can be taken to be scrap which arose in the preparatory stages of the manufacturing process. In that view of the matter we hold that the drums can be considered as scrap in terms of Rule 57F(4) and duty on the same can be demanded under the Tariff Heading and the rate applicable to the scrap as such i.e. the rate applicable to the drums as such in the form these are cleared."

Clearance of waste by service provider

28.6-2 Following provisions will apply to a service provider, who is not a 'manufacturer'-

Inputs becoming waste while providing output service - If some inputs become waste while providing output services, they are 'used in provision of output services'. In such case, no 'amount' or 'duty' is payable when he sells them as scrap, as it cannot be said that he has 'manufactured' them.

Input becoming waste/scrap before putting to use - If the inputs become waste even before taking them out of stores, an 'amount' equal to Cenvat taken will be payable. The reason is that in such case, it cannot be said that the inputs were used 'for providing output services'.

Sale of empty packing material - A service provider availing Cenvat on inputs is not required to pay any 'amount' on packing material/empty drums sold by him, even if he had availed Cenvat on such inputs.

Sale of goods on which no Cenvat was availed - A service provider is not required to pay any 'amount' if he sells/disposes of inputs or goods on which he has not availed Cenvat credit.

Coaches (Condemned) sold by the Railways in auction

The condemned coaches are sold by the Railways on the condition that wheel sets, non-ferrous or stainless steel metal and other goods, as are indicated by the Railways, shall have to be returned by the purchaser to the Railways, and to separate these goods, the purchaser has to dismantle the goods sold in auction in the Railway premises itself. So long as these goods are not returned to the Railways, the purchaser cannot take away the goods obtained as a result of dismantling. Therefore, it is clear that the property in goods (of the goods sold in auction) does not pass to the purchaser so long as the goods returnable to the railways are not returned to them. It is clear that only the goods remaining at the end of dismantling are auctioned, and it will, therefore, be proper to hold that the goods auctioned fall in the category of Iron scrap. Since the work of dismantling is done by the purchaser on behalf of the Railways, therefore, the purchaser cannot be said to be the manufacturer. Scrap Waste Product

The contention of the applicant is that the copper and iron scrap obtained in the process of manufacture of electrical stampings and ceiling fans is waste product which is approximately 52 per cent of the raw material. Their further contention is that the scrap under consideration, being waste products, its sale is exempted in their hands because they are new units and sale of waste product by the new unit is also exempted from tax, as per Circular No. New Unit – 29 dated 24.4.1992 issued by the Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P., Lucknow.

The contention of the Counsel for the applicant is devoid of force that the copper and iron scrap obtained in the process of manufacture of electrical stampings and ceiling fan is waste product, because according to the Oxford Dictionary, "scrap" means the useless bye product of the manufacturer. Scrap is waste material but not the waste product. Scrap is the commodity from which goods may be manufactured after reprocessing it, but waste product cannot be used in remanufacture. Since the scrap is not waste product, it is not exempted from tax. [Khaitan Fans (India) Ltd., NOIDA, decided on 7.1.1994, u/s. 35 by Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P., Lucknow]

After it emptied the contents of these drums which are taken up for manufacturer, the appellant sold these drums without payment of duty to three/four buyers. The notice placed reliance on the provisions of sub-rule(4) of Rule 57F apparently because the appellant took Modvat credit of the duty paid on the oil and other contents of the drums. After considering the cause shown and hearing the assessee the Commissioner has confirmed the demand and imposed penalty equal to the duty. Hence this appeal.

2. Advocate for the appellant puts forth the following contentions. The appellant cannot be considered to have manufactured anything in emptying the drums. Merely emptying drums does not amount to a process of manufacture. The drums leave the factory in the same shape and condition in which they were received except for possible changes to them which have taken place in the course of transport and handling. Even if there is held to be manufacture what resulted was not scrap within the meaning of the term occurring in Note 6(a) to Section XVI of the Tariff. He agrees that there is a decision of the Tribunal in West Cost Industrial Gases Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (83) ELT 358 which concluded that empty drums cleared from the factory after removing calcium carbide which they contained are to be taken as scrap which arise in the preparatory stages of the manufacturing process. He however refers to the later decision of the Tribunal in CC v. Im Kemex India Ltd. - 1996 (86) ELT 95. He relies upon a Supreme Court decision in Khandelwal Engineering Works - 1985 (20) ELT 222, and the decision of the Tribunal in I.O.L. Ltd. v. CCE 1993 (68) ELT 624 saying that drums and barrels cannot be considered to be waste arising out of processing of inputs and a Circular letter No. 22/39/86, dated 5-9-1986 of the Board saying that no duty was payable on such drums.

3. The departmental representative contends that the Commissioner has indicated how the processing of the inputs amounts to manufacture and relies on the decision in West Coast Industrial Gases Ltd. v. CCE.

4. Reference to Rule 57F(4) does not seem very relevant to us. This rule provides in Clause (2)for the nature of utilisation of credit. The departmental representative contends rightly, in our view that even when Modvat credit is not taken if product is held to be the result of manufacture, duty liable to be paid on such waste unless it is exempted. For this to take place, two conditions have to be satisfied. The first is that there has been a process of manufacture and the second is that what emerges is scrap.

5. There is no case when the appellant empties the barrels of their contents and then disposes them of because of the facts they cease to be barrels have been used once, would not fetch the same value as before. The Commissioner himself does not say that is manufacture. He says that the goods have been processed. It cannot be said that emptying the drums, a new commercially different product with a different name and number has emerged. The appellant therefore has not manufactured anything by emptying drums. The Tribunal in West Coast Industrial Gases Ltd. v. CCE has held that drums which were emptied of calcium carbide which they contained must be considered to be scrap which arises in the preparatory stage of manufacturing process. No reasoning has been given to justify this conclusion. Apart from this, the issue before the Tribunal was not one of manufacture. The issue was whether that portion of the credit which was contained in the drums (by reason of the value of drums being added to the value of the inputs) should be reversed for the reason that the drums were not used for the manufacturing process. Computation of Section 80HHC deduction

The deduction under section 80HHC, subject to several other conditions, incorporated in the section, is determined as under: Thus, if the total turnover increases, the advantage which the assessee would get under section 80HHC would decrease because the amount deductible substantially depends upon the ratio between the export turnover and total turnover. If the export turnover is higher, comparatively the amount deductible under section 80HHC would be more; or in other words, if compared to total turnover, export turnover is less the amount deductible from the income under section 80HHC would be reduced. [Para 10]

Meaning of the term 'turnover'

The term 'turnover' had neither been defined in the Act nor has been explained by any of the CBDT circulars. [Para 17]

In the aforesaid circumstances, one has to look at the meaning of the term 'turnover' in ordinary accounting or commercial parlance. [Para 18]

Normally, the term 'turnover' would show the sale effected by a business unit. It may happen that in the course of the business, in addition to the normal sales, the business unit may also sell some other things. [Para 19]

In ordinary accounting parlance, as approved by all accountants and auditors, the term 'sales', when reflected in the profit and loss account, would indicate sale proceeds from sale of the articles or things in which the business unit is dealing. When some other things like old furniture or a capital asset, in which the business unit is not dealing are sold, the sale proceeds therefrom would not be included in 'sales' but it would be shown separately. [Para 20]

In simple words, the word 'turnover' would mean only the amount of sale proceeds received in respect of the goods in which an assessee is dealing in. [Para 21]

So far as the scrap is concerned, the sale proceeds from the scrap may either be shown separately in the profit and loss account or may be deducted from the amount spent by the manufacturing unit on the raw material, which is steel in the case of the respondent-assessee, as the respondent-assessee is using stainless steel as raw material, from which utensils are manufactured. The raw material, which is not capable of being used for manufacturing utensils will have to be either sold as scrap or might have to be re-cycled in the form of sheets of stainless steel, if the manufacturing unit is also having its re-rolling plant. If it is not having such a plant, the manufacturer would dispose of the scrap of steel to someone who would re-cycle the said scrap into steel so that the said steel can be re-used. [Para 22]

When such scrap is sold, the sale proceeds of the scrap cannot be included in the term 'turnover' for the reason that the respondent-unit is engaged primarily in the manufacturing and selling of steel utensils and not scrap of steel. Therefore, the proceeds of such scrap would not be included in 'sales' in the Profit and Loss Account of the respondent-assessee. [Para 23]

The situation would be different in the case of the buyer, who purchases scrap from the respondent-assessee and sells it to someone else. The sale proceeds for such a buyer would be treated as 'turnover' for a simple reason that the buyer of the scrap is a person who is primarily dealing in scrap. In the case on hand, as the respondent-assessee is not primarily dealing in scrap but is a manufacturer of stainless steel utensils, only sale proceeds from sale of utensils would be treated as his 'turnover'. [Para 24]

The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India ('ICAI') has published some material under the head 'Guidance Note on Tax Audit under section 44AB'. The said material has been published so as to guide the members of the ICAI. In our opinion, when a recognized body of Accountants, after due deliberation and consideration publishes certain material for its members, one can rely upon the same. Para 5 of the said Note deals with 'Sales', 'turnover' and 'gross receipts'. The meaning given by the ICAI clearly denotes that in normal accounting parlance the word 'turnover' would mean 'total sales' as explained hereinabove. The said sales would definitely not include the scrap material which is either to be deducted from the cost of raw material or is to be shown separately under a different head. There is no reason for not accepting the meaning of the term 'turnover' given by a body of Accountants, which is having a statutory recognition. [Para 25]

If all accountants, auditors, businessmen, manufacturers etc. are normally interpreting the term 'turnover' as sale proceeds of the commodity in which the business unit is dealing, there is no reason to take a different view than the view normally taken by the persons who are concerned with the said term. [Para 26]
