Scrap, as defined in the explanation to the section only talks about the waste and scrap from the manufacturing or mechanical working. This definition of 'scrap' provides waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials which is definitely not usable shall be treated as scrap. Even the assessee himself had paid TCS in terms of section 206C for the purchase of goods under consideration, it is viewed that the nature of goods shall remain the same i.e scrape and purchase of goods by the assessee shall not change its character . Further the definition of scrap if read in conjunction with sub-section (1A) of section 206C, it clearly suggests that the scrap is only indicative of nature of goods and it is not indicative of the person from whom the TCS is required to be collected. The definition of scrap in view of the Bench, does not suggest that the scrap should be generated by the seller himself. The only condition of the scrap is that the scrap should be waste and scrap from the manufacturing or mechanical working of material, which is definitely not usable as such on account of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. Thus, the provisions of section 206C are applicable to the instant case as the assessee is a trader and dealing in the scrap generated from the mechanical working of the material (breaking of the ship). Further it is not necessary that such mechanical working (breaking of the ship) should be carried out by the assessee himself. The assessee is, therefore, liable to deduct tax at source under section 206C on the sale of scrap. In fact, the admission of the assessee is the best evidence to admit the liability. The assessee himself has admitted that the assessee is dealing in the scrap generated from the breaking of the ship and had purchased the scarp. The contention of the assessee that since the iron scrap like steel, ingots, iron etc. is being used by the industries without any change, is not correct as the nature of goods shall remain same, therefore, it comes under the definition of the scrap. The material sold by the assessee cannot be used as such without any modification by the buyer of the said scrap. As the said material/goods come from the breaking of the ship, these goods were sold to the manufacturer/rerolling mills, as scrap therefore, the goods (scrap) sold by the assessee were not usable as such and therefore, the assessee was required to deduct TCS from the buyer. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Section 2, read with First Schedule, of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 and section 2 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 - Classification - Aluminium dross and skimmings - Tariff Item 2620 4010 specially deals with aluminium dross and Tariff Item 2620 4090 deals with other slag, ash or residues containing mainly aluminium - Hence, aluminium dross, skimmings are clearly specified in Central Excise Tariff - Customs Tariff also includes aluminium dross and skimmings under Tariff sub-heading 2620 40 [Paras 6.1 to 6.3] [In favour of revenue]Central Excise : Aluminium dross and skimmings and similar non-ferrous metal dross and skimmings which arise as a by-product in process of manufacture of aluminium/non-ferrous metal products are manufactured goods and hence excisable with effect from 10-5-2008 in view of explanation added to section 2(d)

Section 2(d), read with section 3, of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 2 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 and section 2 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 - Excisable Goods - Marketability - Customs Tariff is based on Harmonized System of Nomenclature and an entry (heading/sub-heading) is created specifically for a product only when commodity is bought and sold on a regular basis on a substantial scale - This would imply that 'aluminium dross and skimmings' listed in tariff are marketable commodities [Para 6.3] [In favour of revenue]

Section 2(f), read with sections 2(d) and 3, of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Manufacture - General Meaning - Tariff recognises waste and scrap as a distinct and different commodity and seeks to impose a tax on waste and scrap either when it is traded (Customs duty) or when it is manufactured, by way of excise duty - Purpose and object of creating a tariff entry for waste and scrap including 'dross and skimmings' is to make the product liable to tax/duty - Therefore, a specific entry created for purpose of levy of duty/tax cannot be merely wished away or brushed aside, by holding that waste and scrap are not manufactured goods - When dross and skimmings are specifically mentioned in tariff, it would not be unreasonable to assume that such products are manufacture goods even though they arise in course of manufacture of other products - Since they are capable of being bought and sold for a consideration, they are marketable and liable to excise duty - Hence, aluminium dross and skimmings and similar non-ferrous metal dross and skimmings which arise as a by-product in process of manufacture of aluminium/non-ferrous metal products are manufactured goods and hence excisable with effect from 10-05-2008 in view of explanation added to section 2(d) [Paras 6.4 to 8] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: Facts

The assessee is a manufacturer of aluminium sheets and coils falling under CETH 7607 1190 of the Central Excise Tariff using major raw material 'aluminium ingots'.

In the course of manufacture of aluminium sheets/coils, aluminium dross/skimmings emerge as byproducts.

The assessee sells these byproducts on a regular basis.

The department raised demand of duty on 'aluminium dross/skimmings' on ground that it is a manufactured product and liable to excise duty in view of Explanation to section 2(d) to Central Excise Act, 1944.

Assessee's Arguments

Dross skimmings are not manufactured goods.

Explanation was inserted in section 2(d) in order to clarify that the goods which can be bought and sold in the market are deemed to be. The explanation deals with only with the marketability aspect of the question and does not say that even non-manufactured goods are deemed to be manufactured goods.

Revenue's Arguments

Explanation to section 2(d) creates a legal fiction by which any goods which are capable of being bought and sold for a consideration shall be deemed to be marketable and on this basis it was held that aluminium dross and skimmings are liable to duty of excise.

When a product emerges as a by-product in the course of manufacture of some other product, that by-product cannot be treated as a waste just because it is an unintended product arising in the course of manufacture of an intended final product. The by-product would be waste only if it is of no value or negligible value, something which the manufacturer would want to get rid of.

HEADNOTE: Section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction - Exporter (Computation of deduction) - Assessment year 1999-2000 - Assessee's partnership firm was engaged in making bicycle parts for export - Assessee claimed deduction under section 80HHC - While computing deduction, Assessing Officer excluded amount of sale of scrap from 'total turnover' and proportionate profit on sale of scrap from 'profit of business' - Whether Apex court in case of CIT v. Punjab Stainless Steel Industries [2014] 364 ITR 144/46 taxmann.com 68/[2015] 229 Taxman 423, had finally cleared this issue that proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover' for purpose of computation for deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes - Whether in view of same, question regarding inclusion of sale of scrap in total turnover was required to be examined afresh by Assessing Officer in factual matrix of case; thus, matter to be remanded to Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [Partly in favour of assessee/Matter remanded]IT: For purpose of computation of deduction under section 80HHC proceeds generated from sale of scrap would not be included in 'total turnover'

FACT: The assessee, partnership firm was engaged in making of bicycle parts for exports. The assessee filed its return of income declaring total income at Rs. Nil and claimed deduction under section 80HHC. A reopening notice under section 148 was issued and served upon the assessee. Thereafter, the assessee filed return of income declaring Nil income after claiming deduction under section 80HHC. The assessment was finalised by Assessing Officer under section 143(3) and deduction under section 80HHC was restricted to lesser amount as against the claim of the assessee.

While computing deduction under section 80HHC, the Assessing Officer excluded the amount of sale of scrap from the total turnover and the proportionate profit on sale of scrap from the 'profit of the business'.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) decided the issue in favour of the assessee. However, it was clarified that the sale of scrap would not be considered while computing the profits of the business.

On further appeal, the Tribunal recorded that if the sale of scrap was excluded from the purview of 'total turnover', the proportionate profit thereof should also be reduced from the 'Profit of the business' for the purpose of computing deduction under section 80HHC. Thus, the order passed by the Assessing Officer on this aspect was sustained.

On revenue's appeal to the High Court:

HELD: The issue has now been finally decided by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Punjab Stainless Steel Industries [2014] 364 ITR 144/46 taxmann.com 68/[2015] 229 Taxman 423 wherein after considering the relevant statutory provisions and the case law on the point, it was held by the Apex Court that the proceeds generated from the sale of scrap would not be included in the total turnover. It was observed that the intention behind the enactment of section 80HHC was to encourage export so as to earn more foreign exchange. It was concluded that once the Government decides to give some benefit to someone who is helping the nation in bringing foreign exchange, the revenue should also make all possible efforts to encourage such traders or manufacturers by giving such business units more benefits as contemplated under the provisions of law. [Para 6]

In view of the law laid down by the Apex Court in Punjab Stainless Steel Industries's case (supra), for the parties submitted that the question regarding inclusion of sale of scrap in the total turnover is required to be examined afresh by the Assessing Officer in the factual matrix of the case. It was urged that in such circumstances, the orders passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal be set aside and the matter be remanded to the Assessing Officer for passing fresh order after hearing assessee on this issue in accordance with law. [Para 7]

Handling of tetraethyl lead compound

.

80. (1) Tetraethyl lead compound shall not be unloaded from a ship unless—

(a)

it is packed in specially constructed steel drums of substantial construction, sealed with an inner and outer bung, and fitted with rolling roofs on to the shell as an added precaution;

(b)

all receptacles containing tetraethyl lead compound are distinctively and durably marked with the words "Tetraethyl Lead Compound Poison"; and

(c)

two sets of protective equipment comprising the following are provided and kept readily available for use in the event of any leakage of tetraethyl lead compound—

(i)

rubber gloves,

(ii)

rubber boots,

(iii)

rubber apron or oilskin suit, and

(iv)

suitable respirator, which should be either of canister type containing minimum of 50cc. of activated charcoal or an airline respirator with an independent fresh air supply.

(2) Following measures shall be taken while unloading tetraethyl lead compound:—

(a)

no receptacle containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be opened within the limits of the port;

(b)

before commencement of the unloading operations, the consignment of tetraethyl lead compound shall be inspected on board the vessel by a responsible person. No tetraethyl lead compound drums showing any sign of leakage shall be unloaded until suitably repaired or placed in a larger receptacle or container offering sufficient precautions from leakage;

(c)

drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be discharged under the supervision of a responsible person;

(d)

drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be loaded discharged in rope slings with a maximum of two drums at a separate sling for each drum. Hooks shall on no account be used;

(e)

dock workers handling drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be provided with heavy gloves of canvas or leather and shall use such gloves; and

(f)

adequate quantities of non-inflammable solvent or kerosene and soap and water to deal with any leakages of tetraethyl lead compound shall be kept readily available where the work of handling of the tetraethyl lead compound is carried on.

(3) Following measures shall be taken in the event of leakage of tetraethyl lead compound:—

(a)

the area on which the leakage of tetraethyl lead compound has occurred (including the outside of a drum) shall be treated as follows:—

(i)

flush with kerosene or some other light oil solvent followed by water. If the surface permits, wash thoroughly with soap working up as much lather as possible, and again flush with water;

(ii)

if it is possible to obtain quickly a supply of common bleaching lime (Ca O Cl2) the area should first be treated generously with a mixture of bleaching lime and water in the form of thin slurry (NEVER use the dry powder) alternatively a five per cent solution of sulphury! chloride (SO2 Cl2) in kerosene may be used;

(b)

if contamination of absorbent material such as wooden flooring, dunnage, or other packing material has taken place, then such material shall, after treatment as above, be removed from the place where tetraethyl lead compound is being handled;

(c)

any clothing which becomes contaminated by tetraethyl lead compound shall be removed immediately and cleaned by repeated rinsing in a non-inflammable dry cleaning fluid;

(d)

if tetraethyl lead compound can be smelled, dock workers not assigned to deal with the leakage of tetraethyl lead compound shall be removed from that place; and

(e)

dock workers assigned to deal with leakage of tetraethyl lead compound shall wear the protective equipment described under sub-regulation 1(c).

(4) Suitable protective clothing shall be provided for handling of tetraethyl lead compound in refrigerated spaces.

9. Procedure for Cutting permission.—

(1)

The competent authority may grant permission for cutting operations within a maximum period of two working days upon satisfactory verification of following items, namely: —

(a)

A certificate from the State Pollution Control Board that all kinds of oils, cargo residues and other loose hazardous wastes are completely removed and respective holds and tanks are decontaminated.

(b)

"Safe for entry and safe for hot work" certificate has to be issued by the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organization/PESO for cargo and slop tanks of petroleum tankers, or by any competent agency authorized by the Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH under the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948);

(c)

Inspection shall be carried out by the Safety officer of Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH or authorized person of Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH to ensure -

(i)

ignitable materials are completely removed from confined spaces that need to be certified for hot work;

(ii)

areas in engine room are practically gas free with proper venting and well within explosive limits by use of calibrated multi-gas monitoring meter. On satisfactory compliance of this inspection, Safe for entry and safe for hot work permission shall be issued for engine room;

(iii)

bunker area and those common areas of ships where there is likelihood of ignitable gases generations need to be properly ventilated and ensure that spaces are well within explosive limits by use of calibrated portable gas meters.

(2)

In case any short coming is noted then the same shall be communicated in writing within two working days to enable the recycler to re-submit the request upon necessary corrections.

10. Monitoring of worker safety and hazardous material during dismantling activity.—

(1)

Worker safety:

(a)

A Safety officer/Safety Officer as per the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948) shall be engaged by ship recycling facility.

(b)

A competent person shall be engaged for issuance and continuous monitoring of conditions based on which safe for entry and safe for hot work permits issued as per the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948).

(c)

All the equipment such as crane, winch, chain rope and shackles, generator set and any other safety equipment installed in the ship recycling facility or hired for the purpose of recycling shall be installed and maintained in accordance with the provisions of the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948) and rules made thereunder and any other relevant Acts and rules.

(d)

A safety officer/Safety Supervisor is responsible for conducting meetings prior to starting any activity, briefing the risks involved in the activity and control measures taken to minimize such risks.

(e)

A placard displaying important precautions (do's and don'ts) to be followed during ship recycling activity is installed at prominent places within the premises and that such display is made in English and other language(s) as understood by the workers involved in recycling.

(f)

A calibrated explosive gas detector, a multi gas monitor including hydrogen sulphide (H2S) gas monitor, portable gas meters and an oxygen percentage analyzer are available on the site in working condition.

(g)

Adequate lighting arrangement is made in the common areas of yard and in the spaces where activity is carried out. The SRF should conspicuously mark and maintain an emergency exit route and such route should always be free from any obstructions.

(h)

The emergency response plan drill should be conducted once in 6 months. Further, an off-site emergency plan for the whole district should be prepared and to be conducted once in a year.

(2)

Handling, storage and disposal of hazardous material:

(a)

One Safety Officer/One Safety supervisor as per section 41C(b) of the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948) shall be engaged by ship recycling facility.

(b)

Supervisor shall ensure that hazardous materials are handled, stored, transported and disposed as per the approved ship recycling plan and in accordance with local legislations.

3.2 Bagasse held non-manufactured by Supreme Court : The Circular aforesaid was challenged successfully in Balrampur Chini Mills Ltd. v. UOI [2013] 30 taxmann.com 175 (Allahabad) and CCE v. DSCL Sugar [2014] 41 taxmann.com 64/43 GST 151 (Allahabad) and also in CCE v. KCP Sugar & Industries Corporation Ltd. - 2015 (321) ELT A223 (A.P.) on ground that even though marketable, Bagasse was non-manufactured product and therefore, not excisable and even payment under rule 6 would not be required. The Department went in appeal before Supreme Court in UOI v. DSCL Sugar Ltd. 2015 (322) E.L.T. 769, wherein it was held as follows :

Facts : Assessee was manufacturing sugarcane and molasses. In the process of manufacture of sugar, sugarcane is crushed, its juice is extracted and Bagasse emerges as residue/waste of sugarcane. Since Bagasse was liable to Nil rate of duty, department argued that it was 'exempted goods' and demanded Cenvat reversal under rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Held :

No manufacture/deemed manufacture : Bagasse is only an agriculture waste and residue and not result of any process; hence, it is not covered in definition of 'manufacture' under section 2(f) of Central Excise Act, 1944. Further, there is no Chapter note or Section note in Central Excise Tariff declaring process in respect of bagasse as amounting to manufacture.

Not excisable, even if deemed to be marketable : Hence, notwithstanding amendment in 2008 in section 2(d) ibid, creating a fiction of deemed marketability, bagasse is not excisable as it is not passing test of 'manufacture'.

Cenvat Rule 6 inapplicable [for period prior to 1-3-2015] : Since bagasse is not excisable, hence, even if NIL-rated, cenvat rule 6 is inapplicable thereto. Therefore, denial of credit on electricity on ground that bagasse is excisable exempted goods, was incorrect.

3.3 Zinc Dross also held to be non-manufactured by Bombay High Court : The Bombay High Court in Hindalco Industries Ltd. v. UOI [2015] 49 GST 429 opined that Aluminium dross and skimmings, etc. not 'manufactured' goods and not liable to duty, even if marketable/bought and sold. The facts and judgment are :

Facts : In course of manufacture of aluminium sheets/coils, aluminium dross/skimmings emerged as byproducts. Department demanded duty thereon arguing that in view of Explanation to section 2(d), said goods were marketable. Assessee argued that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' were not 'manufactured goods' and were not, therefore, liable to duty.

Held : Conditions contemplated under section 2(d) (excisable goods, movability and marketability) and section 2(f) (manufacture) have to be satisfied conjunctively in order to entail imposition of excise duty. Merely because goods satisfy test of being marketed and saleable and merely because goods are listed in tariff, it does not mean that they are 'manufactured goods'. In various judgments, Supreme Court held that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' are not manufactured goods and said view was followed in context of 'zinc dross and flux skimming'. Hence, impugned goods were not manufactured goods and could not, therefore, be charged to excise duty.

CENTRAL EXCISE - HAZARDOUS WASTE DISPOSAL AS PER GPCB GUIDELINES BY A MANUFACTURING UNIT

1. We present our query in following words :

Facts : An automobile ancillary manufacturing unit wants to dispose hazardous waste material generated from manufacturing process after the concerned input material is put to use and used for manufacturing process as per GPCB [Gujarat Pollution Control Board] Guidelines to GPCB approved entity.

Description and Category of Material :

[a]

Caustic Soda (liquid) - Die Cleaning material - Process material - to be removed after being used (not as such)

[b]

IPA - Cleaning Material - Process Material - to be removed after being used (not as such )

[c]

Coating Sludge (mix of Nokoluk flux, DHM, WS1, Diluent M) -Mix of Coating Materials - Mix of Raw Material - to be removed after being put to use and used in manufacturing (not as such) - All material of coating sludge are our Raw Material - CENVAT Credit is regularly taken of this material when there is inward of it

[d]

Hydraulic oil – Lubricant in one of our manufacturing process – Process material - CENVAT taken on inward of this material - to be removed after being put to use and used for manufacturing ( not as such)

We are going to send these materials for disposal to GPCB approved agency. We will pay them fees for this technical service for sample testing as well as disposal process. No consideration would be receivable or have been received from the consignee i.e., GPCB approved agency situated in Gujarat, India in whatsoever manner against this removal/disposal. In nutshell from sample test to disposal, it is our statutory liability and at our expense, we do it.

Question of Excise Law

[a]

Whether we need to remove this material (all or few or any one) under Excise Invoice ?

[b]

How to value these material supposing it attracts excise, given the fact that we don't have any consideration receivable against this removal.

[c]

What is the general convention/standard operating procedure in manufacturing sector in regard with removing this material under excise invoice and valuation for excise purpose where there is no consideration or similar transaction/removal for comparison ?

Sincere thanks for the read and we request you to respond to the same.

We take this liberty to summarize your query in few words :

Whether disposal of waste arising out of inputs as per pollution control laws has any central excise implication, when such disposal does not result in any consideration and in fact, results in expenditure.

Having summarized your query, let us come direct to position of law :

Removal of inputs as such attracts reversal of Cenvat credit under rule 3(5) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. However, in this case, the inputs have been used and only hazardous waste is being removed. Such removal would, therefore, not attract rule 3(5) and therefore, no statutory invoice is required.

As per section 3 of the Central Excise Act, 1944, excise duty is charged on production or manufacture of excisable goods. It appears that waste is waste of raw material and has not undergone manufacture. Even assuming manufacture, it is not 'goods' as it is not marketable. Definition of marketability under Explanation to section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, provides that goods are deemed to be marketable, if they are capable of being bought and sold for a consideration. The disposal of hazardous waste is mandatory under pollution control laws and can be made only to specified agencies and further leads to expenditure at your end. Hence, same cannot be treated as marketable, as no one would buy it. Therefore, there is no charge of excise duty thereon and consequent, statutory procedures under Excise law cannot be applied.

In view of the above, there are no excise or cenvat implications in the matter.

In evidence of the aforesaid, you are required to generate a normal removal challan for removal of waste citing applicable laws. You should preserve relevant documents in support of the aforesaid claims.

Inclusive Part

5. The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

In Indo Rama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (219) ELT 122 (Bom.), the High Court held that the credit of duty paid on the goods or fuel used in the generation of electricity is available, provided the electricity is used for the manufacture of final product. The use of electricity must have nexus with goods manufactured in the factory.

5.1 Primary packing material - In Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 201 (Punj. & Har.), it was held that it is not a matter of dispute that chewing gum/bubble gums manufactured by the assessees are directly or primarily packed with the printed aluminium foils without tattoos. It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

CENTRAL EXCISE - TREATMENT OF WASTE

1. We have two factories registered under central excise with the following details —

1st Factory - Manufacturer of fine chemicals falling under Chapter 34

2nd Factory - Declared as job worker (a bottling plant) of first factory.

We sent 100 Kgs. of chemicals to be packed in 100 gms. bottles to bottling plant. After completion of packing in small packs we received only 90 Kgs. chemicals packed in small container. What would be the treatment of non-collectible waste of 10% (10 Kgs. out of every lot of 100 kgs.) ?

It is clearly stated by you that both the factories are registered separately. In this case the manufacturing factory is clearing 100 Kgs. to job-worker and receiving back the same in entirety (subject to processing loss). The process loss of 10% will not be chargeable to duty, only if the same is normal process loss.

The benefit may be claimed under rule 21 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, as —

the same is due to natural causes or unavoidable reasons, and

is incurred prior to removal of finished goods from the factory.

An alternative view may be that only 90 Kg. is the manufactured product, because manufacture under section 2(f) is complete only after the completion of all incidental or ancillary processes, which include packing/bottling.

In any case, the duty can be levied only on 90 Kgs.

CENTRAL EXCISE - WHETHER IN CASE OF EXPORT UNDER CLAIM OF REBATE, EXCISE DUTY MAY BE PAID THROUGH CENVAT CREDIT

2. We are exporters of a final product. Export is made under claim of rebate. Please clarify whether we can set-off/adjust excise duty payable under the option of "Export under claim of Rebate" through Cenvat credit or not ? Whether rebate would be allowed even in that case ?

As per rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, credit is allowed of duty or tax paid on inputs or input services or capital goods used in factory/manufacture purposes.

The said credit may be used to pay duty on final product. Goods exported under claim of rebate are cleared on payment of duty and said duty can very well be paid by using Cenvat credit as per rule 3(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In fact, Form ARE-1 itself in Part A provides for certification as follows —

Certified that 1. duty has been paid by debit entry in the Personal Ledger Account No. .........and/or CENVAT Account Entry No. .……or recorded as payable in Daily Stock Account, on the goods described overleaf.

(Emphasis Supplied)

Therefore, for purpose of export under claim of rebate, duty may be paid using balance in Cenvat Credit Account.

CENVAT CREDIT - ROTARY MILL AND WOODEN BALL - CAPITAL GOODS V. INPUT

3. We are availing of credit of duty paid on Rotary Mill and Wooden Ball falling under Tariff Items 44219050 and 44219050, respectively, and use it for grinding Propellant Powder as input. The said goods are machinery and are being capitalized in our financial accounts and depreciation is being claimed. Whether Cenvat credit availed by us is in order ?

The query has been replied in two parts —

Part - I : Input v. Capital Goods

Taking classification put forth by you to be correct, since the goods are classifiable under Chapter 44, they are not listed in any of the categories of capital goods as provided in rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. However, if —

they are purchased as 'components or spares or accessories' of some other machinery ; and

such other machinery is a capital goods under rule 2(a)(A)(i) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004,

then the said mill/ball would be classifiable as capital goods under rule 2(a)(A)(iii) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In any other event the same would be eligible for credit as an 'input', as the same is presumably used within the factory.

Part - II : Relevant treatment under Financial Accounts

The classification and treatment under financial accounts is not relevant for the purpose of deciding eligibility to Cenvat credit.

In other words, even if the said goods are inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, they may be 'fixed assets' under the accounting standards issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and would, accordingly, be eligible for depreciation.

The two things must be viewed separately.

(g) Capital goods installed elsewhere - The capital goods should be installed in the very factory of manufacturer of final products. Even if it is subsidiary company, credit will not be available - Sumangala Spinning Mills (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1999 (113) ELT 84 (Tribunal). (h) Capital goods at job worker’s premises - Capital goods used at job worker’s premises, for work on inputs are not eligible for Cenvat credit - Majestic Auto Ltd. v. CCE 1999 (107) ELT 133 (Tribunal).

(i) Outside factory premises - Capital goods used outside the factory premises, are not eligible for CENVAT Credit.

(j) Capital goods used in manufacture of exempt intermediate product - Capital goods may be used in the manufacture of an exempt intermediate product but the final product may be dutiable. In such case, CENVAT Credit is available on such capital goods, if final product is chargeable to duty - CBEC Circular No. 665/56/2002-CX, dated 25-9-2002.

(k) Project imports - These are also eligible for CENVAT Credit. If some capital goods are eligible while some may not be eligible, the breakup value of capital goods eligible for CENVAT can be certified by a Cost Accountant in the prescribed form - MF (DR) Circular No. 351/67/97-CX., dated 5-11-1997.

(l) Capital goods used both for dutiable and non-dutiable finished goods - The definition merely says that the capital goods must be used in the factory of the manufacturer and does not in specific terms, say that the use must be exclusively of the excisable finished goods.

(m) Exclusion of equipment/appliances used in an office - Rule 2 specifically excludes use of capital goods like equipment or appliances in an office.

(n) Other capital goods - Capital goods other than those mentioned above, are not eligible for CENVAT Credit.

(o) Capital goods removed as scrap after use - In such circumstances, it cannot be said that these are removal ‘as such’. Hence, no excise duty is payable. Wear/Tear cannot be said to be manufactured, and is not liable for duty - CCE v. Birla Corpn. Ltd. 2005 (181) ELT 263 (Tri. - Delhi).

(p) Sale of factory - If factory is sold, it is not removal of capital goods ‘as such’. Hence, no duty is payable on capital goods - Jamna Auto Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2001 (130) ELT 181 (Tri. - Delhi).

(q) Capital goods removed after use for some years - As per the Board’s Circular No. 643/34/2002, CX, dated 1-7-2002 the value on which the supplier of capital goods has paid duty would be a reasonable basis for paying duty with depreciation as per Letter F. No. 495/16/93, CUS VI, dated 26-5-1993.

(r) Use of capital goods by service provider - In case of output service provider, the capital goods should be used for providing output services. The use may be anywhere and even part use is sufficient.

(s) Installation is not required for taking CENVAT Credit - Installation or use is not a precondition for taking CENVAT Credit. On mere receipt in the factory, CENVAT Credit can be availed on capital goods.

(t) Eligibility to be decided on the basis of date of receipt - Eligibility of CENVAT Credit on capital goods is required to be decided on the basis of eligibility on the date when goods were received in the factory. Subsequent eligibility will not help - CCE v. Surya Roshini Ltd. 2003 (155) ELT 581 (Tri. - Delhi).

(u) Capital goods used by service provider - Service provider can also send out capital goods for providing output service, but they should be brought back within 180 days.

Difference between CENVAT Credit on capital goods and Input

4. The difference between Cenvat Credit on capital goods & inputs is explained hereunder :

(a)In the case of inputs, CENVAT Credit is available as soon as input is received in the factory, whereas for capital goods up to 50 per cent Credit is available in current year and balance in subsequent year.

(b)CENVAT Credit utilised on inputs has to be reversed on stock of inputs, when the assessee opts out of CENVAT. This rule is not applicable for capital goods.

(c)The eligible inputs and capital goods have been given in CENVAT Rules.

(d)Inputs are to be used in or in relation to manufacture while in respect of capital goods the only requirement is that it should be used in the factory.

Inter-Unit Transfers Allowed- Goods can be transferred from one MOOWR unit to another.

CHALLENGES AND FUTURE UNCERTAINTY

While MOOWR is a beneficial scheme, these challenges are hindering its performance.

Complex compliance: Filing multiple BOEs for each DTA sale is time-consuming and complex.

No depreciation is allowed when capital goods are sold in the domestic market—duty is on full import value.

No RODTEP or Drawback: MOOWR-based exports are less competitive given they are not eligible for RODTEP scrips or Drawback. Typically benefits RODTEP and Drawback would be in the range of 4-5% of the value of exported good, which is significant for a lot of exporters.

New concern: The Finance Act 2024 empowered the Government of India to exclude certain goods or operations from the applicability of MOOWR scheme. This adds unpredictability, making long-term planning difficult for businesses relying on this scheme and creating an unease in doing business.

Takeaways

If you are importing raw materials or machinery regularly, consider obtaining a MOOWR license.

Be prepared for higher compliance costs.

Evaluate if loss of RODTEP/Drawback is offset by duty deferment benefits.

MOOWR is one of the most flexible and cash-flow-friendly customs schemes available in India. It's ideal for businesses that import raw material or machinery and sell their finished goods either in domestic market or export market.

Small and Mid-sized manufacturers initially hesitate to register under MOOWR because of compliance worries. But once they set up the systems, the cash flow benefits are too significant to ignore.

1965, only sales made in nature of any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure or any sales in connection with or ancillary to such trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure were taxable. Thus, intention of doing the business measured by volume, frequency, continuity or regularity as well as profit motive was essential to tax a sale transaction. Any sale of goods done without intention of doing a business in those goods or without profit motive was not taxable. In this context Apex Court in the case of State of Gujarat v. Raipur Manufacturing Co. Ltd. [1967] 19 STC 1 had taken a view that to bring ancillary sales under tax net it must be shown by the revenue that they were made with an intention to do business and earn profit. It relied on its own decision in the case of State Of Andhra Pradesh v. Abdul Bakhi and Bros AIR 1965 SC 531. It was held that when a person in the course of carrying on a business is required to dispose of what may be called his fixed assets or his discarded goods acquired in the course of the business, an inference that he desired to carry on the business of selling his machinery or fixed assets or discarded goods would not ordinarily arise. Hence, the same will not be taxable.

Legislators amended the definition of 'business' by providing that any sale made in the nature of any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure; whether or not there was intention of makingany gain or profit; as well as sales in connection with or incidental orancillary to such trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure shall be covered.

First important decision on the issue post the amendment was rendered by the Hon. Supreme Court in the case of State of Tamil Nadu v. Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Co of India Ltd. [1973] AIR 1045. In this case the respondent under the Factories Act had to supply tea and edibles to its workmen for the Canteen established by it. It also supplied to its distributors calendars, purses and key chains. They also periodically sold items such as scraps, unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, rims, etc., Issue before the Court was whether these sales were 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' to the business ?

Before the above case, the Hon. Madras High Court in the case of Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. Sri Thirumagal Mills Limited [1967] 20 STC 287 had taken a view that even if by way of amendment to the definition of 'business' profit motive is deleted as an ingredient, still the ancillary activity has to be of commercial nature. It should still partake the nature of 'trade, commerce, manufacture, etc.' specified in the first limb and only then it can be taxed. Hence, it was held that turnover of fair price shop run for the employees will not be leviable to tax.

The Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court on the contrary in the case of Hyderabad Asbestos Cement Products Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh [1969] 24 STC 487 (SC) had taken a view that for an ancillary sale to be taxed it is not required that the same must be done with an intention of doing business. Any ancillary sale connected with the business shall be taxable.

The Hon. Supreme Court in the case of Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Co. of India Ltd. (supra) did not agree with the decision of the Hon. Madras High Court and affirmed the ratio decided by the Hon. Andhra Pradesh High Court.

It held that the Hon. Madras High Court had not paid sufficient attention to word 'such' as appearing in clause 'any transaction in connection with, or incidental or ancillary to, such trade, commerce, manufacture,adventure or concern'. Hence, it held that after the omission of profitmotive, any sale which is ancillary to business whether or not made with an intention to do business of such ancillary goods shall be taxable. The Hon. Supreme Court thus held that once a transaction is covered within the ambit of terms 'in connection with or incidental or ancillary' the same shall be taxable, whether or not there was any intention to do business in the commercial sense of 'business' in these ancillary goods.

In the given case the Apex Court held that whether sale of scrap such unserviceable oil drums, rubber hoses, jerry cans, etc, is ancillary to the business is a finding of fact. However, it observed that as the respondent was an oil company, all those items were parts of the business activity of trading in oil and, hence, the same were taxable. In respect of marketing items like calendars, wallets, etc. it was observed that such goods were given to dealers for increasing the sales. Hence, the same were also ancillary to business. With regard to canteen sales it was observed that Government Order specifically provided for exemption to sales made by canteen and, hence, the same must be considered by lower authorities.

CENTRAL EXCISE - WRONG SCN - WHETHER COMPENSATION CAN BE CLAIMED FROM THE DEPARTMENT ?

1. Though our Query is academic, we would like to know whether where any officer, purely out of ill-will, creates allegations against the assessees by issuance of unwarranted show-cause notices, can assessees seek compensation from the department of all the expenses ? What about filing of civil suit ?

Section 40 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and corresponding provisions under various other laws provide protection to Central Government and its officers.

Section 40(1) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 provides that -

no suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie

against the Central Government or any officer of the Central Government or a State Government

for anything which is done, or intended to be done,

in good faith, in pursuance of this Act or any rule made thereunder.

Further, section 40(2) provides that no proceeding, other than a suit, shall be initiated against the Central Government or any officer of the Central Government or a State Government for anything done or purported to have been done in pursuance of this Act or any rule made thereunder, -

without giving the Central Government or such officer a month's previous notice in writing of the intended proceeding and of the cause thereof, or

after the expiration of three months from the accrual of such cause.

Thus, any of the proposed actions must conform to the requirements of section 40 and corresponding provisions in other law.

Further, unless otherwise proved with clear evidence, the benefit of doubt goes to the Central Government and its officers, etc.

A criminal proceeding is generally entertained subject to evidence and time-bar created in section 40(2). A civil proceeding entails voluminous work/evidences.

Introduction

1. To be liable to excise duty, a product must be manufactured, movable, marketable and mentioned in First Schedule to Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 as subject to duty of excise duty. From 1-3-2015, even if goods are non-excisable, they continue to be exempted goods and, therefore, credit relatable thereto has to be reversed.

Demand of duty on Bagasse/Zinc-Dross, etc. has been subject matter of repeated litigation since decades. The Department has been making all efforts (and CBEC upholding said efforts by issuance of circulars) to demand excise duty on Bagasse/Zinc-Dross. However, the Courts have been holding otherwise.

This article makes an attempt to analyse the position of law vis-à-vis recent landmark judgments on the issue and Circular No.1027/15/2016-CX, dated 25-4-2016.

Position prior to 10-5-2008

2. Prior to 10-5-2008, concept of marketability was not defined in the Central Excise Act, 1944 and for being marketable, goods were required to be known as such in market and capability of being commercially bought and sold as 'goods'. Thus, waste and residue of many kinds were held non-marketable. In this regard, to be brief, we may be conclude that —

bagasse was held not excisable goods in Commissioner v. Balrampur Chini Mills Ltd. - 2015 (320) ELT A258 (SC)]. This view was accepted by CBEC itself in its Circular No. 941/2/2011-CX., dated 14-2-2011

zinc dross was held non-manufactured/non-marketable in Collector v. Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. - 2004 (165) ELT 386 (SC) and Commissioner v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 2006 (203) ELT 3 (SC).

The Department's demand of excise duty on said goods was therefore, set aside. The Department's demand of reversal of credit under rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 (and its earlier counterparts) was set aside on ground that since they were not marketable and non-excisable, hence, they were not even 'exempted goods' as defined in the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Hence, no payment of duty/credit was required prior to 10-5-2008.

Period 10-5-2008 to 28-2-2015

3. Vide amendment by Finance Act, 2008, as Explanation was inserted in section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 defining the concept of marketability. It was provided that "goods" includes any article, material or substance which is capable of being bought and sold for a consideration and such goods shall be deemed to be marketable. Thus, capability of being bought and sold for a consideration would constitute marketability and there would be no need for the goods to be commercially tradeable or known as such in the market.

3.1 Circular of 2009 and 2011 : Relying upon this amendment, the CBEC issued Circular No. 904/24/2009-CX., dated 28-10-2009 (reiterated in Circular No. 941/2/2011-CX., dated 14-2-2011) that (paras 2 to 5 of the Circular of 2009, relevant extracts) :

Excisability of bagasse and similar waste products arising during the course of manufacture has been under dispute for a long period of time.

In the budget of 2008, the definition of "excisable goods" in clause (d) of section 2 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 was amended by adding an explanation that for the purposes of this clause, "goods" include any article, material or substance which is capable of being bought and sold for a consideration and such goods shall be deemed to be marketable.

It is clarified that with this amendment in section 2(d), the bagasse, aluminium/zinc dross and other such products termed as waste, residue or refuse which arise during the course of manufacture and are capable of being sold for consideration would be excisable goods and chargeable to payment of excise duty.

CENTRAL EXCISE - JOB-WORK - DIRECT EXPORT

1. We purchased wire rods, availed Cenvat credit thereon and sent them to the job worker [who is a related party] for drawing them [procedure under rule 4(5)(a) has been followed]. The job worker is an exporter also. Instead of sending the drawn rods back to us, it was decided that the job-workers would export the same to its own customers. Can it be done ? We are ready to pay duty on cost (raw material plus job work charges plus 10% net profit margin) by issuing invoice in name of job worker. Will it be in accordance with law ? You may please advise us as regards any other formality to be observed under the law ?

One can presume that yourself (the principal manufacturer) want to sell the finished goods to the job-worker himself and the job-worker would export the same. There is absolutely no embargo thereupon i.e., you may sell the goods to job-worker. In fact, rule 4(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 permits direct clearance from factory of job-worker. Instead of receiving finished goods back and again selling them to job-worker, you may definitely raise a sale bill in the name of job-worker.

Since it is claimed that you are related parties, the value of 'drawn rods' (final product) would be determined as per rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000, read with rules 9 and 10 ibid.

Since the job-worker would act as merchant exporter, he may avail of facilities under rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, i.e., procurement without payment of duty or any other export incentive for which necessary procedures would have to be complied with. If the facility under rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 in relation to procurement of goods without payment of duty for export is availed, no duty would be payable on drawn rods.

It is advised that an informed decision be made, after analyzing pros and cons.

2. We are manufacturers of TV sets. In some cases we purchase completed TV sets from third parties and sell them to customers. We are availing of marketing services. Please clarify whether we can take service tax credit of marketing services in relation to the units not manufactured by us and sold to customers.

Purchase and sale of goods does not amount to 'manufacture'. Further, the same does not amount to an 'output service' under rule 2(p) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, as first of all, the same is not a service under section 65B(44) of the Finance Act, 1994 and secondly, the same falls in negative list under section 66D(e) of the Finance Act, 1994 [Trading of Goods].

Since trading of goods is neither manufacture nor provision of service, any service used therefor is not eligible for credit under rule 3, read with rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In case you have taken credit, you are advised to reverse the same to avoid applicability of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

2. Rule 3(5) and 3(5A)/(5B) defines four types of situations and provides guidelines what is to be done. All these situations are detailed below.

Here there is no question of bona fide or mala fide intention due to which no penalty provision would be attracted.

(a) Capital goods removed ‘as such’ - ‘As such’ means, in the same position in which purchase is done. Whatever Cenvat Credit is taken/availed, it has to be paid to the account of the Central Government. No such type of payment is required to be made if the capital goods is/are removed for providing output service.

(b) Capital goods removed ‘as scrap’ - If capital goods are removed ‘as scrap’, then manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the duty leviable on transaction value.

(c) Capital goods removed ‘before put to use’ - Here manufacturer is required to pay full amount of duty which has been taken as Cenvat credit. This situation is different from the situation given in (a) above, as here it might be possible that the capital goods which are purchased may not be in ‘intact’ position, say, for example machines are purchased and installed and are made ready to use, but ultimately it is decided that these should not be used but to be removed.

(d) Capital goods removed ‘after put to use’ - What amount of Cenvat credit has been taken in the books of account is required to be depreciated by 2.5 per cent (i.e., reduced) per quarter and the balance amount is required to be paid to the account of the Central Government.

What if capital goods are sent for jobwork outside factory or office premises and not received back in 180 days ?

3. Rule 4(5a ) clarifies this situation. Once capital goods which are purchased are removed from the factory or the premises of the service provider for providing output taxable services, then such capital goods must be received back in the factory or the premises of service provider within the period of 180 days. If such capital goods are not received within the abovesaid period, then manufacturer or service provider (as the case may be) shall pay an amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the inputs or capital goods by debiting the Cenvat credit account or otherwise. Here the option of payment by debiting cenvat account is given.

4. This is new provision which has been introduced under rule 6. It is made clear that Cenvat credit is not allowed for the input/capital goods/input services which are used in the process of manufacture of non-excisable goods or for providing non-taxable services.

However, this new provision allows the manufacturer or service provider to take 100 per cent Cenvat credit, by paying 10 per cent of the value of exempted goods (for manufacturer) or 8 per cent of the value of exempted services (for service provider).

(i)Under the original rule, if the capital goods, on which MODVAT credit was taken were removed from the factory, the assessee was required to clear the same on payment of duty, not lesser than the amount of credit which was previously taken thereon. As per the amended notification, this requirement applies only where the capital equipment is sought to be removed from the factory without being used in the manufacture of excisable goods.

As per the amendment, if the machinery is sought to be removed from the factory after being used therein, then the payment of excise duty has to be made after allowing a deduction of 2.5 per cent of the credit taken earlier for each quarter of a year of usage from the date of taking the credit. The amended notification further provides that if the machinery has been sold for any reason as scrap, this duty shall be paid at the rate applicable to such scrap.

It would appear that the normal life of the machinery, for this purpose, is estimated at 10 years, and a distinction is drawn between used and unused machinery and also between usable and scrapped machinery.

(ii)A new sub-rule has also been added, permitting removal of capital goods for tests or repairs for reconditioning, provided the same are returned to the factory for further use as capital goods. (iii)The earlier requirement was that before the assessee takes MODVAT credit on capital goods, such goods have to be verified by the Excise Superintendent. This requirement, which was considered impractical and susceptible to misuse, has now been removed by another amended notification.

(iv)Yet another welcome amendment is that the assessee can now take credit on capital goods on the basis of an invoice or bill of entry or other duty-paying document as against the cumbersome procedure prescribed earlier.

These amendments are in the right direction, as a result of which, most of the practical difficulties are considered to have been removed.

2.4 Case of goods obtained on lease or hire purchase - According to the existing provisions, MODVAT credit on capital goods is not permissible in respect of the equipment acquired on lease or hire purchase. It was reported that the Government has decided to amend the relevant rules so as to extend MODVAT credit to capital goods acquired through leasing and hire purchase also. 2.5 MODVAT credit vs. Depreciation - It is specifically provided that no credit of the duty paid on capital goods shall be allowed, if the assessee claims depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 on that part of the value of capital goods which represents the amount of specified duty paid on such goods. In other words, a manufacturer has the option to claim MODVAT credit on the duty paid or forego the same if he opts to claim income-tax depreciation on the duty portion of the capital goods. If the manufacturer has opted for taking MODVAT credit, income-tax depreciation on such capital goods can be claimed only on the net cost as reduced by the duty paid thereon.

definition of ‘manufacture’ as contained in the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The term ‘manufacture’ is borrowed from the Central Excise Act, 1944 and this is one of the terms which never reached finality in the matter of dispute regarding process to be considered as a manufacture or not. There is a catena of judgments on the subject ‘Manufacture’, and there are books written on this subject which show the significance of the term under the Excise Law. The definition under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act can be divided into three parts:

First part of the definition refers to "any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product". This term has been interpreted by various forums including the Apex Court and what emerges out is presence of the following criteria to constitute manufacture:

u A process should be carried out.

u Such process should result into a distinctly new product, commercially known as such.

u The resultant product should be moveable and marketable.

For example, processes like Electroplating, Teflon Coating, Anodising, Heat Treatment, Powder Coating, etc., are no doubt a process carried out, but no new product emerges out of such process and, hence, this cannot be described as process amounting to manufacture and job workers undertaking the above activities are required to pay service tax.

The second part of the definition under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 is introduced from March 1, 1986, which reads as under:

"‘Manufacture’ includes any process,—

(i )** ** **

(ii )which is specified in relation to any goods in the section or Chapter Notes of the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 as amounting to manufacture;"

This is a major change in the definition of ‘Manufacture’ and the interesting aspect of this definition is that whatever is mentioned in the Section Notes or Chapter Notes will be applicable to only those goods falling in the respective Sections/Chapter of the Tariff. For example, in respect of food preparations, chemicals and pharmaceutical products, even the process of labelling and re-labelling, repacking from bulk packs to retail packs or adoption of any other treatment to render the product marketable to the consumer, shall amount to manufacture. If the product falling under the respective Chapters undergoes the above process, it will be treated as ‘Manufacture’ and all excise formalities will have to be complied with. To appreciate and understand whether a particular process amounts to manufacture or not, one has to refer to Section Notes and Chapter Notes under the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

The third part of the definition is a recent addition which came into effect from March 1, 2003 which reads as under:

"‘Manufacture’ includes any process,—

(i )and (ii) ** ** **

(iii )which, in relation to the goods specified in the Third Schedule, involves packing or repacking of such goods in a unit container or labelling or re-labelling of containers including the declaration or alteration of retail sale price on it or adoption of any other treatment on the goods to render the product marketable to the consumer,"

The above definition applies only to goods specified in the Third Schedule which comprises of 99 items which are incidentally same items which attract excise duty based on MRP/RSP under section 4A of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

Thus, the term ‘Manufacture’ spreads its wings all over, which leaves very little scope for escape from excise levy. When the manufacturers themselves are contesting the term ‘Manufacture’ with the Excise authorities resulting in never ending disputes arising out of the same, it is time for job workers to understand and appreciate the concept which is now defined in a detailed way as explained above.

Business Auxiliary Service, meaning of

4. It is interesting to note that production or processing of goods for or on behalf of the client is one of the notified services under the term ‘Business Auxiliary Service’. The definition ends with a clear note that the term ‘Business Auxiliary Service’ does not include any activity that amounts to manufacture within the meaning of clause (f) of section 2 of the Central Excise Act, 1944. Therefore, if the job worker carries out any manufacturing process under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 falling under one of the three categories of the definition discussed above, he can safely remain out of service tax net. On account of introduction of service tax on job work, it will be a tough time for job workers to convince the excise authorities that the process carried out by them amounts to manufacture. Before introduction of service tax on job work, the job workers were fighting with the department that the process carried out by them does not amount to manufacture to remain out of the excise net, whereas the present scenario is a reverse situation. One has to go by the decisions of the Tribunal, High Court or Supreme Court when claim is made for remaining away from service tax net on the ground that the process carried out amounts to manufacture.

If the job workers carry out the process on the material supplied to them which amounts to manufacture, service tax is not payable in view of the definition of ‘Business Auxiliary Service’ as discussed above.

5. We send scrap (say, 100 kg.) to the job worker for further processing. Job-worker returns 80 kg. scrap after processing under job work agreement issued under delivery challan. The job worker does not receive any service charges for this, but, in lieu thereof, takes 20 kg. as the service charge. No financial transaction takes place. Whether these type of transactions are allowed under excise law ? Will there be any liability on our (principal manufacturer's) part ? Kindly clarify

Assuming that process amounts to manufacture, liability to pay duty is of the manufacturer : in this case, job-worker. Hence, in case of 80 kg. manufactured on job-work basis and returned to principal manufacturer, the value will be determined as per rule 10A(iii) of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 read with Ujagar Prints (SC)'s case.

The job-work charges would form part of the value and since, in this case, the job-work charges are in kind in form of retention of 20 kg. scrap, the value would be determined based on value of scrap retained by the job-worker.

When job-worker sells 20 kg. (after processing), duty thereon would be payable separately at the time of removal.

CENVAT CREDIT - REVERSAL ON EXEMPTED SERVICE AND SERVICES COVERED UNDER FULL REVERSE CHARGE ?

6. We are manufacturing goods which are 100% excisable and are also providing Goods Transport Agency's Services, which are exempt as per mega exemption notification (transport of defence and military equipments). When taking and availing cenvat, is it necessary to reverse cenvat on exempted service as per rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 ? Is it necessary to reverse credit, even if service is provided on reverse charge mechanism ? Kindly clarify.

Reversal under rule 6 would apply to exempted services provided by service provider. Hence, it would equally apply to exempt Goods Transport Agency's Services.

However, where services are covered under reverse charge, they cease to be 'output service' and hence, no credit can be availed in respect thereof. Hence, any wrongly taken credit has to be reversed.

SERVICE TAX - SUPPLY OF BEDS IN TRAINS v. ABATEMENT

7. Whether supply of bed rolls in the trains attracts Service tax before 1-10-2012 and whether there is any abatement of 30% after 1-10-2012 on the same service ? If yes, under which notification ?

Supply of bed rolls in trains is a taxable service and is not eligible for any exemption or abatement. The abatement relates only to 'transport of passengers by railways' and the service in question is altogether different.

SERVICE TAX - OUTDOOR CATERING v. FACTORY CANTEEN

8. If outdoor caterer is providing catering service in a mess within the factory premises : Is the service exempt as per the mega exemption notification ?

Entries 19 and 19A of the Mega Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012 read as follows :

"19. Services provided in relation to serving of food or beverages by a restaurant, eating joint or a mess, other than those having the facility of air-conditioning or central air-heating in any part of the establishment, at any time during the year;";

19A. Services provided in relation to serving of food or beverages by a canteen maintained in a factory covered under the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948), having the facility of air-conditioning or central air-heating at any time during the year."

It appears that mess would be covered by Entry 19A (if maintained as per Factories Act and having AC) or Entry 19 (if non-AC).

Some experts would suggest that mess services are provided by company to employees and not by outdoor caterer and hence, exemption cannot be availed. However, the most important fact to be noted is that 'company has hired outdoor caterer to run mess' in compliance with law and therefore, mess is run/operated by caterer and mess services would thus, be exempt as aforesaid. Employer-company is not the service provider; in fact, it is duty bound to arrange for canteen and canteen/mess services are provided only by the caterer.

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture and sale of different varieties of metallic wires and in the course of such manufacturing activity, waste material, viz., scrap metal, was obtained. The assessee's claim for deduction under section 80HH in respect of profits attributable to sale proceeds of scrap and drums and value of scrap at close of the accounting year was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the impugned profits could not be said to have been derived from the industrial undertakings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim on the ground that scrap metal was a direct offshoot of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and eventually it could not be put into a different category other than the one from which the main product was derived. HELD: Section 41(1 ) brings to tax certain amounts by a fiction of law. Therefore, the operation of such fiction should be limited to the language of the section. Where the assessee has incurred a loss or expenditure or trading liability and this trading liability has been allowed as deduction in an earlier year and something has later on been recovered in respect of such liability or such liability has either been remitted or has ceased to exist, section 41( 1) comes into operation. But according to the facts in the present case, nothing happened as contemplated by section 41(1) . Sale proceeds derived were for the sale of the particular product and not recoupment of earlier purchase. Accordingly, section 41(1) had no application to the facts of the instant case.

The sale proceeds of drums used for storing water and which had become useless could not, however, be said to be directly derived from the industrial undertaking considering the manufactur-ing activity in which the assessee was involved. This surplus was also of the nature falling under section 41(2 ). Therefore, the assessee was not entitled to relief in respect of profits attributable to sale of drums.
