HELD: As per sub-clause (1) of section 206C, every seller shall collect from the buyer of any goods specified, a sum equal to the amounts specified. In this case, the petitioner has awarded contracts to various bar owners to run the bar adjacent to the retail shows run by the petitioner. [Para 73] As mentioned, the licensees who have been issued licenses to run the bar adjacent to the retail outlets/shops of the petitioner were required to offer their bid to run the bar under a tender process under Tamil Nadu Liquor Retail Vending (in Shops and Bars) Rules, 2003. In the bar, the bar contractors (successful licensees) are entitled to sell food items (short eats) and collect the leftover bottles by the consumers, who after consuming liquor from the retail outlet leave it in the licensed premises albeit the 'bars' licensed under Tamil Nadu Liquor Retail Vending (in Shops and Bars) Rules, 2003 to the bar licensees. [Para 74]

To attract the liability under section 206C, it is incumbent on the part of the Department to establish that the bottles left by buyers of liquor who consume liquor in the bars attached to the petitioner TASMAC's retail shops satisfies the definition of 'Scrap' within the meaning of (vi) to table to sub-section (1) and section 206C. The expression 'Scrap' has been defined to mean waste and scrap from the 'manufacture' or 'mechanical working of materials' which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. [Para 76]

The expression 'Scrap' would mean 'Waste' and 'Scrap from Manufacture' or 'Mechanical Working of Material'. The definition is furnished qualified. Such waste is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons. It has to take within its meaning those activities which will amount to manufacture under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, read with relevant Chapter notes. [Para 77]

Section 2(29BA), defined the expression 'manufacture', with its grammatical variations to mean a change in a non-living physical object or article or thing,—

(a)

resulting in transformation of the object or article or thing into a new and distinct object or article or thing having a different name, character and use; or

(b)

bringing into existence of a new and distinct object or article or thing with a different chemical composition or integral structure. [Para 78]

The expression 'mechanical working of materials' in the definition of 'scrap' in clause to Explanation (b) to section 206(c) has not been defined separately. [Para 79]

Both manufacture and 'mechanical working of material' can generate 'scrap'. Although, an activity may not amount to 'manufacture' yet waste and scrap can be generated from 'mechanical working of material'. [Para 82]

The expression 'mechanical working' is not new to taxing enactments. It has been used in the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 and under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. Section Note 8(a) to section XV of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 uses the expression 'waste generated during mechanical working of metal in the workshop'. [Para 84]

The test of manufacture under section 2(f) of Central Excise Act, 1944 is well known. An activity which has to lead to emergence of a new product in the market is a manufacturing activity. [Para 85]

It was in this context, the Courts have held levy of Central Excise duty on various 'scrap' generated from either manufacture or 'mechanical working of materials' are liable to tax provided such waste is also specified in the 1st schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1955. [Para 86]

'Scrap' was treated as 'excisable goods' for the purpose of section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, for levy under Central Excise Act, 1944, provided it satisfied the above requirements. [Para 87]

Though the expression 'manufacture' has been defined in Income-tax Act, 1961, the expression 'mechanical working of material' has not been defined in Income-tax Act, 1961. In the 9th Ed. of Oxford's Dictionary, the expression "mechanical" has been defined as follows:-

(a)

operated by power from an engine;

(b)

connected with machines and engines;

(c)

connected with the physical laws of movement and cause and effect. [Para 88]

However, dictionary meaning of the word 'mechanical' by itself does not help in resolving the legal issue in this case. Therefore, other rules of interpretation have to be looked for and applied. [Para 89]

The respondents availed of deemed credit facility for waste and scrap of iron and steel and used the goods as inputs for their final products. The Department held that the scrap/waste was not duty paid, hence the respondents were not entitled to the deemed credit facility.

Dutiability of waste and scrap

3.3 Waste and scrap is practically treated as 'final product' for excise purposes. As discussed above earlier, there was view that dross, skimmings, remnants, bagasse etc. arising during manufacture are not 'goods' even if they fetch some price. Now, this view may not be valid after 10-5-2008.

Thus, waste and scrap can be 'goods' but dutiable only if 'manufactured' and are mentioned in Tariff.

Following discussions and case law is relevant even after 10-5-2008.

Meaning of scrap - The dictionary meaning of 'scrap' is 'a small piece or amount of something especially one that is left over after the greater part had been used or material, especially metal, discarded after processing' - Baby Varghese v. State of Kerala (2008) 16 VST 448 (SC).

Waste and scrap is 'final product' under Cenvat - Board has clarified that waste and scrap is treated as 'final product' under rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules [that time rule 57AA(c)] and its clearance is as if it is a final product. - MFDR TRU No. 345/2/2000-TRU dated 29-8-2000 (However, this is so if waste is 'manufactured'. Further, waste is not 'final product' if not mentioned in Central Excise Tariff. In any case, this view has not been fully endorsed by Tribunal).

Scrap can be 'goods' - In Khandelwal Metal and Engg. Works v. UOI - 1985 (Supp) 1 SCR 750 = 1985 (20) ELT 222 (SC) = AIR 1985 SC 1211 = (1985) 3 SCC 620, Apex Court held that scrap would be liable to duty, if it is known in commercial parlance by that name and has an established market - followed in Dhrunal Chhotalal Patel v. UOI - 1993 (63) ELT 27 (Bom HC).

In Greysham v. CCE 2000(117) ELT 350 (CEGAT), it was held that waste and scrap of steel arising during manufacture is dutiable as it is marketable and specifically mentioned in tariff.

Iron scrap recovered from slag arising out of manufacture of iron in blast furnace is excisable commodity - Steel Authority of India v. CCE 2006 (197) ELT 113 (CESTAT).

Cotton waste arising in the course of manufacture of cotton yarn and acid sludge arising in the course of refining of crude oil into kerosene can be treated as 'intended manufacture' as they arise regularly and also sold regularly from time to time. - CST v. Bharat Petroleum 1995(77) ELT 790 = 85 STC 220 (SC).

[Earlier, a view was held waste and scrap is not 'manufactured' but arises during the course of manufacture. It is not obtained by any process of manufacture but is obtained in course of manufacture of end product. Waste or scrap is in nature of rubbish and has no distinguishing name character or use and hence it is not goods. However, in view of subsequent judgments of Supreme Court, these judgments are no more valid.]

In Windorz India v. CCE 2002(145) ELT 148 (CEGAT), it was held that cut pieces of Aluminium rods, bars etc. arising during manufacture of Aluminium windows is 'scrap' as defined in CETA and is dutiable.

Duty is payable on waste arising during manufacture of exempted product - CCE v. AG Flats (2012) 277 ELT 96 (CESTAT).

Goods rejected during testing - If finished product is rejected at testing stage, it is to be classified as scrap. - Durgapur Steel Plant v. CCE 2001(132) ELT 784 (CEGAT).

Defective products not usable as such are 'waste and scrap' - Defective products unusable have to be taken as 'scrap and waste' - Panchmahal Steels Ltd. v. CCE 1997(93) ELT 516 (CEGAT).

In CCE v. MRF Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 595 (CEGAT - 3 member bench), it was held that rubber scrap obtained by cutting defective rubber tubes are not 'goods'.

Calcium carbide slag is waste and not marketable. It is not excisable goods - CCE v. DCW Ltd. (2008) 222 ELT 79 (CESTAT).

Just because assessee has found some use of waste, it does not mean that the waste is marketable, if it has no specific composition or identity - Gujarat State Fertilisers v. CCE (2009) 234 ELT 532 (CESTAT).

In UP State Sugar Corpn v. CCE 2000(119) ELT 74 (CEGAT), it was held that press-mud arising during manufacture of sugar is only a residual waste. It is not marketable and is not excisable. - view upheld in CCE v. Titawi Sugar Complex 2003(152) ELT 21 (SC)- - - followed in CCE v. Cheyyar Coop Sugar Mills (2009) 240 ELT 417 (CESTAT SMB) accepted by department - CBEC circular No. 730/46/2003-CX dated 31-7-2003 [However, in another matter, departmental appeal has been admitted - 199 ELT A70].

In CCE v. Tony Electronics 2000(119) ELT 139 (CEGAT), it was held that waste and scrap in the course of manufacture of audio/video magnetic tape is not marketable and hence not excisable.

Waste like floor sweeping, processed defective cakes etc. are not marketable.- CCE v. Delta Foods (2011) 30 STT 121 (CESTAT SMB) * Delta Foods v. CCE (2012) 277 ELT 352 (CESTAT) (Hence rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules is not applicable as payment of 'amount' is not required)

Stray or distress sale does not mean goods are 'marketable'.

3.2-2 Stray or distress sale does not prove marketability

Stray sale does not mean goods are marketable - If the product is generally not sold, stray sales do not mean that the product is marketable - Gujarat State Fertilizers v. CCE - (1996) 84 ELT 539 (CEGAT) - correct decision as 'one swallow does not make a summer'.

In CCE v. Ranger Breweries Ltd. 2000(122) ELT 447 = 39 RLT 1065 (CEGAT), it was observed that stray incidents of sale does not give characteristics of marketability to the goods - same view in CCE v. Karnataka Vidyuth Karkhane (2009) 239 ELT 165 (CESTAT).

Distress sale does not mean goods are marketable - In Britannia Industries Ltd. v. CCE 1997(93) ELT 719 (CEGAT), it was held that waste cannot be treated as excisable goods merely because it is capable of fetching some sale price, if such sale is distress sale and sale price is determined at the whims of the buyers as there is no ready market for regular sale.

13. (1) The Scrapping Yard shall be set up in an adequate area having space for vehicular movement, storing the vehicles or items received and recyclable material recovered, commensurate to the size and voluminous nature of the scraps to be handled by the facility.

(2) The Scrapping Yard shall be a gated area to handle, depollute and dismantle End-of-Life Vehicles, white goods and other scraps along with facility for measuring radiation as is followed for import of scrap.

(3) Material handling machines shall be utilised to minimise human intervention and create safe work places.

(4) All Scrapping Yards shall engage competent and trained manpower to process the End-of-Life vehicles, goods and other scraps.

(5) The Scrapping Yard shall have dry areas (free from water logging), impermeable surfaces like asphalt or concrete flooring, asphalt or concrete roads, adequate workshop facilities for in-house maintenance, fire protection systems etc. to maintain safe work places and all other required measures for keeping pollution under control.

(6) Scrapping Yard shall be equipped with a depollution system, preferably with zero discharge system and dismantling work shall be done using technology for processing the End-of-Life vehicles, goods and other scraps.

(7) The Scrapping Yard shall comply with relevant health and safety legislation or regulation and environmental norms.

(8) The Scrapping yard shall have,-

(a)

Suitable earmarked area for parking of waste vehicles on non-permeable asphalt or concrete or epoxy coated flooring with adequate drainage facility and no waste or potentially waste vehicle shall be parked on roads or public spaces even during processing of applications for deposit and shall be accommodated within the premises of the Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facility only.

(b)

Certified de-polluting equipment to ensure zero leakage of pollutants during draining of fuels or fluids or gases and liquids, certified de-risking equipment for safe neutralization or removal of airbags, pre-tensioner etc., appropriate dismantling equipment for the activities defined (such as de-risking, de-polluting, dismantling, shredding, shearing, bailing etc.), designated areas for storing the segregated scrap, adequate space for storage and handling of segregated spares, designated space for temporary storage of automotive hazardous waste such as tyres, batteries, fuel, oils, liquids and gases, suitable safety and occupational health equipment, material handling equipment for the safe transportation of spares, scrap etc.

(c)

Appropriate Industrial grade lighting and ventilation systems, conformity to noise pollution norms and appropriate effluent treatment plants or water recycling plants.

(9) Scrapping Yards shall accredit themselves with the latest version of quality standards viz. ISO 9001 (Quality management system), ISO14001 (Environmental Management System) and ISO 45001 (Occupational health and safety) within twelve months of commencement of operations.

(10) In case Scrapping Yards do not have adequate capability or provisions for responsible recycling of hazardous waste (like e-waste, lead acid batteries, lithium-ion components, or for recovery of rare earth metals, etc.), or for recycling of scrap material which is outside its scope, then such materials shall be sold to duly authorised recyclers or agencies, who have adequate capability and licence.

In order to set over this controversy in the above definition of ‘input’, the Legislature has clarified that even if an item is not contained in the final product still it would be classifiable as an ‘input’ under the above definition. In other words, it has been clarified by the definition of ‘input’ that the following considerations will not be relevant :

(a)Use of input in the manufacturing process be it direct or indirect; and (b)even if the input is not contained in the ‘final product’ it would still be covered by the definition.

These considerations have been made irrelevant by the use of expression ‘goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ which, as stated above, is the crucial requirement of the definition of ‘input’. In this regard, some case laws are cited hereunder :

In J.K. Cement Works v. CCE 2010 (252) ELT 249 (Trib. - Delhi), it was held that only those goods which form part of the process carried out by a manufacturer for converting raw material into finished goods can be considered as inputs and the goods which are not integrally connected with the process of manufacture resulting in utilization of such product directly or indirectly in the manufacture of finished product cannot be said to be input. Therefore, oxygen, helium and acetylene gases used for repair and maintenance of plant and machinery are not covered by the definition of ‘input’.

In Reva Electric Car Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (250) ELT 149 (Trib. - Bang.), the Tribunal held that it is unambiguously clear that the rejection was at the pre-manufacturing stage and for no reasons attributable to the appellant. Rejection at the pre-manufacturing stage is also indispensable for quality control. It can be said that any rejection of input without ulterior motive or oblique purpose may not disentitle an assessee from the benefit of law relating to CENVAT credit.

It did not appear that the car manufacturer had escaped duty. The revenue should, therefore, allow entitlement of CENVAT credit in the absence of any violation of law. Accordingly, the demand of Rs. 6,90,150 on the count of using of inputs for R&D was unsustainable in the absence of any finding to show that the R&D had not resulted in finished goods and that finished goods had escaped duty. Exercise of Research having resulted in the finished goods and that had suffered duty, CENVAT credit was admissible for which demand of Rs. 6,90,150 was set aside.

In HIM Technoforge Ltd.’s case (supra), the respondent was a manufacturer of rough forgings and forging articles of steel falling under Chapter 7326 of the CETA, 1985. They also availed CENVAT credit of inputs and capital goods. The dispute related to ‘metal band saw blades’ and ‘steel shots’ as to whether they could be considered as capital goods as contended by the department or could be treated as inputs as claimed by the respondent. The original authority after taking note of the duration of use of these items and the purpose for which they were used held that they were capital goods.

The Commissioner (Appeals) treated the above products as ‘inputs’. He held that under the CENVAT Credit Rules, the term ‘input’ has been defined to mean all goods, except HSD oil, LSD and motor spirit used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. In view of this above definition of the ‘input’ under the CENVAT Credit Rules, both the items, namely, ‘metal saw blade’ and ‘steel shots’ used by the appellants in connection with the production of goods on consumable would merit classification under inputs only and, therefore, the credit taken by them was in order.

The Tribunal held that if the role and period of usage as recorded by the original authority was taken into account, the decision of Commissioner (Appeals) had clearly held that the same were in the nature of consumables used in relation to manufacture of final products and, therefore, appropriately to be treated as inputs.

CCE 2010 (258) ELT 111 (Trib. - Ahd.), a small amount of Rs. 9,456 stood denied to the appellant on the ground that the credit had been availed on the waste and scrap, which could not be considered as an input for the appellant’s final product. The lower authorities had nowhere discussed as to how the waste and scrap could not be considered as an input. The cable waste of cut length was being utilized and consumed by the appellant in its own factory in the manufacture of finished goods. The duty paid cable waste received in the factory had been accounted for in the input register and its consumption had been shown in the manufacture of the final product. The final product manufactured out of the same was accounted for in the RG-1 Part I Register, which stood cleared on payment of duty. As such to deny the benefit of waste and scrap on the ground that the same was not an input was not justified.

Since the definition of the term ‘manufacture’ given in section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 has been replaced by section 4 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, the existing Chapters of Central Excise Tariff Act have been governed by relevant Chapter Notes and Section Notes. 3. For the same, there are 3 points :

u Whether it is an excisable good in terms of the relevant Chapter Notes or Section Notes;

u Whether it arises during the course of manufacturing process;

u Whether it is marketable, if not, then it is not called as an excisable commodity. Mere fetching a nominal value has no relevance.

Any waste and scrap arising from manufacture or mechanical working of input/raw materials (i.e., due to manufacturing process) is only liable to duty - Hindalco Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (144) ELT 339 (Trib. - Delhi) provided that the same shall be marketable. Scrap arising through dismantling of buildings, repair of machinery, etc., is not liable to duty - Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (144) ELT 555 (Trib. - Bang.), National Winder v. CCE 2002 (147) ELT 463 (Trib. - Delhi). However, scrap generated in workshop used for maintenance of plant other than old part or scrap generated by dismantling of used machinery shall be liable to pay duty - Budhewal Co-op. Sugar Mills Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (141) ELT 490 (Trib. - Delhi) but subject to fulfilment of other conditions. However, packing materials of inputs/raw materials could not be treated to be waste arising out of processing of the input for which credit has been taken - CCE v. West Coast Industrial Gases Ltd. 2003 (155) ELT 11 (SC).

However, packing materials of inputs/raw materials could not be treated to be waste arising out of processing of the input for which credit has been taken - CCE v. West Coast Industrial Gases Ltd. 2003 (155) ELT 11 (SC). In other words, the waste and scrap arising out of capital goods on which no credit has been availed, shall not be dutiable - Southern Agrifurane Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2003 (158) ELT 323 (Trib. - Chennai), provided that no Cenvat credit on such capital goods was taken - Kesoram Rayon v. CCE 2003 (162) ELT 620 (Trib. - Kol.).

If any waste is not marketable, the same shall not be dutiable - CCE v. Indian Tube Co. Ltd. 1995 (77) ELT 21 (SC); Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd.’s case (supra). For example, refuse, rubbish and ashes thrown up in the course of manufacture are not goods even if they may fetch some prices - CCE v. Tata Iron & Steels Co. Ltd. 2004 (165) ELT 386 (SC). If the resultant waste (after process of a waste) is same having almost identical chemical and physical properties, resultant waste could not be said as manufactured waste - Indian Organic Chemicals Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (88) ELT 644 (SC).

Waste and scrap is dutiable only when it is a manufactured product and not otherwise - Elphinstone Metal Rolling Mills v. CCE 2004 (167) ELT 481 (SC)

A by-product is something of value, which is produced in making main product or it is a substance obtained in the course of a specific process, but it is not the primary product. If it is not marketable (although sold in market in few occasions), the same will not be dutiable - Gujarat State Fertilizers Co. Ltd. v. CCE 1997 (90) ELT 149 (Trib. - New Delhi). For example, by-product obtained during the course of processing of rice in the rice mill, not fit for human consumption, does not fall within the ambit of definition of ‘vegetable oil’ contained in section 3(h) of the National Oil Seeds and Vegetable Oil Development Board Act - A.P. Rice Bran Solvent Extractors Association v. Union of India 1998 (103) ELT 481 (SC).

And waste and scrap arising out of manufacture of exempted goods are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise vide Notification No. 89/95-CE, dated May 18, 1995, provided that in such factory, any other excisable goods (other than exempted goods) shall not be manufactured - see also E.P. Electropressings (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2002 (140) ELT 230 (Trib. - Delhi).

CENVAT CREDIT - FAQs (PART 3)

In this article, the author has discussed some very common questions in respect of capital goods used by manufacturer of excisable goods or provider of taxable services.

Is Cenvat credit available on capital goods if acquired on lease, hire-purchase or loan ?

1. YES, it is allowed under rule 4(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

What if capital goods are removed from factory/service premises ‘as such’ or ‘if removed as scrap’ or ‘before put to use’ or ‘after being used’?

2. Rule 3(5) and 3(5A)/(5B) defines four types of situations and provides guidelines what is to be done. All these situations are detailed below.

Here there is no question of bona fide or mala fide intention due to which no penalty provision would be attracted.

(a) Capital goods removed ‘as such’ - ‘As such’ means, in the same position in which purchase is done. Whatever Cenvat Credit is taken/availed, it has to be paid to the account of the Central Government. No such type of payment is required to be made if the capital goods is/are removed for providing output service.

(b) Capital goods removed ‘as scrap’ - If capital goods are removed ‘as scrap’, then manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the duty leviable on transaction value.

(c) Capital goods removed ‘before put to use’ - Here manufacturer is required to pay full amount of duty which has been taken as Cenvat credit. This situation is different from the situation given in (a) above, as here it might be possible that the capital goods which are purchased may not be in ‘intact’ position, say, for example machines are purchased and installed and are made ready to use, but ultimately it is decided that these should not be used but to be removed.

(d) Capital goods removed ‘after put to use’ - What amount of Cenvat credit has been taken in the books of account is required to be depreciated by 2.5 per cent (i.e., reduced) per quarter and the balance amount is required to be paid to the account of the Central Government.

What if capital goods are sent for jobwork outside factory or office premises and not received back in 180 days ?

3. Rule 4(5a ) clarifies this situation. Once capital goods which are purchased are removed from the factory or the premises of the service provider for providing output taxable services, then such capital goods must be received back in the factory or the premises of service provider within the period of 180 days. If such capital goods are not received within the abovesaid period, then manufacturer or service provider (as the case may be) shall pay an amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the inputs or capital goods by debiting the Cenvat credit account or otherwise. Here the option of payment by debiting cenvat account is given.

What is 8 per cent/10 per cent option which is newly introduced under rule 6 ?

4. This is new provision which has been introduced under rule 6. It is made clear that Cenvat credit is not allowed for the input/capital goods/input services which are used in the process of manufacture of non-excisable goods or for providing non-taxable services.

However, this new provision allows the manufacturer or service provider to take 100 per cent Cenvat credit, by paying 10 per cent of the value of exempted goods (for manufacturer) or 8 per cent of the value of exempted services (for service provider).

Is Cenvat credit on mobile phone available ?

5. Yes, this is a very debatable issue, but the same has been resolved by Circular No. 59/8/2003-ST, dated June 20, 2003 in the context of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002.

As per the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002, Cenvat credit for service tax paid on telephone bills which are installed in office premises was available.

However, under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the same condition was totally removed. This rule came in force with effect from September 10, 2004.

: Where assessee-State owned liquor giant had exclusive monopoly for retail and wholesale of Indian Made Foreign Spirits (IMFS) in entire State of Tamil Nadu and it floated tenders to select third-party bar contractors (licensees) to sell eatables and collect empty bottles left by consumers at bars situated adjacent to/within assessee's retail shop of liquor, since empty bottles were neither 'scrap' nor a property of either assessee or bar licensee, liability under section 206C was not attracted Section 206C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection of tax at source (Sale of scrap) - Assessment years 2016-17 and 2023-24 - Assessee-Company owned by Tamil Nadu Government had exclusive monopoly for retail and wholesale of Indian Made Foreign Spirits (IMFS) in entire state of Tamil Nadu - Assessee floated tenders to select third-party bar contractors (licensees) to sell eatables and collect empty bottles left by consumers at bars situated adjacent to/within assessee's retail shop of liquor - Assessee acting as an agent merely collected tender/licence amount from successful tenderer and remitted 99 per cent of same to Government retaining 1 per cent commission - Revenue treated assessee as assessee-in-default for failure to collect tax at source under section 206C on amount tendered by successful bar licensee from sale of empty bottles by treating sale of bottles as scrap - However, it was observed that only such 'scrap' generated from either 'manufacturing activity' or from 'mechanical working of material' could be construed to be in contemplation of section 206C - Mere opening, breaking or uncorking of a liquor bottle by mere twisting seal in a liquor bottle will not amount to generation of 'scrap' from 'mechanical working of material' for purpose of section 206C - Further, to be a seller of used bottle, assessee should be owner of bottle, however, neither assessee nor licensee were owners of waste bottles - Empty bottles were neither generated in manufacturing, nor in mechanical working of material - Whether therefore, invocation of sections 206C, 206CC and 206CCA was wholly misplaced and unwarranted under circumstances against assessee for alleged failure to collect tax at 1 per cent on 99 per cent of license fee payable to Government and 1 per cent retained as agency commission - Held, yes - Whether thus, question of paying simple interest under section 206C(7) could not be countenanced with - Held, yes [Paras 97, 101, 102, 105, 107, 108 and 109] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications: Circular No. 7/2016, dated 7-3-2016 and Circular No. 525 dated 24-11-1998

FACT: The assessee-Company owned by the Tamil Nadu Govt. had the exclusive monopoly for retail and wholesale of Indian Made Foreign Spirits (IMFS) in the entire state of Tamil Nadu. Assessee floated tenders to select third-party bar contractors (licensees) to sell eatables and collect empty bottles left by the consumers at the bars situated adjacent to/within the assessee's retail shop of liquor. Assessee acting as an agent merely collected the tender/licence amount from the successful tenderer and remitted 99 per cent of the same to the Government retaining 1 per cent commission.

Revenue treated the assessee as assessee-in-default for failure to collect tax at source under section 206C(1) on the amount tendered by the successful bar licensee from sale of empty bottles by treating the sale of bottles as scrap and thus demanded tax for the aforesaid period in dispute together with interest under section 206C(7).

Assessee argued that empty bottles left over by the consumers in the bar did not qualify as scrap under Explanation to section 206C as the assessee was not engaged in manufacture or generation of waste from mechanical working of materials from which scrap had arisen, it was merely selling liquor in its retail shops. The empty liquor bottles left by the consumers were in the bar and not the property of the assessee and in any event not sold by it. Assessee also submitted that the bar contractors collected and sold empty bottles in their own right and not on behalf of the assessee and the consideration was also retained by the contractors.

HELD: As per sub-clause (1) of section 206C, every seller shall collect from the buyer of any goods specified, a sum equal to the amounts specified. In this case, the petitioner has awarded contracts to various bar owners to run the bar adjacent to the retail shows run by the petitioner. [Para 73]

80. (1) Tetraethyl lead compound shall not be unloaded from a ship unless—

(a)

it is packed in specially constructed steel drums of substantial construction, sealed with an inner and outer bung, and fitted with rolling roofs on to the shell as an added precaution;

(b)

all receptacles containing tetraethyl lead compound are distinctively and durably marked with the words "Tetraethyl Lead Compound Poison"; and

(c)

two sets of protective equipment comprising the following are provided and kept readily available for use in the event of any leakage of tetraethyl lead compound—

(i)

rubber gloves,

(ii)

rubber boots,

(iii)

rubber apron or oilskin suit, and

(iv)

suitable respirator, which should be either of canister type containing minimum of 50cc. of activated charcoal or an airline respirator with an independent fresh air supply.

(2) Following measures shall be taken while unloading tetraethyl lead compound:—

(a)

no receptacle containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be opened within the limits of the port;

(b)

before commencement of the unloading operations, the consignment of tetraethyl lead compound shall be inspected on board the vessel by a responsible person. No tetraethyl lead compound drums showing any sign of leakage shall be unloaded until suitably repaired or placed in a larger receptacle or container offering sufficient precautions from leakage;

(c)

drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be discharged under the supervision of a responsible person;

(d)

drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be loaded discharged in rope slings with a maximum of two drums at a separate sling for each drum. Hooks shall on no account be used;

(e)

dock workers handling drums containing tetraethyl lead compound shall be provided with heavy gloves of canvas or leather and shall use such gloves; and

(f)

adequate quantities of non-inflammable solvent or kerosene and soap and water to deal with any leakages of tetraethyl lead compound shall be kept readily available where the work of handling of the tetraethyl lead compound is carried on.

(3) Following measures shall be taken in the event of leakage of tetraethyl lead compound:—

(a)

the area on which the leakage of tetraethyl lead compound has occurred (including the outside of a drum) shall be treated as follows:—

(i)

flush with kerosene or some other light oil solvent followed by water. If the surface permits, wash thoroughly with soap working up as much lather as possible, and again flush with water;

(ii)

if it is possible to obtain quickly a supply of common bleaching lime (Ca O Cl2) the area should first be treated generously with a mixture of bleaching lime and water in the form of thin slurry (NEVER use the dry powder) alternatively a five per cent solution of sulphury! chloride (SO2 Cl2) in kerosene may be used;

(b)

if contamination of absorbent material such as wooden flooring, dunnage, or other packing material has taken place, then such material shall, after treatment as above, be removed from the place where tetraethyl lead compound is being handled;

(c)

any clothing which becomes contaminated by tetraethyl lead compound shall be removed immediately and cleaned by repeated rinsing in a non-inflammable dry cleaning fluid;

(d)

if tetraethyl lead compound can be smelled, dock workers not assigned to deal with the leakage of tetraethyl lead compound shall be removed from that place; and

(e)

dock workers assigned to deal with leakage of tetraethyl lead compound shall wear the protective equipment described under sub-regulation 1(c).

(4) Suitable protective clothing shall be provided for handling of tetraethyl lead compound in refrigerated spaces.

The Bombay High Court observed that, though the main ratio laid down in the said decision that incidental sale of goods can be brought to tax only if done with an intention of doing business in those goods is not applicable in view of amendment to the definition, still the fact that incidental sales of "unserviceable or discarded" goods intended only for reduction of the space and to save accommodation were not so integrated with (or connected with) the main business even if they were of considerable volume and frequency. Bombay High Court held that sale of three used motor cars by the assessee, who was a dealer carrying on business of manufacturing, selling and supplying of chemicals, did not amount to sale by a dealer within the meaning of section 3, read with clauses (11) and (5A) of section 2 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959 as it was not 'in connection with or incidental to or ancillary to' the business of supplying chemicals.

"Sale of used or discarded cars by the assessee in the present case would be governed by proposition No. 7 emerging from decision of Supreme Court in Raipur Manufacturing Co. [1967] 19 STC 1 which is reproduced below:

'7. Where a person in the course of carrying on a business is required to dispose of what may be called his fixed assets or his discarded goods acquired in the course of his business, an inference that he desired to carry on the business of selling his fixed assets or discarded goods would not ordinarily arise.'

Following the same, such sales cannot be held to be part of or incidentof the main business of the assessee, which in the present case comprised of manufacture and sale of chemicals. No sales tax can,therefore, be levied under the Act on such sales.

Recently, further notifications and clarifications were issued on May 20, 1994, in order to overcome these difficulties. The following are the important points to be noted from these amendments :

(i)Under the original rule, if the capital goods, on which MODVAT credit was taken were removed from the factory, the assessee was required to clear the same on payment of duty, not lesser than the amount of credit which was previously taken thereon. As per the amended notification, this requirement applies only where the capital equipment is sought to be removed from the factory without being used in the manufacture of excisable goods.

As per the amendment, if the machinery is sought to be removed from the factory after being used therein, then the payment of excise duty has to be made after allowing a deduction of 2.5 per cent of the credit taken earlier for each quarter of a year of usage from the date of taking the credit. The amended notification further provides that if the machinery has been sold for any reason as scrap, this duty shall be paid at the rate applicable to such scrap.

It would appear that the normal life of the machinery, for this purpose, is estimated at 10 years, and a distinction is drawn between used and unused machinery and also between usable and scrapped machinery.

(ii)A new sub-rule has also been added, permitting removal of capital goods for tests or repairs for reconditioning, provided the same are returned to the factory for further use as capital goods. Prior to this amendment, it was thought that even in such cases of removal of capital goods duty was required to be reimbursed.

(iii)The earlier requirement was that before the assessee takes MODVAT credit on capital goods, such goods have to be verified by the Excise Superintendent. This requirement, which was considered impractical and susceptible to misuse, has now been removed by another amended notification.

(iv)Yet another welcome amendment is that the assessee can now take credit on capital goods on the basis of an invoice or bill of entry or other duty-paying document as against the cumbersome procedure prescribed earlier.

These amendments are in the right direction, as a result of which, most of the practical difficulties are considered to have been removed.

2.4 Case of goods obtained on lease or hire purchase - According to the existing provisions, MODVAT credit on capital goods is not permissible in respect of the equipment acquired on lease or hire purchase. Several representations were made in this regard by the industry. It was reported that the Government has decided to amend the relevant rules so as to extend MODVAT credit to capital goods acquired through leasing and hire purchase also. But the relevant notification has not yet been issued and it is hoped that it would be done soon.

2.5 MODVAT credit vs. Depreciation - It is specifically provided that no credit of the duty paid on capital goods shall be allowed, if the assessee claims depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 on that part of the value of capital goods which represents the amount of specified duty paid on such goods. In other words, a manufacturer has the option to claim MODVAT credit on the duty paid or forego the same if he opts to claim income-tax depreciation on the duty portion of the capital goods. If the manufacturer has opted for taking MODVAT credit, income-tax depreciation on such capital goods can be claimed only on the net cost as reduced by the duty paid thereon.

Accounting treatment - General observation

3. The accounting treatment of MODVAT credit on capital goods should be such that it would not vitiate the objective with which the credit is granted, but should aid in promoting the desired objective of industrial growth. If need be, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) should bring out suitable amendments to the existing Accounting Stan dards or Guidance Notes or bring out a specific Guidance Note in this regard.

Accounting problems likely to arise

4. Accounting of MODVAT credit on capital goods is likely to pose many problems.

The basic question is whether the MODVAT credit is to be reduced from the cost of related asset.

If MODVAT credit is reduced from the cost of the asset and if such reduced cost is reflected in the accounts, it is likely to result in the following problems for the manufacturer :

(i)The quantum of term finance by lending institutions would be far less, if it is based on the net cost of the assets. In the case of an existing manufacturer, if MODVAT credit is not substantial and is utilised in the year of purchase itself, there might not be much of a problem in such a case.

However, now, Central Excise Tariff has specific headings for dross and slag with effect from February 28, 2005. These are sold and have market value. Should it be held as ‘goods’ with effect from February 28, 2005? It is true that in Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 268 (SC) = AIR 1995 SC 1580 = 1995 Supp (2) SCC 465 = 1995 AIR SCW 2436 = 1995 (58) ECR 612 (SC 3-member Bench judgment), it was held that ‘dross and skimmings’ arising during manufacture of Aluminium is not ‘excisable goods’. They are merely refuse or ashes given out in process of removing impurities from raw material. Hence they are not ‘excisable goods’ as understood in commercial parlance, even if they are sold and they fetch some price. This was followed in CCE v. Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. 2004 AIR SCW 1948 = 165 ELT 386 = 61 RLT 239 (SC 3-member Bench), where it was held that zinc dross and skimmings are merely refuse, scum or rubbish. It is not result of treatment, labour or manipulation, even if it fetches some price in market. Everything which is sold is not necessarily a marketable commodity known to commerce and worthwhile to trade in.

In CC v. Universal Cables 149 ELT 968 (CEGAT 3- member Bench), it was held that dross and skimming of Aluminium obtained in manufacture of Aluminium rods is not excisable. - Departmental appeal dismissed by the Supreme Court on July 9, 1996 - 151 ELT A 175.

However, now CETA has following specific entries with effect from February 28, 2005 - ‘Brass Dross’ (2620 30 10), ‘Aluminium Dross’ (2620 40 10) and slag/dross from manufacture of iron or steel (2619).

In Balaji Enterprises v. CCE 1997 AIR SCW 2026 = 92 ELT 3 (SC) = AIR 1997 SC 2170, it has been observed and noted that whenever things like waste and scrap have been sought to be taxed in the Central Excise Act, specific entries have been made for this purpose. Supreme Court has noted various specific examples from the old tariff in this regard.

Waste is not obtained by any process of manufacturing but in the course of manufacturing and processing to produce the end product. The intention of legislature to cover waste or scrap in relation to manufacture is required to be specifically mentioned in tariff item before liability to pay duty on waste or scrap arises - Plastics Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1991 (51) ELT 271 (Bom HC). In Shree Synthetic Ltd. v. CCE - 1991 (52) ELT 238 (CEGAT), it was held - "Waste is normally not considered as ‘goods’ except where it is deemed to be ‘goods’ by way of legal fiction and specific mention in any provision, rule or the tariff."

‘Waste or scrap’ will be ‘goods’ and hence taxable only if specifically mentioned in CETA (Tariff) - Kamath Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1992 (60) ELT 666 (CEGAT).

Hence, in my view, these may get covered as dutiable with effect from February 28, 2005.

(h) Capital goods at job worker’s premises - Capital goods used at job worker’s premises, for work on inputs are not eligible for Cenvat credit - Majestic Auto Ltd. v. CCE 1999 (107) ELT 133 (Tribunal).

(i) Outside factory premises - Capital goods used outside the factory premises, are not eligible for CENVAT Credit.

(j) Capital goods used in manufacture of exempt intermediate product - Capital goods may be used in the manufacture of an exempt intermediate product but the final product may be dutiable. In such case, CENVAT Credit is available on such capital goods, if final product is chargeable to duty - CBEC Circular No. 665/56/2002-CX, dated 25-9-2002.

(k) Project imports - These are also eligible for CENVAT Credit. If some capital goods are eligible while some may not be eligible, the breakup value of capital goods eligible for CENVAT can be certified by a Cost Accountant in the prescribed form - MF (DR) Circular No. 351/67/97-CX., dated 5-11-1997.

(l) Capital goods used both for dutiable and non-dutiable finished goods - The definition merely says that the capital goods must be used in the factory of the manufacturer and does not in specific terms, say that the use must be exclusively of the excisable finished goods.

(m) Exclusion of equipment/appliances used in an office - Rule 2 specifically excludes use of capital goods like equipment or appliances in an office.

(n) Other capital goods - Capital goods other than those mentioned above, are not eligible for CENVAT Credit.

(o) Capital goods removed as scrap after use - In such circumstances, it cannot be said that these are removal ‘as such’. Hence, no excise duty is payable. Wear/Tear cannot be said to be manufactured, and is not liable for duty - CCE v. Birla Corpn. Ltd. 2005 (181) ELT 263 (Tri. - Delhi).

(p) Sale of factory - If factory is sold, it is not removal of capital goods ‘as such’. Hence, no duty is payable on capital goods - Jamna Auto Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2001 (130) ELT 181 (Tri. - Delhi).

(q) Capital goods removed after use for some years - As per the Board’s Circular No. 643/34/2002, CX, dated 1-7-2002 the value on which the supplier of capital goods has paid duty would be a reasonable basis for paying duty with depreciation as per Letter F. No. 495/16/93, CUS VI, dated 26-5-1993.

(r) Use of capital goods by service provider - In case of output service provider, the capital goods should be used for providing output services. The use may be anywhere and even part use is sufficient.

(s) Installation is not required for taking CENVAT Credit - Installation or use is not a precondition for taking CENVAT Credit. On mere receipt in the factory, CENVAT Credit can be availed on capital goods.

(t) Eligibility to be decided on the basis of date of receipt - Eligibility of CENVAT Credit on capital goods is required to be decided on the basis of eligibility on the date when goods were received in the factory. Subsequent eligibility will not help - CCE v. Surya Roshini Ltd. 2003 (155) ELT 581 (Tri. - Delhi).

(u) Capital goods used by service provider - Service provider can also send out capital goods for providing output service, but they should be brought back within 180 days.

Difference between CENVAT Credit on capital goods and Input

4. The difference between Cenvat Credit on capital goods & inputs is explained hereunder :

(a)In the case of inputs, CENVAT Credit is available as soon as input is received in the factory, whereas for capital goods up to 50 per cent Credit is available in current year and balance in subsequent year.

(b)CENVAT Credit utilised on inputs has to be reversed on stock of inputs, when the assessee opts out of CENVAT. This rule is not applicable for capital goods.

(c)The eligible inputs and capital goods have been given in CENVAT Rules.

(d)Inputs are to be used in or in relation to manufacture while in respect of capital goods the only requirement is that it should be used in the factory.

9. Procedure for Cutting permission.—

(1)

The competent authority may grant permission for cutting operations within a maximum period of two working days upon satisfactory verification of following items, namely: —

(a)

A certificate from the State Pollution Control Board that all kinds of oils, cargo residues and other loose hazardous wastes are completely removed and respective holds and tanks are decontaminated.

(b)

"Safe for entry and safe for hot work" certificate has to be issued by the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organization/PESO for cargo and slop tanks of petroleum tankers, or by any competent agency authorized by the Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH under the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948);

(c)

Inspection shall be carried out by the Safety officer of Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH or authorized person of Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health/DISH to ensure -

(i)

ignitable materials are completely removed from confined spaces that need to be certified for hot work;

(ii)

areas in engine room are practically gas free with proper venting and well within explosive limits by use of calibrated multi-gas monitoring meter. On satisfactory compliance of this inspection, Safe for entry and safe for hot work permission shall be issued for engine room;

(iii)

bunker area and those common areas of ships where there is likelihood of ignitable gases generations need to be properly ventilated and ensure that spaces are well within explosive limits by use of calibrated portable gas meters.

(2)

In case any short coming is noted then the same shall be communicated in writing within two working days to enable the recycler to re-submit the request upon necessary corrections.

10. Monitoring of worker safety and hazardous material during dismantling activity.—

(1)

Worker safety:

(a)

A Safety officer/Safety Officer as per the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948) shall be engaged by ship recycling facility.

(b)

A competent person shall be engaged for issuance and continuous monitoring of conditions based on which safe for entry and safe for hot work permits issued as per the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948).

(c)

All the equipment such as crane, winch, chain rope and shackles, generator set and any other safety equipment installed in the ship recycling facility or hired for the purpose of recycling shall be installed and maintained in accordance with the provisions of the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948) and rules made thereunder and any other relevant Acts and rules.

(d)

A safety officer/Safety Supervisor is responsible for conducting meetings prior to starting any activity, briefing the risks involved in the activity and control measures taken to minimize such risks.

(e)

A placard displaying important precautions (do's and don'ts) to be followed during ship recycling activity is installed at prominent places within the premises and that such display is made in English and other language(s) as understood by the workers involved in recycling.

(f)

A calibrated explosive gas detector, a multi gas monitor including hydrogen sulphide (H2S) gas monitor, portable gas meters and an oxygen percentage analyzer are available on the site in working condition.

(g)

Adequate lighting arrangement is made in the common areas of yard and in the spaces where activity is carried out. The SRF should conspicuously mark and maintain an emergency exit route and such route should always be free from any obstructions.

(h)

The emergency response plan drill should be conducted once in 6 months. Further, an off-site emergency plan for the whole district should be prepared and to be conducted once in a year.

(2)

Handling, storage and disposal of hazardous material:

(a)

One Safety Officer/One Safety supervisor as per section 41C(b) of the Factories Act 1948 (63 of 1948) shall be engaged by ship recycling facility.

(b)

Supervisor shall ensure that hazardous materials are handled, stored, transported and disposed as per the approved ship recycling plan and in accordance with local legislations.

It is clarified that with this amendment in section 2(d), the bagasse, aluminium/zinc dross and other such products termed as waste, residue or refuse which arise during the course of manufacture and are capable of being sold for consideration would be excisable goods and chargeable to payment of excise duty. It is further clarified that in case the rate of duty in respect of such products is Nil in the tariff or they are exempt from duty in terms of any exemption notification, and if Cenvat Credit has been taken on the inputs which are used for manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods, then in terms of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the assessee is required to reverse the proportionate credit or pay percentage-based amount.

3.2 Bagasse held non-manufactured by Supreme Court : The Circular aforesaid was challenged successfully in Balrampur Chini Mills Ltd. v. UOI [2013] 30 taxmann.com 175 (Allahabad) and CCE v. DSCL Sugar [2014] 41 taxmann.com 64/43 GST 151 (Allahabad) and also in CCE v. KCP Sugar & Industries Corporation Ltd. - 2015 (321) ELT A223 (A.P.) on ground that even though marketable, Bagasse was non-manufactured product and therefore, not excisable and even payment under rule 6 would not be required. The Department went in appeal before Supreme Court in UOI v. DSCL Sugar Ltd. 2015 (322) E.L.T. 769, wherein it was held as follows :

Facts : Assessee was manufacturing sugarcane and molasses. In the process of manufacture of sugar, sugarcane is crushed, its juice is extracted and Bagasse emerges as residue/waste of sugarcane. Since Bagasse was liable to Nil rate of duty, department argued that it was 'exempted goods' and demanded Cenvat reversal under rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Held :

No manufacture/deemed manufacture : Bagasse is only an agriculture waste and residue and not result of any process; hence, it is not covered in definition of 'manufacture' under section 2(f) of Central Excise Act, 1944. Further, there is no Chapter note or Section note in Central Excise Tariff declaring process in respect of bagasse as amounting to manufacture.

Not excisable, even if deemed to be marketable : Hence, notwithstanding amendment in 2008 in section 2(d) ibid, creating a fiction of deemed marketability, bagasse is not excisable as it is not passing test of 'manufacture'.

Cenvat Rule 6 inapplicable [for period prior to 1-3-2015] : Since bagasse is not excisable, hence, even if NIL-rated, cenvat rule 6 is inapplicable thereto. Therefore, denial of credit on electricity on ground that bagasse is excisable exempted goods, was incorrect.

3.3 Zinc Dross also held to be non-manufactured by Bombay High Court : The Bombay High Court in Hindalco Industries Ltd. v. UOI [2015] 49 GST 429 opined that Aluminium dross and skimmings, etc. not 'manufactured' goods and not liable to duty, even if marketable/bought and sold. The facts and judgment are :

Facts : In course of manufacture of aluminium sheets/coils, aluminium dross/skimmings emerged as byproducts. Department demanded duty thereon arguing that in view of Explanation to section 2(d), said goods were marketable. Assessee argued that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' were not 'manufactured goods' and were not, therefore, liable to duty.

Held : Conditions contemplated under section 2(d) (excisable goods, movability and marketability) and section 2(f) (manufacture) have to be satisfied conjunctively in order to entail imposition of excise duty. Merely because goods satisfy test of being marketed and saleable and merely because goods are listed in tariff, it does not mean that they are 'manufactured goods'. In various judgments, Supreme Court held that 'aluminium dross/skimmings' are not manufactured goods and said view was followed in context of 'zinc dross and flux skimming'. Hence, impugned goods were not manufactured goods and could not, therefore, be charged to excise duty.

1. We present our query in following words :

Facts : An automobile ancillary manufacturing unit wants to dispose hazardous waste material generated from manufacturing process after the concerned input material is put to use and used for manufacturing process as per GPCB [Gujarat Pollution Control Board] Guidelines to GPCB approved entity.

Description and Category of Material :

[a]

Caustic Soda (liquid) - Die Cleaning material - Process material - to be removed after being used (not as such)

[b]

IPA - Cleaning Material - Process Material - to be removed after being used (not as such )

[c]

Coating Sludge (mix of Nokoluk flux, DHM, WS1, Diluent M) -Mix of Coating Materials - Mix of Raw Material - to be removed after being put to use and used in manufacturing (not as such) - All material of coating sludge are our Raw Material - CENVAT Credit is regularly taken of this material when there is inward of it

[d]

Hydraulic oil – Lubricant in one of our manufacturing process – Process material - CENVAT taken on inward of this material - to be removed after being put to use and used for manufacturing ( not as such)

We are going to send these materials for disposal to GPCB approved agency. We will pay them fees for this technical service for sample testing as well as disposal process. No consideration would be receivable or have been received from the consignee i.e., GPCB approved agency situated in Gujarat, India in whatsoever manner against this removal/disposal. In nutshell from sample test to disposal, it is our statutory liability and at our expense, we do it.

Question of Excise Law

[a]

Whether we need to remove this material (all or few or any one) under Excise Invoice ?

[b]

How to value these material supposing it attracts excise, given the fact that we don't have any consideration receivable against this removal.

[c]

What is the general convention/standard operating procedure in manufacturing sector in regard with removing this material under excise invoice and valuation for excise purpose where there is no consideration or similar transaction/removal for comparison ?

Sincere thanks for the read and we request you to respond to the same.

We take this liberty to summarize your query in few words :

Whether disposal of waste arising out of inputs as per pollution control laws has any central excise implication, when such disposal does not result in any consideration and in fact, results in expenditure.

Having summarized your query, let us come direct to position of law :

Removal of inputs as such attracts reversal of Cenvat credit under rule 3(5) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. However, in this case, the inputs have been used and only hazardous waste is being removed. Such removal would, therefore, not attract rule 3(5) and therefore, no statutory invoice is required.

As per section 3 of the Central Excise Act, 1944, excise duty is charged on production or manufacture of excisable goods. It appears that waste is waste of raw material and has not undergone manufacture. Even assuming manufacture, it is not 'goods' as it is not marketable. Definition of marketability under Explanation to section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, provides that goods are deemed to be marketable, if they are capable of being bought and sold for a consideration. The disposal of hazardous waste is mandatory under pollution control laws and can be made only to specified agencies and further leads to expenditure at your end. Hence, same cannot be treated as marketable, as no one would buy it. Therefore, there is no charge of excise duty thereon and consequent, statutory procedures under Excise law cannot be applied.

In view of the above, there are no excise or cenvat implications in the matter.

In evidence of the aforesaid, you are required to generate a normal removal challan for removal of waste citing applicable laws. You should preserve relevant documents in support of the aforesaid claims.

The assessee is a manufacturer of aluminium sheets and coils falling under CETH 7607 1190 of the Central Excise Tariff using major raw material 'aluminium ingots'.

Dross skimmings are not manufactured goods.

Revenue's Arguments

Explanation to section 2(d) creates a legal fiction by which any goods which are capable of being bought and sold for a consideration shall be deemed to be marketable and on this basis it was held that aluminium dross and skimmings are liable to duty of excise.

When a product emerges as a by-product in the course of manufacture of some other product, that by-product cannot be treated as a waste just because it is an unintended product arising in the course of manufacture of an intended final product. In the facts of the case before us, aluminium dross and skimmings emerges as by-product during the course of manufacture of aluminium sheets/coils from aluminium ingots. These dross and skimmings have a substantial commercial value and cannot be treated as 'waste'.

HEADNOTE: Section 2, read with First Schedule, of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 and section 2 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 - Classification - Aluminium dross and skimmings - Tariff Item 2620 4010 specially deals with aluminium dross and Tariff Item 2620 4090 deals with other slag, ash or residues containing mainly aluminium - Hence, aluminium dross, skimmings are clearly specified in Central Excise Tariff - Customs Tariff also includes aluminium dross and skimmings under Tariff sub-heading 2620 40 [Paras 6.1 to 6.3] [In favour of revenue]Central Excise : Aluminium dross and skimmings and similar non-ferrous metal dross and skimmings which arise as a by-product in process of manufacture of aluminium/non-ferrous metal products are manufactured goods and hence excisable with effect from 10-5-2008 in view of explanation added to section 2(d)

Section 2(d), read with section 3, of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 2 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 and section 2 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 - Excisable Goods - Marketability - Customs Tariff is based on Harmonized System of Nomenclature and an entry (heading/sub-heading) is created specifically for a product only when commodity is bought and sold on a regular basis on a substantial scale - This would imply that 'aluminium dross and skimmings' listed in tariff are marketable commodities [Para 6.3] [In favour of revenue]

Section 2(f), read with sections 2(d) and 3, of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Manufacture - General Meaning - Tariff recognises waste and scrap as a distinct and different commodity and seeks to impose a tax on waste and scrap either when it is traded (Customs duty) or when it is manufactured, by way of excise duty - Purpose and object of creating a tariff entry for waste and scrap including 'dross and skimmings' is to make the product liable to tax/duty - Therefore, a specific entry created for purpose of levy of duty/tax cannot be merely wished away or brushed aside, by holding that waste and scrap are not manufactured goods - When dross and skimmings are specifically mentioned in tariff, it would not be unreasonable to assume that such products are manufacture goods even though they arise in course of manufacture of other products - Since they are capable of being bought and sold for a consideration, they are marketable and liable to excise duty - Hence, aluminium dross and skimmings and similar non-ferrous metal dross and skimmings which arise as a by-product in process of manufacture of aluminium/non-ferrous metal products are manufactured goods and hence excisable with effect from 10-05-2008 in view of explanation added to section 2(d) [Paras 6.4 to 8] [In favour of revenue]

When a product emerges as a by-product in the course of manufacture of some other product, that by-product cannot be treated as a waste just because it is an unintended product arising in the course of manufacture of an intended final product. The by-product would be waste only if it is of no value or negligible value, something which the manufacturer would want to get rid of. In the facts of the case before us, aluminium dross and skimmings emerges as by-product during the course of manufacture of aluminium sheets/coils from aluminium ingots. These dross and skimmings have a substantial commercial value and cannot be treated as 'waste'.

Issue Involved

Whether Aluminium Dross and Skimmings or similar Non-ferrous Metal Dross and Skimmings, which arise in the process of manufacture of aluminium/Non ferrous metal products can be considered as a 'manufactured goods' and hence excisable for the period post 10-5-2008 in view of the Explanation added to section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 ?

HELD: I. Aluminium dross, skimmings are listed in Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 :

In the Central Excise Tariff, Chapter 26 deals with Ores, Slag and Ash. Sub-heading 2620 40 deals with slag, ash or residues containing mainly aluminium. CETH 2620 4010 specially deals with aluminium dross and CETH 2620 4090 deals with other slag, ash or residues containing mainly aluminium. Thus, the aluminium dross, skimmings are clearly specified in the Central Excise Tariff and there is no dispute in this regard. [Paras 6.1 and 6.2]

II. Aluminium dross, skimmings are 'marketable' :

Explanation added to section 2(d) vide Finance Act, 2008 provides that, for the purpose of the said clause 'goods' includes any article, material or substance which is capable of being bought and sold for a consideration and such goods shall be deemed to be marketable'. It is not in dispute that aluminium dross and skimmings are capable of being bought and sold for a consideration and are, in fact, regularly bought and sold. The Customs Tariff also includes aluminium dross and skimmings under CTH 2620 40. Customs Tariff is based on the Harmonized System of Nomenclature and an entry (heading/sub-heading) is created specifically for a product only when the commodity is bought and sold on a regular basis on a substantial scale. This would imply that aluminium dross and skimmings are marketable commodities. Therefore, the only question left for consideration is whether they are 'manufactured' goods. [Para 6.3]

III. Aluminium dross, skimmings are presumed to be 'manufactured', as listed in Tariff :

Nobody deliberately manufactures waste and scrap. Waste and scrap emerge as a by-product in the course of manufacture of other products. In fact both the Central Excise and Customs Tariff provide for separate headings/sub-headings in respect of waste and scrap of various materials such as plastics, rubber, paper, textile, iron and steel, non-ferrous metals, glass and glassware, precious metals and so on.

Therefore, the tariff recognises waste and scrap as a distinct and different commodity and seeks to impose a tax on waste and scrap either when it is traded (Customs duty) or when it is manufactured, by way of excise duty. In other words, the purpose and object of creating a tariff entry for waste and scrap including 'dross and skimmings' is to make the product liable to tax/duty.

It is also equally well understood that nobody undertakes, either deliberately or purposefully, manufacture of waste and scrap, whether it be of aluminium or other metals or of plastics, rubber, textiles, glass, etc. Waste arises in the manufacturing process of various products. It is to tax such waste and scrap which arise in the course of manufacture of other products, separate entries are created in the tariff, including those for aluminium dross and skimmings. Thus, the intent of the legislature is very clear. Therefore, a specific entry created for the purpose of levy of duty/tax cannot be merely wished away or brushed aside, by holding that waste and scrap are not manufactured goods.

It is a settled principle in taxation that no part of the law should be interpreted in such a way so as to make it non-effective or odious. Viewed from this perspective, when dross and skimmings are specifically mentioned in the tariff, it would not be unreasonable to assume that such products are manufacture goods even though they arise in the course of manufacture of other products.

6.3-1 In Jawahar Mills Ltd. v. CCE 1999 (108) ELT 47 (Tri. - Delhi) it was held that for being covered by the definition of 'capital goods' an item need not have direct nexus with final products being produced.

6.3-2 In Thermax Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (281) ELT 305 (Tri. Mum.) the Tribunal held that there was no doubt that the appellant had taken CENVAT credit in the years in which the capital goods, were falling under heading 6804 of the First Schedule of the Excise Tariff Act. Therefore, the appellant was entitled to 100% of the CENVAT credit as per the provisions of Rule 4(2)(b) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

6.4 Credit for supporting structures

6.4-1 In Shakumbari Sugar & Allied India Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (283) ELT 216 (Tri. - Delhi) it was held that the supporting structure for machinery being covered by the term 'plant' would be covered by the definition of capital goods and, hence, the MS angles, channels, sections, etc, being components of such supporting structures would also be covered by the definition of 'capital goods'. The impugned order denying the credit in respect of MS Angle, Channels, Sections, CTD bars, etc., used for supporting structures was not sustainable.

6.5 Reversal of CENVAT credit

6.5-1 In Shree Rajasthan Syntec Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (280) ELT 470 (Tri. - Delhi) the duty was confirmed against the applicant on the ground that at the time of reversal of old and used capital goods, the appellant was required to reverse CENVAT credit availed by it at the time of receipt of the said capital goods. It was held that full credit was not to be reversed as removal of old used capital goods was not treatable as removal of capital goods 'as such'.

6.6 Interpretation of the words 'as such'

6.6-1 In CCE v. Khalsa Cotspin (P.) Ltd. 2012 (280) ELT 438/[2010] 1 taxmann.com 509 (New Delhi - CESTAT) the Tribunal found that undisputedly the capital goods had been installed in the premises of the respondents and were put to use. The goods removal after use could not be treated as cleared 'as such'. The plea of the Department was that at the time of sale, goods were capable of being used for purpose for which they were being used by assessee in factory was rejected by the Tribunal.

6.6-2 In Harsh International (Khasini) (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (281) ELT 714 (Delhi) the appellant had purchased the capital goods in period between 2003 and 2005 and used them in the factory till they were sold in June and July, 2007. Thus, the capital goods were used for a period of 2 to 4 years. They could not, therefore, be stated to be sold as capital goods, but were sold as used capital goods. The Court held that the appellant was not liable to pay excise duty in accordance with Rule 3(5) when it removed the used capital goods.

6.7 Transfer of capital goods to the depots

6.7-1 In Suyra Color Products (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (280) ELT 455 (Tri. - Bang.) the issue involved was whether the appellant was eligible to avail of CENVAT credit on the capital goods, which were purchased by him and the CENVAT credit availed on transfer to their depots situated in various States. The lower authorities proceeded on the ground that the appellant had not used these machines in the factory of manufacturer of final products. The Tribunal held that the provision of Rule 4(5)(a) allowed an assessee to avail of the credit on capital goods even if they were sent to job worker for any other purpose. If the provisions of Rule 4(5)(a) were examined, then relief to the appellant under the provisions of Rule 4(5)(a) could not be denied.

United Phosphorus Ltd. 2000 (117) ELT 529 (SC) unless proved otherwise. The Supreme Court in the case of Indian Cable Co. Ltd. (supra) has expressed that marketability is a decisive test for durability. It only means ‘saleable’ or ‘suitable for sale’. It need not be, in fact, marketed. The article should be capable of being sold or being sold to consumers in the market, as it is without anything more. In the absence of a finding, that the goods are ‘marketable’, i.e., saleable or suitable for sale, it could not be said to be a good, which may be subject to excisability.

The Apex Court in the case of Union of India v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. 1995 (58) ECR 612 has reiterated that marketability is a question of fact to be decided on the facts of each case. It was held that it may be possible to recover something from a particular thing, they can, therefore, be sold but that does not make them a marketable commodity. In other words, everything, which is sold, is not necessarily a marketable commodity as known to the commercial world and, it may be worthwhile to trade in. Since marketability test is essentially a question of fact - Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (181) ELT 170 (SC), there must be some serious attempts to go to market and collect proper evidences, but it cannot be established on basis of mere stability. Sufficient proof that product is commercially known is required - Gujarat Nermada Valley Fert. Co. Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (184) ELT 128 (SC) which could not be viewed through a hawker’s eye - Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (190) ELT 301 (Trib. - LB) unless the product is capable of being marketed and is known to those who are in the market, as having an identity as a distinct identifiable commodity, that the article is subject to excise duty. Fact that articles fall within Schedule, not make them marketable. Actual sale is not necessary but article must be capable of being sold in market or known in market as good - Gujarat Nermada Valley Fert. Co. Ltd.’s case (supra ). Actual purchase and sale, or fact of their being marketed or their general availability in market is not required to be proved- Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd.’s case (supra).

Article is not eligible to be taxed only because it is having saleable value. CCE v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. 2006 (203) ELT 3 (SC). Mention of an item in an exemption notification is not determinative of its excisability. New Shorrock Mills v. CCE 2006 (202) ELT 192 (Trib. - LB); Indore Wire Co. Ltd. v. Union of India 2006 (203) ELT 179 (SC). Mere listing of an item in the Schedule to the Act is not sufficient to make it excisable - Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd.’s case (supra). Mere mention of item in ISI is also not sufficient - Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India 2004 (164) ELT 372 (SC).

Once marketability of an article is established, the fact that it is not actually sold but is entirely consumed captively or that it is sold only to one or two buyers has no relevance. However, mere manufacturing activity by itself, does not prove marketability. Inter-unit transfer of an item does not prove its marketability. Product produced must be a distinct commodity known in common parlance to commercial community for the purpose of buying and selling - Cipla Ltd. v. CCE 2008 (225) ELT 403 (SC).

Accordingly, articles like storage units, running counters, wall and kitchen units normally not capable to be removed without cannibalizing, are not furniture and not excisable goods - Craft Interiors (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (203) ELT 529 (SC). The goods, which are removed and used for mandatory quality control test and are destroyed during such test, cannot be considered as amounting to removal and as such do not fall under category of ‘excisable goods’ - CCE v. Tarco Cable Co. Ltd. 2001 (127) ELT A49 (SC). Intellectual property or information technology being an intangible asset if once put on a paper, cassette, diskettes or any other thing to supply the same, fall under the category of ‘excisable goods’ just like drawings, designs, manuals and technical materials - Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. CCE 2001 (128) ELT 21 (SC).

CENTRAL EXCISE - JOB-WORK - DIRECT EXPORT

1. We purchased wire rods, availed Cenvat credit thereon and sent them to the job worker [who is a related party] for drawing them [procedure under rule 4(5)(a) has been followed]. The job worker is an exporter also. Instead of sending the drawn rods back to us, it was decided that the job-workers would export the same to its own customers. Can it be done ? We are ready to pay duty on cost (raw material plus job work charges plus 10% net profit margin) by issuing invoice in name of job worker. Will it be in accordance with law ? You may please advise us as regards any other formality to be observed under the law ?

One can presume that yourself (the principal manufacturer) want to sell the finished goods to the job-worker himself and the job-worker would export the same. There is absolutely no embargo thereupon i.e., you may sell the goods to job-worker. In fact, rule 4(6) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 permits direct clearance from factory of job-worker. Instead of receiving finished goods back and again selling them to job-worker, you may definitely raise a sale bill in the name of job-worker.

Since it is claimed that you are related parties, the value of 'drawn rods' (final product) would be determined as per rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000, read with rules 9 and 10 ibid.

Since the job-worker would act as merchant exporter, he may avail of facilities under rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, i.e., procurement without payment of duty or any other export incentive for which necessary procedures would have to be complied with. If the facility under rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 in relation to procurement of goods without payment of duty for export is availed, no duty would be payable on drawn rods.

It is advised that an informed decision be made, after analyzing pros and cons.

CENVAT CREDIT - TRADER NOT ELIGIBLE TO TAKE CREDIT

2. We are manufacturers of TV sets. In some cases we purchase completed TV sets from third parties and sell them to customers. We are availing of marketing services. Please clarify whether we can take service tax credit of marketing services in relation to the units not manufactured by us and sold to customers.

Purchase and sale of goods does not amount to 'manufacture'. Further, the same does not amount to an 'output service' under rule 2(p) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, as first of all, the same is not a service under section 65B(44) of the Finance Act, 1994 and secondly, the same falls in negative list under section 66D(e) of the Finance Act, 1994 [Trading of Goods].

Since trading of goods is neither manufacture nor provision of service, any service used therefor is not eligible for credit under rule 3, read with rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

In case you have taken credit, you are advised to reverse the same to avoid applicability of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.
